lessons.title: V3·A1 — Records and value equality
lessons.summary: You already know a record gives you value equality for free. This sector is about what the compiler actually generated, where that generated equality is wrong for your domain, and how to repair it without losing `with`. The array member is the trap that catches everyone.

# V3·A1 — Records and value equality

`06_structs_records` taught you the shape: `record Point(int X, int Y)`, two
instances with the same numbers compare equal, `with` makes a modified copy.
That is the tourist version. This sector opens the hood, because the moment a
record holds anything more interesting than an `int` — an array, a cached
field, a base record — the free equality either stops being free or quietly
starts being wrong, and it never tells you.

The honest one-line summary of a record is: **a class with a compiler-generated
equality implementation based on its fields, plus a copy constructor exposed
through `with`.** Every surprise in this sector follows from one of the three
nouns in that sentence — *generated*, *fields*, *copy*.

## Concept — what the compiler actually writes

Given `public record Person(string Name, int Age)`, the compiler synthesises
something very close to this:

```csharp
public class Person : IEquatable<Person>
{
    protected virtual Type EqualityContract => typeof(Person);

    public string Name { get; init; }
    public int Age { get; init; }

    public virtual bool Equals(Person? other) =>
        other is not null
        && EqualityContract == other.EqualityContract
        && EqualityComparer<string>.Default.Equals(_name, other._name)
        && EqualityComparer<int>.Default.Equals(_age, other._age);

    public override bool Equals(object? obj) => Equals(obj as Person);
    public override int GetHashCode() => /* contract + each field, combined */;

    public static bool operator ==(Person? a, Person? b) =>
        ReferenceEquals(a, b) || (a is not null && a.Equals(b));
    public static bool operator !=(Person? a, Person? b) => !(a == b);

    protected Person(Person original) { _name = original._name; _age = original._age; }
    public virtual Person Clone() => new Person(this);   // really named <Clone>$

    public void Deconstruct(out string Name, out int Age) { ... }
    protected virtual bool PrintMembers(StringBuilder b) { ... }
    public override string ToString() { /* "Person { Name = Ada, Age = 36 }" */ }
}
```

Six things in that listing are worth stopping on.

**`Equals` compares fields, not properties.** It reads backing fields directly.
A computed property (`public string Initials => Name[..1];`) is not a field, so
it plays no part in equality — correct, since it is derived. But a *lazily
cached* field does participate: add `private string? _cached;` and two
otherwise identical records compare unequal purely because one of them has been
asked for the cached value and the other has not. That is a real bug and it is
invisible at the call site, because the field you forgot about is the one you
added for performance.

**`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` does the per-field comparison**, so each field
is compared the way *that type* defines equality. For `string` and `int`, fine.
For `string[]`, `EqualityComparer<string[]>.Default` falls back to reference
equality, because arrays do not override `Equals`. Two records holding arrays
with identical contents are not equal. Nothing warns you. This is the single
most expensive thing to learn late.

**`EqualityContract` is the runtime-type check.** It is a virtual property, so
a derived record overrides it with its own `typeof`. That is what makes
`new Person("Ada", 36)` unequal to an `Employee("Ada", 36, ...)` even when you
compare through a `Person`-typed variable — and it is why the comparison stays
*symmetric*, which a naive hand-written `obj is Person` check would not be.

**`operator ==` is static and non-virtual**, but the generated one delegates to
the virtual `Equals(Person?)`, so it behaves polymorphically anyway. Records
quietly fix a classic hand-rolled-equality bug for you here; lesson 8 shows the
version you have to get right yourself.

**The clone method and the protected copy constructor are what `with` uses.**
`p with { Age = 37 }` lowers to "call the clone, then assign `Age` through its
`init` setter". It does *not* call your primary constructor. If your validation
lives in the constructor body, `with` walks straight past it.

**`PrintMembers` is the override point for `ToString`.** It is the sanctioned
way to redact a secret or add a computed value to the printed form, and its
accessibility depends on whether the record is sealed.

## Exercise 1 — `with`, deconstruction, and what stayed put

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex1.cs`. `Seat` is
`record Seat(string Row, int Number)`. Implement `NextSeat()` returning the
same row with `Number + 1`, `Label()` returning `"A12"` via deconstruction, and
`SameRowAs(Seat other)`.

The gate keeps a reference to the original seat and checks it is untouched
after `NextSeat()`, and that `seat.NextSeat().NextSeat()` reads `A14` starting
from `A12`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — three kinds of equality, one table

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex2.cs`. Three tiny types are declared for
you as stubs: `Tag` (must become a `record`), `Label` (must stay a plain
`class` with no equality members), `Cell` (must become a
`readonly record struct`). Implement `EqualitySurvey.Report()` returning
exactly

```
tag=True label=False cell=True boxedCell=True
```

where each value compares two separately constructed instances holding
identical data, and the last one compares them after both have been assigned to
`object`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the array member

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex3.cs`. `Playlist` is
`record Playlist(string Name, string[] Tracks)`, and right now two playlists
with the same name and the same track titles are **not** equal. Fix it by
writing your own `Equals(Playlist? other)` and `GetHashCode()` that compare the
tracks element by element.

You must not swap the member for a `List<T>` — that changes nothing — and you
must not write your own `operator ==`. The gate checks that `==`, `Equals` and
a `HashSet<Playlist>` all agree, so `GetHashCode` has to move with `Equals`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — validation that survives `with`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex4.cs`. `Discount` validates `Percent` in its
constructor body, and `new Discount(10) with { Percent = 900 }` sails straight
through. Move the check so `with` cannot produce an invalid value, throwing
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` whose `ParamName` is `"Percent"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — `PrintMembers` and the redacted token

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex5.cs`. `Credentials` holds a user and an API
token, and `ToString()` currently prints the token in full. Override
`PrintMembers` so the output is exactly

```
Credentials { User = ada, Token = ***, Fingerprint = 3f }
```

where `Fingerprint` is computed from the token, not stored. The record is
deliberately not `sealed`; getting the accessibility of your override right is
part of the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — `EqualityContract`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex6.cs`. `Shape` is a record with a `Sides`
member; `Circle : Shape` adds nothing but a type name. Implement
`ShapeFacts.BaseEqualsDerived()`, which must construct both, compare them
through `Shape`-typed variables, and return the answer — `false`. Then
implement `SameGeometryAs`, which deliberately ignores the runtime type and
compares only the declared members, so a `Shape` and a `Circle` with the same
`Sides` report `true`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — a record struct as a dictionary key

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex7.cs`. `SkuKey` is a
`readonly record struct SkuKey(string Code)` that must compare and hash
case-insensitively (ordinal), so `"AB-1"` and `"ab-1"` are one key. Implement
`Equals(SkuKey other)` and `GetHashCode()`, then `SkuIndex.Lookup`, which finds
the entry whatever the caller's casing and never boxes the key.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — an immutable aggregate with a cached hash

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex8.cs`. `Basket` holds an
`ImmutableArray<BasketLine>`. Implement `Add`, `RemoveAt` and `Replace` in
terms of `with`, structural equality over the lines, and a hash code computed
**once**, in the constructor, into a field that must play no part in equality.

That last clause is the whole exercise: a cached field is still a field, and a
record's generated members would happily use it. You are writing the equality
by hand precisely so it does not.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex8
```

## Challenge — replaying changes

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Challenge.cs`. `Snapshot` starts empty and
applies an ordered sequence of `Change(string Field, string Value)` records.
Identical changes appear more than once in the stream and must be applied only
once; the last distinct write to a field wins; the final `ToString()` must be
stable and sorted by field name. Value equality does the deduplication, `with`
does the application, `PrintMembers` does the printing.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is a `Measurement` whose `CapturedAt` timestamp must play no part in
equality — the same idea as ex8's cached field arriving from the opposite
direction, in a domain where the excluded field is meaningful but not
identifying.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality review1
```

# Reading - csharp/v3ca01_records_value_equality

## Notes

**A record is a class with generated members, and you can replace any of them.**
The compiler only synthesises a member if you have not written one with a
matching signature. Write `public virtual bool Equals(Playlist? other)` and the
generated one disappears; the generated `Equals(object?)`, `operator ==` and
`operator !=` remain and route through yours. That is the mechanism behind ex3
and ex8: you keep the whole record experience and replace exactly the piece
that was wrong. The one member you cannot replace is the clone method — it is
name-mangled specifically so you cannot.

**Field-based, not property-based.** The generated `Equals` reads backing
fields. For a positional record that is the same set of things as the
properties, which is why the distinction is invisible until you add a private
field. Anything you store — a memoised hash, a lazily built index, a
`Random` — becomes part of identity. The rule to carry: **if you add a private
field to a record, you have changed its equality**, and you should decide
whether that was intended in the same commit.

**`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` is the recursion step.** Each field is compared
using the default comparer for its type, which uses `IEquatable<T>` if the type
implements it and `object.Equals` otherwise. Records, strings, primitives and
tuples all behave. Arrays, `List<T>`, `Dictionary<,>` and most mutable
collections do not: they inherit reference equality, so two collections with
identical contents are different values. `ImmutableArray<T>` is not a rescue
either — its `Equals` compares the wrapped array reference.

**`with` is a copy, then a set.** The lowering is: call the protected copy
constructor to make a shallow clone, then run each `init` assignment on the
clone. Two consequences. First, the copy is *shallow*: a `with` on a record
holding a `List<T>` gives you a second record pointing at the same list, and
mutating it changes both. Second, the primary constructor body never runs, so
constructor validation is bypassed — the fix is to validate inside the `init`
accessor, which `with` does call.

**Inheritance and `EqualityContract`.** The generated equality demands that
both sides report the same contract type. This gives you the property most
hand-written equality gets wrong: `a.Equals(b) == b.Equals(a)` even when the
two are at different levels of a hierarchy. The cost is that a base and a
derived instance are never equal, however identical their data — which is
usually right and occasionally not, and ex6 makes you write the "usually not"
version explicitly rather than by accident.

**Record structs.** `record struct` gives value equality that is field-wise and
`IEquatable<T>`-based, which is strictly better than the `ValueType.Equals`
reflection path a plain struct falls back to (lesson 7 measures that path).
Positional `record struct` members are mutable `get; set;` unless you declare
the type `readonly record struct`, in which case they are `get; init;`. A
mutable value type used as a dictionary key is a bug waiting for a maintainer,
so reach for `readonly record struct` by default.

## ex1

Warm-up, but with one real assertion in it: the gate holds the original seat
and checks it after `NextSeat()`. `with` cannot mutate the receiver — there is
no code path in the generated members that writes to `this` — and seeing that
proved once is worth more than reading it.

Deconstruction in `Label()` is there so you use the generated `Deconstruct`
rather than the properties. Both work; the point is knowing it exists, because
positional patterns in lesson 2 depend on it.

## ex2

The interesting cell in the table is `label=False`. A plain class inherits
`object.Equals`, which is reference equality, so two identically populated
instances are different. Everyone knows that abstractly and half of people
still expect `True` when the class has only data in it.

`boxedCell=True` is the other one. Boxing a `readonly record struct` and
comparing through `object` still gives the value answer, because the generated
`Equals(object?)` override is what `object.Equals` dispatches to. Compare that
with lesson 7, where boxing a plain struct reaches `ValueType.Equals` and pays
for reflection to get the same answer.

## ex3

The array trap, and the reason it is worth a whole exercise: the code looks
right, the tests you would naturally write pass (a record equals itself), and
the failure only shows up when two independently constructed values ought to
match. Deduplicating a list of playlists silently keeps duplicates.

`SequenceEqual` handles the comparison; `HashCode`'s `Add` in a loop handles
the hash. The gate insists a `HashSet<Playlist>` agrees because that is the
consumer that punishes an `Equals`/`GetHashCode` mismatch, and it punishes it
by silently doing nothing rather than by throwing.

Notice what you did *not* have to write: `operator ==`, `Equals(object?)`,
`ToString`, the copy constructor. Replacing one generated member left the rest
in place, and the operator now routes through your comparison.

## ex4

Constructor validation on a record is a half-measure, and `with` is where it
shows. Moving the check into the `init` accessor covers both paths, because the
primary constructor's parameter assignment also goes through `init`.

The wrinkle is that a positional record's `init` accessor is generated, so you
have to stop being positional for that member — declare the property yourself
with an explicit backing field. That is the trade the exercise wants you to
feel: positional syntax is a convenience, and the moment you need behaviour in
an accessor you write the property out longhand.

## ex5

`PrintMembers` returns `bool` — `true` if it wrote anything — because the base
`ToString` uses the return value to decide whether to emit a separating comma
for a derived record's members. Return `false` after writing and the punctuation
comes out wrong for subclasses.

The accessibility rule is the trap: in an unsealed record the synthesised
member is `protected virtual bool PrintMembers(StringBuilder)`, and in a sealed
one it is `private bool PrintMembers(StringBuilder)`. Match the wrong one and
the compiler tells you, but the message is about hiding an inherited member,
which is not obviously about this.

## ex6

`BaseEqualsDerived` has to compare through `Shape`-typed variables, otherwise
the compiler picks the wrong overload and the question you are asking is not
the question you meant. The answer is `false`, and the reason is one virtual
property.

`SameGeometryAs` is the deliberate opt-out. Writing it makes the point that
records give you *one* equality, the identity one, and a domain often wants a
second, weaker comparison. The right home for that second comparison is a named
method or an `IEqualityComparer<T>` — never an override that makes `Equals`
lie, because collections believe `Equals`.

## ex7

Two ideas collide here. The hashing must be case-insensitive *and* consistent
with the comparison, so both go through `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`.
Ordinal, not culture: a culture-sensitive comparer makes your dictionary
behave differently in Istanbul, and lesson 8's challenge revisits exactly that.

"Must not box" is checkable: `Dictionary<SkuKey, T>` uses
`EqualityComparer<SkuKey>.Default`, which finds your `IEquatable<SkuKey>`
implementation — generated for record structs — and calls `Equals(SkuKey)`
directly on the struct. Fail to keep the strongly typed overload and every
lookup boxes twice.

## ex8

Caching a hash is a legitimate optimisation for a deep immutable aggregate, and
it is also the field that must not participate in equality. Writing both
members by hand is the only way to have it: computed once in the constructor,
read by `GetHashCode`, ignored by `Equals`.

Building `Add`/`RemoveAt`/`Replace` on `with` gives you the second idea —
structural sharing. `ImmutableArray<T>.Add` copies the array, which is O(n) and
honest; a real basket would use `ImmutableList<T>` for O(log n) at the cost of
a worse constant. Knowing which you have is the point; both are wrong if you
call them in a loop, which is what the challenge does deliberately.

## challenge

Deduplicating with a `HashSet<Change>` only works because `Change` is a record,
so this is the whole sector in one line. Order matters for the *result* (last
write wins) but not for the *dedup*, and getting those two facts to coexist is
the design work.

Sorting the output in `PrintMembers` is what makes the printed form testable at
all. Any type whose `ToString` iterates a dictionary is untestable in principle,
because hash ordering is not contractual — a good habit to take away
independently of records.

## review1

Excluding a field from equality is the same operation as ex8's cached hash,
but here the field is business data, which makes the decision a domain
decision rather than a technical one. Two readings of 20.5 C from sensor 3 are
"the same measurement" for deduplication and clearly not the same event for
auditing. The lesson is to write down which question your `Equals` answers,
because the collection classes will hold you to it.

# V3·A1 — Records and value equality (archive)

A record is a class whose equality, hashing, printing and copying are written
for you by the compiler. That generosity is the feature and the hazard: the
generated code is *good*, and it is generated from your fields, so it is only
as correct as your field list is honest about what identity means.

## The generated member list, in full

For `public record Person(string Name, int Age)` you get:

| Member | Notes |
|---|---|
| `EqualityContract` | `protected virtual Type`, overridden by each derived record |
| `Equals(Person?)` | `public virtual`, field-by-field via `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` |
| `Equals(object?)` | `public override`, delegates to the typed overload |
| `GetHashCode()` | `public override`, combines the contract and every field |
| `operator ==` / `!=` | `public static`, delegate to the virtual `Equals` |
| copy constructor | `protected Person(Person original)`, shallow |
| clone method | `public virtual`, name-mangled, drives `with` |
| `Deconstruct` | positional records only, one `out` per parameter |
| `PrintMembers` | `protected virtual` (unsealed) / `private` (sealed) |
| `ToString()` | `public override`, `Type { A = 1, B = 2 }` |

Write any of them yourself (except the clone) and the compiler stops generating
that one. That is the whole customisation story.

## Worked example — repairing equality for a collection member

```csharp
public record Playlist(string Name, string[] Tracks)
{
    public virtual bool Equals(Playlist? other) =>
        other is not null
        && EqualityContract == other.EqualityContract
        && Name == other.Name
        && Tracks.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(other.Tracks);

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        HashCode hash = new HashCode();
        hash.Add(Name);
        foreach (string track in Tracks) hash.Add(track);
        return hash.ToHashCode();
    }
}
```

Three details carry the example. `virtual` on the typed `Equals` is required —
a record's `Equals(T)` is virtual, and the compiler will not accept a
non-virtual replacement in an unsealed record. Keeping the `EqualityContract`
check preserves the symmetry the generated code had. And `HashCode` is used
rather than an XOR fold, because XOR is commutative and would hash
`["a","b"]` and `["b","a"]` identically.

## Worked example — validation that `with` respects

```csharp
public record Discount
{
    private readonly int _percent;

    public Discount(int percent) => Percent = percent;

    public int Percent
    {
        get => _percent;
        init => _percent = value is >= 0 and <= 100
            ? value
            : throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(Percent), value, "0-100.");
    }
}
```

`with` calls the `init` accessor, so this holds on both paths. Note the record
is no longer positional for that member; you cannot attach behaviour to a
generated accessor.

## Worked example — a second, weaker comparison

```csharp
public sealed class SameGeometryComparer : IEqualityComparer<Shape>
{
    public bool Equals(Shape? a, Shape? b) => a?.Sides == b?.Sides;
    public int GetHashCode(Shape shape) => shape.Sides.GetHashCode();
}
```

When the domain wants two notions of "same", the second one goes in a comparer
or a named method, never in an `Equals` override. Every collection type in the
BCL takes an `IEqualityComparer<T>`; use that door.

## Worked example — the shallow copy nobody expects

```csharp
public record Order(string Id, List<string> Notes);

Order first = new Order("A1", new List<string> { "gift wrap" });
Order second = first with { Id = "A2" };

second.Notes.Add("fragile");
Console.WriteLine(first.Notes.Count);   // 2
```

`with` copied the *reference*, so both orders share one list. This is not a
record defect — it is what a shallow copy means, and every clone-based API in
the BCL behaves the same way. The fix is to hold an immutable member type, so
that "add a note" produces a new collection and a new record:

```csharp
public record Order(string Id, ImmutableList<string> Notes)
{
    public Order WithNote(string note) => this with { Notes = Notes.Add(note) };
}
```

Do that consistently and a record becomes genuinely immutable rather than
merely unassignable. Leave one mutable member in place and every guarantee you
were relying on has a hole in it, in the one place you will not look.

## Worked example — excluding a field, on purpose

```csharp
public record Reading(string Sensor, double Value, DateTimeOffset At)
{
    public virtual bool Equals(Reading? other) =>
        other is not null
        && EqualityContract == other.EqualityContract
        && Sensor == other.Sensor
        && Value.Equals(other.Value);

    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Sensor, Value);
}
```

Excluding a field is the safest kind of custom equality, because it cannot
break reflexivity, symmetry or transitivity — you are simply comparing a
smaller tuple. Compare that with "equal if within 0.1", which breaks
transitivity (`a~b`, `b~c`, but not `a~c`) and quietly corrupts every hash
container it touches. If your equality has a tolerance in it, it is not
equality; it is a comparison method with a name.

## Common mistakes

1. **Assuming a record with an array or list member has value equality.** It
   does not. Two identical playlists are unequal, and your deduplication
   silently keeps both.
2. **Adding a private cached field.** It joins the equality set. Symptoms are
   maddening: equality that depends on whether anyone has read a property.
3. **Validating in the constructor body.** `with` bypasses it. Validate in
   `init`.
4. **Assuming `with` deep-copies.** It is a shallow copy; both records share
   the same mutable member.
5. **Overriding `Equals(object?)` instead of `Equals(T)`.** You end up with two
   disagreeing implementations, because the generated typed overload remains
   and `==` prefers it.
6. **Forgetting `GetHashCode` when you write `Equals`.** `HashSet` and
   `Dictionary` will fail to find things and will not tell you why.
7. **Using a mutable record as a dictionary key.** `init` makes the *properties*
   read-only, but a `List<T>` member is still mutable, and mutating it after
   insertion strands the entry.
8. **Expecting base and derived records to compare equal.** `EqualityContract`
   says no, on purpose.
9. **Sealing a record and then writing `protected virtual bool PrintMembers`.**
   In a sealed record the member is `private`.
10. **Reaching for `record` for an entity.** A customer with an id is equal to
    another customer when the ids match, whatever the other 20 fields say.
    That is identity equality, and a record fights you.

## In an interview

*"What is the difference between a record and a class?"* — A record is a class.
The compiler adds value-based `Equals`/`GetHashCode`/`==`, a `ToString` that
prints members, a protected copy constructor and a clone used by `with`, and,
for positional records, a `Deconstruct`. Nothing about the runtime type system
changes: records are reference types, they participate in inheritance, and a
`record struct` is a struct with the same generated set.

*"How does record equality actually work?"* — It compares the runtime
`EqualityContract` first, then each backing field with
`EqualityComparer<T>.Default`. So it is field-based, and any field whose type
uses reference equality — arrays, `List<T>` — makes the record use reference
equality for that part.

*"When would you not use a record?"* — Entities with identity; anything EF Core
tracks and mutates; large payloads you would `with` inside a loop, since each
`with` is a full shallow copy; and types where equality is genuinely a domain
question with more than one answer.

## Check yourself

1. Which generated member does `with` call, and which does it not?
2. `record A(int X)` and `record B(int X) : A(X)`. Is `new A(1) == new B(1)`?
   Which member decides?
3. You add `private int _callCount;` to a record and increment it in a method.
   What breaks?
4. Why is `EqualityComparer<string[]>.Default.Equals(a, b)` reference equality?
5. Write `GetHashCode` for a record with a `string` and a `string[]` member.
6. What is the return value of `PrintMembers` used for?
7. Where do you put validation so that both the constructor and `with` enforce
   it, and what syntax do you have to give up?
8. A `readonly record struct` compared through two `object` variables: value or
   reference equality, and which member is called?
9. Why does a positional `record struct` with mutable members make a poor
   dictionary key?
10. Give two ways to express "equal for this purpose but not for identity".
11. Does replacing `Equals(T)` also replace `operator ==`? What routes to what?
12. Why can you not write your own clone method for a record?
13. `p with { }` — what does it produce, and how many objects exist afterwards?
14. Your record holds an `ImmutableArray<int>`. Is equality structural?

# Long read — how records are built, and what they cost

## Where they came from

Before C# 9, "a small immutable type with value semantics" was a page of
boilerplate: a constructor, read-only properties, `Equals(T)`, `Equals(object)`,
`GetHashCode`, `==`, `!=`, and a `ToString` nobody kept up to date. Teams
either wrote it, generated it with a ReSharper template that drifted out of
sync, or used `Tuple`/`ValueTuple` and lost the names. The BCL itself is full of
hand-written examples of exactly this: `System.Version`, `TimeSpan`,
`KeyValuePair<,>`.

C# 9 (November 2020, .NET 5) added `record` — strictly a *language* feature.
No runtime support was added, no new IL, no new CLR type kind. A record is a
class the compiler decorated. You can prove it: `typeof(Person).IsClass` is
`true`, and the only trace in metadata is a compiler-generated
`<Clone>$` method plus, since C# 10, an `IsExternalInit` modreq on the `init`
setters. C# 10 added `record struct` and `readonly record struct`; C# 12 added
primary constructors to ordinary classes and structs, which are *not* the same
feature and generate none of the equality members.

## The lowering, in detail

Take `public record Person(string Name, int Age);`.

The positional parameters become `public string Name { get; init; }` and
`public int Age { get; init; }`, with backing fields, plus a constructor that
assigns them. `init` is a normal setter with a `modreq(IsExternalInit)` on it:
that modreq is what stops other compilers, and later versions of your own
assembly, from calling it outside an object initialiser. It is a compile-time
guarantee only — reflection can set the backing field, which is exactly how
every deserialiser materialises records.

`Equals(Person? other)` is emitted as a chain: null check, then
`EqualityContract == other.EqualityContract`, then one
`EqualityComparer<T>.Default.Equals(field, other.field)` per field. The
`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` calls are why field comparison is not free: for
`string` it lands in `string.Equals` after a devirtualised call; for a struct
implementing `IEquatable<T>` the JIT usually inlines it; for an arbitrary
reference type it is a virtual call into `object.Equals`.

`GetHashCode` combines `EqualityComparer<Type>.Default.GetHashCode(
EqualityContract)` with each field's hash using the same multiply-and-add
pattern `HashCode` uses. Because the contract is included, a base and a derived
record hash differently even with identical data — consistent with the equality
that will reject them.

`with` lowers to two steps you can see in IL: `callvirt <Clone>$`, then a store
per initialiser. The clone calls the protected copy constructor, which does a
member-by-member copy of every field, including compiler-generated ones. That
is O(fields), it allocates one object, and it is *shallow* — a `List<T>` member
is shared by both. The virtual clone is what makes `with` work correctly on a
variable statically typed as the base record: cloning an `Employee` held in a
`Person` variable gives an `Employee`.

## Performance, honestly

A `with` is one allocation plus a field copy. That is cheap in absolute terms
and expensive in a loop: folding a thousand changes into a record by `with` per
change allocates a thousand objects, all immediately garbage. Gen0 collection
is fast, so this is usually fine and occasionally the whole problem — the
allocation profiler will tell you which. The functional idiom "build a new
value each step" is not free the way it is in a language with a compacting
nursery tuned for it; it is merely usually affordable.

Equality on a record with N fields is N comparisons and no reflection, which
makes it dramatically faster than `ValueType.Equals` on a plain struct (that
one walks fields with reflection unless the type is blittable — lesson 7 has
the numbers). A `record struct` used as a dictionary key is one of the better
performance decisions available in modern C#: `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`
finds the generated `IEquatable<T>`, the call is devirtualised, and no boxing
happens on lookup.

The generated `ToString` builds a `StringBuilder` and appends every member. It
is convenient in logs and it is not free; a hot logging path that interpolates
a large record into a debug message pays for the whole render even when the log
level discards it. Use the structured-logging pattern that defers formatting.

## Record structs, and why they are the better default for small values

`record struct` arrived in C# 10 and is the most under-used member of the
family. A plain struct that does not override `Equals` inherits
`ValueType.Equals(object)`, which boxes the argument and then — unless the type
is blittable, meaning no references and no padding — walks the fields with
reflection. That path is roughly an order of magnitude slower than a written
comparison and allocates on every call. A `record struct` gets a generated
`IEquatable<T>.Equals(T)`, so `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` finds it, the JIT
usually inlines it, and a dictionary lookup keyed on the struct never boxes.

`readonly record struct` goes one step further and makes every generated
property `get; init;`, which matters for a reason lesson 7 develops in detail:
a non-readonly struct passed by `in` forces the compiler to take a defensive
copy before every member access, so the "optimisation" of passing by reference
makes the code slower. Declaring the type `readonly` removes the need for those
copies entirely.

The one thing to watch is `with` on a large record struct: it copies the whole
value, on the stack, per expression. For a three-field struct that is free; for
a forty-field struct in a loop it is not, and the profiler will show it as time
in the method rather than as allocation, which makes it harder to spot.

## The parts people misuse

**Records as DTOs over the wire.** Fine, with a caveat: `init` and `required`
are compile-time constructs, and a JSON deserialiser will happily produce a
record with `null` in a non-nullable `string` member. Validation still belongs
somewhere real.

**Records as EF Core entities.** The change tracker wants to mutate the
instance it handed you and to identify rows by key. A record's value equality
means two different rows with the same column values are "the same entity" to
any set operation you perform in memory, and `init` members mean the tracker
has to use reflection to write. It works and it fights you the whole way.

**Deep hierarchies of records.** Legal, and `EqualityContract` keeps equality
sane, but the more levels you have the more places a `with` on a base-typed
variable does something you did not picture. Two levels is plenty, for the same
reasons `04_inheritance_polymorphism` gave.

**`record` for anything mutable.** Nothing stops you writing
`public record Cart { public List<Item> Items { get; set; } = new(); }`. You
now have a type with value equality over a mutable member, which is the exact
combination that strands entries in hash containers.

## When not to use it

Use a class when the type has identity (an id, a handle, a database row), when
it is going to be mutated in place, when it participates in a framework that
expects to construct and populate it in two steps, or when equality is a
domain question you want to answer explicitly rather than have generated. Use a
`readonly record struct` when the value is small and copied often; a
`record class` when it is large, shared, or polymorphic. Reach for `class` +
hand-written `IEquatable<T>` — lesson 8 — when you need equality that is
deliberately not the field list.

## Further reading

- [Records (C# reference)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record)
  — the normative list of synthesised members, including the accessibility
  rules for `PrintMembers` in sealed records.
- [C# 9.0 records feature specification](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/main/proposals/csharp-9.0/records.md)
  — the lowering, in the language designers' own words; read the "Synthesized
  equality members" section when you need to argue about symmetry.
- [`init`-only setters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/init)
  — what the `IsExternalInit` modreq guarantees and does not guarantee.
- [`System.HashCode`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.hashcode)
  — `Combine` for a fixed set of fields, `Add` in a loop for collections, and
  why the seed is randomised per process.
- [Choosing between class, record and struct](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/choosing-between-class-and-struct)
  — the design-guideline framing of the identity-versus-value question.


## Hint 1

Three of the four answers are decided by which keyword you put in front of the
type name; only one of them is decided by anything you write inside `Report`.

Before you write a line, predict all four values and write your predictions
down. The one people get wrong is the last.

## Hint 2

Boxing looks like this:

```csharp
object left = someStruct;
object right = someOtherStruct;
bool same = left.Equals(right);
```

`left.Equals` is a virtual call on `object`. Which method it lands in depends
on what the struct's type overrode — and a `record struct` overrides
`Equals(object?)` for you.

## Hint 3

`Report` is a handful of local variables and one interpolated string. Compare
with `Equals` rather than `==` for the boxed pair, because `==` on two `object`

## Hint 1

Approach it as four separate questions about *where the comparison ends up*:

1. `Tag` — which type declares the `Equals` that runs?
2. `Label` — same question. There is only one candidate.
3. `Cell` — same question again.
4. Boxed `Cell` — the call starts at `object`. Where does it land?

Three of those land in generated code. One lands in `System.Object`.

## Hint 2

`object.Equals(object?)` is virtual and its default implementation is:

```csharp
public virtual bool Equals(object? obj) => ReferenceEquals(this, obj);
```

which is why two identically populated `Label`s are different objects and
therefore unequal — and why adding data to a class never changes its equality.

## Exercise 3 — the array member

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex3.cs`.

```csharp
public record Playlist(string Name, string[] Tracks);
```

Two playlists built from separate arrays with identical contents are currently
**not** equal. Make them equal by replacing the generated equality:

```csharp
public virtual bool Equals(Playlist? other);
public override int GetHashCode();
```

Rules:

- do not change `string[]` to another collection type
- do not write `operator ==` or `operator !=`
- do not write `Equals(object?)`

Worked expectations, with `a = new Playlist("mix", ["one", "two"])`:

- `a == new Playlist("mix", ["one", "two"])` -> `true`
- `a == new Playlist("mix", ["two", "one"])` -> `false` (order is part of the value)
- `a == new Playlist("other", ["one", "two"])` -> `false`
- `new HashSet<Playlist> { a, new Playlist("mix", ["one", "two"]) }.Count` -> `1`

That last assertion is the one that fails if you write `Equals` and forget
`GetHashCode`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The generated `Equals` compares each field with
`EqualityComparer<T>.Default`. For `string` that is a real character
comparison. For `string[]` it is reference equality, because arrays never
overrode `Equals`. Same code, two completely different meanings, decided by the
member's type.

So you are not fixing a bug in the compiler — you are telling it that for this
type, "same tracks" means something it had no way to guess.

## Hint 2

A structural comparison of two arrays, and a hash that matches it:

```csharp
bool same = left.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(right.AsSpan());

HashCode hash = new HashCode();
foreach (string item in left) hash.Add(item);
int code = hash.ToHashCode();
```

`HashCode.Add` in a loop is the collection-shaped counterpart to
`HashCode.Combine` for a fixed field list. Do not fold with `^`: XOR is
commutative, so it would give `["a","b"]` and `["b","a"]` the same hash, and
then your hash would disagree with an `Equals` that cares about order.

## Hint 3

Your `Equals` needs four things in order: a null check on `other`, the runtime
type check the generated version had, the name comparison, and the element
comparison. Keep the type check — dropping it is how hand-written equality
stops being symmetric.

The signature must be `public virtual bool Equals(Playlist? other)`. `virtual`
is not optional in an unsealed record; the compiler rejects a non-virtual
replacement.

Left to you: whether to compare arrays with `SequenceEqual` over spans, over
`IEnumerable<T>`, or with an index loop. All three pass; one of them allocates
two enumerators.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reproduce the failure before you fix it. In a scratch file:

```csharp
string[] one = ["a"];
string[] two = ["a"];
Console.WriteLine(one.Equals(two));                              // ?
Console.WriteLine(EqualityComparer<string[]>.Default.Equals(one, two)); // ?
```

Both print `False`. Everything about this exercise follows from that, including
why `List<T>` would not have helped.

## Hint 2

Think about which member the `HashSet` assertion is really testing. A hash set
does two things on insert: it computes a bucket from `GetHashCode`, then it
compares candidates in that bucket with `Equals`. If your hash codes differ,
the two playlists land in different buckets and `Equals` is never even called —
so the set holds two items and your `Equals` looks broken when it is not.

That is the whole reason the rule "override them together" exists, and it is
also why the failure is silent: nothing throws, you just get a wrong count.

## Hint 3

Write `GetHashCode` first, then `Equals`. Doing it in that order forces you to
decide what "the value" of a playlist is — name plus ordered tracks — and then
`Equals` is just the same decision spelled with comparisons.

Left to you: whether to include the runtime type in the hash the way the
generated version did. It changes nothing here because nothing derives from
`Playlist`, and it changes everything the day something does.

## Exercise 4 — validation that survives `with`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex4.cs`. Today `Discount` looks like this:

```csharp
public record Discount(int Percent)
{
    public Discount(int Percent) : this(Percent) =>
        ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative(Percent);   // never runs for `with`
}
```

Rewrite it so that **every** path into a `Discount` enforces
`0 <= Percent <= 100`:

- `new Discount(10)` -> works, `Percent` is `10`
- `new Discount(-1)` -> `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, `ParamName == "Percent"`
- `new Discount(101)` -> `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, `ParamName == "Percent"`
- `new Discount(10) with { Percent = 900 }` -> `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`,
  `ParamName == "Percent"`
- `new Discount(10) with { Percent = 20 }` -> `Percent` is `20`
- value equality still works: `new Discount(10) == new Discount(10)` -> `true`

The last line is the constraint that stops you turning the record into a class.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`with` never calls your constructor. It calls a generated copy constructor and
then assigns through each property's `init` accessor. So there is exactly one
place a check can sit and be on both paths, and the positional syntax is
currently hiding that place from you.

## Hint 2

A record with an explicitly written property looks like this:

```csharp
public record Temperature
{
    private readonly double _celsius;

    public Temperature(double celsius) => Celsius = celsius;

    public double Celsius
    {
        get => _celsius;
        init => _celsius = double.IsFinite(value)
            ? value
            : throw new ArgumentException("Not a temperature.", nameof(Celsius));
    }
}
```

Note the constructor assigns *the property*, not the field. That is what makes
one check cover both entry points.

## Hint 3

Drop the positional parameter list, declare the backing field `readonly`, and
put the range test in `init`. `ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfLessThan` and
`ThrowIfGreaterThan` exist in .NET 8 and take a `paramName` argument — but note
what they infer by default, and check it is the name the gate wants.

Left to you: whether to throw from an expression-bodied `init` with a
conditional, or from a statement body with a guard clause. The second reads
better once there are two bounds.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write down the two call paths as machine steps:

- `new Discount(10)` — constructor body runs, assigns the member.
- `d with { Percent = 900 }` — copy constructor runs (field-to-field, no
  validation possible), then `set_Percent` runs with `900`.

Now ask: which single method appears in both lists? That is where the check
goes, and everything else in this exercise is consequence.

## Hint 2

There is a tempting wrong answer worth ruling out explicitly: adding validation
to a second, non-primary constructor.

```csharp
public Discount(int percent, bool validate) { ... }   // does not help
```

`with` calls none of your constructors. Any design where the check lives in *a*
constructor loses to `with`, however many constructors you write.

## Hint 3

Once the property is written longhand, the equality question answers itself:
the record still has exactly one field, so the generated `Equals` and
`GetHashCode` still compare exactly that field. You have changed how the value
gets in, not what the value is.

Left to you: the exception message. The gate only checks the type and
`ParamName`, so say something a caller could act on — which value arrived and
what the bounds are.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — `PrintMembers` and the redacted token

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex5.cs`.

```csharp
public record Credentials(string User, string Token);
```

`ToString()` currently prints the token in full, which means one careless log
line leaks a secret. Override `PrintMembers` so that

```csharp
new Credentials("ada", "sk-live-9f3a").ToString()
```

returns exactly

```
Credentials { User = ada, Token = ***, Fingerprint = 3f }
```

`Fingerprint` is the last two characters of the token, lower-cased, and is not
stored anywhere — it is computed inside `PrintMembers`. A token shorter than
two characters prints `Fingerprint = ??`.

The record is deliberately **not** sealed, which decides the accessibility and
the modifier your override needs. The gate also asserts that equality is
unchanged: two `Credentials` with the same user and token are still equal.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ToString()` on a record is not the interesting member. It writes the type
name, a brace, calls `PrintMembers`, and writes the closing brace. Everything
between the braces is `PrintMembers`'s output, so that is the only thing you
have to write.

The signature is fixed and the compiler will tell you if you get it wrong — but
the error message talks about hiding an inherited member, which is not an
obvious way of saying "wrong accessibility".

## Hint 2

The shape of a hand-written `PrintMembers`:

```csharp
protected virtual bool PrintMembers(StringBuilder builder)
{
    builder.Append("Kind = ").Append(Kind);
    builder.Append(", Size = ").Append(Size);
    return true;
}
```

Note there is no leading or trailing space and no comma before the first
member: `ToString` writes `"TypeName { "` and `" }"` around whatever you
append.

## Hint 3

Three appends, separated by `", "`, then `return true`. The return value is not
decoration — a derived record's `ToString` uses it to decide whether it needs a
comma before its own members, so returning `false` after writing produces
broken punctuation for subclasses.

The fingerprint is `Token[^2..]` when the token is long enough. Left to you:
whether to write the short-token case as a conditional expression or an early
branch, and whether `??` is a good sentinel for your team.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from what you are defending against. `ToString` is called by string
interpolation, by most logging frameworks when you pass an object, and by the
debugger. A record's generous default prints every member, so a record is the
easiest way in C# to leak a secret into a log file — and the leak is
invisible in review, because the call site just says `logger.LogDebug("{Creds}",
creds)`.

That framing tells you the fix must live on the type, not at the call sites.

## Hint 2

A rejected alternative worth understanding: overriding `ToString` itself.

```csharp
public override string ToString() => $"Credentials {{ User = {User}, ... }}";
```

It passes this exercise's assertion and it is the wrong tool. You have now
hand-written the brace-and-comma formatting that the compiler maintains for
you, and a derived record inherits your string, including the wrong type name.
`PrintMembers` exists exactly so the type name and punctuation stay generated.

## Hint 3

Deal with the sealed-versus-unsealed question deliberately rather than by trial
and error: in an unsealed record the synthesised member is
`protected virtual bool PrintMembers(StringBuilder)`, and in a sealed record it
is `private bool PrintMembers(StringBuilder)`. Yours must match the record you
have.

Left to you: whether the fingerprint is computed inline in the append chain or
in a small private helper. The helper is easier to unit test, and nothing in
the gate cares.

## Exercise 6 — `EqualityContract`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Ex6.cs`.

```csharp
public record Shape(int Sides);
public record Circle() : Shape(0);

public static class ShapeFacts
{
    public static bool BaseEqualsDerived();
    public static bool SameGeometryAs(Shape left, Shape right);
}
```

`BaseEqualsDerived` must construct a `Shape` with `0` sides and a `Circle`,
hold **both in `Shape`-typed variables**, compare them with `==`, and return
the result. The gate asserts it is `false`, and asserts it is `false` in both
directions — `a == b` and `b == a`.

`SameGeometryAs` ignores the runtime type and compares only `Sides`:

- `SameGeometryAs(new Shape(0), new Circle())` -> `true`
- `SameGeometryAs(new Shape(3), new Circle())` -> `false`
- `SameGeometryAs(new Circle(), new Circle())` -> `true`

The gate also checks that `new Shape(0).Equals(new Circle())` and
`new Circle().Equals(new Shape(0))` agree with each other. Say why in a comment
before you write the code.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two records with identical data are unequal here, and no field explains it. The
member responsible is one you never wrote and cannot see: a virtual property
returning `typeof(this class)`, which each derived record overrides.

Both generated `Equals` implementations compare that property before they look
at any data — which is why the answer is the same whichever side you ask.

## Hint 2

Roughly what the generated comparison does:

```csharp
public virtual bool Equals(Shape? other) =>
    other is not null
    && EqualityContract == other.EqualityContract   // typeof(Shape) vs typeof(Circle)
    && Sides == other.Sides;
```

Contrast that with the naive hand-written version people write instead:

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj) => obj is Shape s && s.Sides == Sides;
```

That one says a `Circle` *is* a `Shape`, so `shape.Equals(circle)` is `true` —
while `Circle`'s own override would say `false`. Asymmetric equality, and a
`HashSet` whose contents depend on insertion order.

## Hint 3

`BaseEqualsDerived` is three lines: two locals typed `Shape`, one comparison,
one `return`. Type the variables as `Shape` deliberately — with `var` you get
`Shape` and `Circle`, the compiler picks a different overload, and you are
answering a different question.

`SameGeometryAs` is one comparison on one property. Left to you: whether it
should also handle `null` arguments, and what it should do if it did. The gate
never passes null; your judgment about a public static helper is separate.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the contract rather than the code. Equality is supposed to be
symmetric: `a.Equals(b)` and `b.Equals(a)` must agree, always. Now put yourself
in the compiler's position, generating `Equals` for a record that might be
derived from, and try to satisfy that rule using only `is` checks. You cannot —
`circle is Shape` is true while `shape is Circle` is false.

The only symmetric test available is "do these two report the same exact
type?", and that is what `EqualityContract` provides.

## Hint 2

You can see the member from outside, indirectly:

```csharp
Shape a = new Shape(0);
Shape b = new Circle();
Console.WriteLine(a.GetType() == b.GetType());   // False
```

`EqualityContract` is the virtual, inheritance-aware version of that check. It
is a property rather than a `GetType()` call so that a derived record *could*
override it to claim its base's contract — which is the escape hatch for the
rare hierarchy that genuinely wants cross-level equality, and which you should
almost never take.

## Hint 3

Think about where `SameGeometryAs` belongs long-term. Written as a static
helper it is honest: a second, weaker notion of sameness with a name that says
what it means. Written as an `Equals` override it would be a trap, because
every `Dictionary`, `HashSet`, `Distinct` and `Contains` in the codebase
believes `Equals`.

Left to you: whether you would promote it to an `IEqualityComparer<Shape>` in
real code. The BCL takes one everywhere for exactly this situation.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The generated `Equals` for a record struct compares each field with the default
comparer, which for `string` is ordinal *case-sensitive*. You want a different
comparison, so you replace exactly that one member — and, because you changed
what "equal" means, the hash has to move with it.

The comparison and the hash must come from the same source of truth, or the
dictionary will look in the wrong bucket and find nothing.

## Hint 2

`StringComparer` gives you both halves from one object:

```csharp
StringComparer comparer = StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase;
bool same = comparer.Equals(left, right);
int code = comparer.GetHashCode(value);
```

Using the comparer for both is the discipline that keeps them consistent. Roll
your own with `ToUpperInvariant()` on each side and you have two independent
places to get it wrong, plus a string allocation per comparison.

## Hint 3

For a record struct the replacement signature is
`public bool Equals(SkuKey other)` — no `virtual`, because a struct cannot be
derived from, and no null check, because `other` cannot be null.

`SkuIndex` is a thin wrapper: a `Dictionary<SkuKey, int>` field, an `Add` that
wraps the string in a `SkuKey`, and a `TryLookup` that does the same and
forwards to `TryGetValue`.

Left to you: what `Add` should do when the same code arrives twice in different
casing. The gate does not test it; decide and be consistent.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the boxing question, because it is the reason this is a
`record struct` and not a `class`.

`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` with no comparer argument uses
`EqualityComparer<TKey>.Default`. For a type implementing `IEquatable<TKey>`
that resolves to a comparer that calls your strongly typed `Equals(TKey)`
directly on the value — no boxing, no `object` in sight. A record struct
implements `IEquatable<T>` for you. Keep the typed overload and the whole
lookup path stays allocation-free.

## Hint 2

The culture assertion is not trivia. Under `tr-TR`, `"I".ToLower()` is `"ı"`,
not `"i"` — the dotless i. Any case-insensitive comparison built out of
`ToLower()`/`ToUpper()` without an explicit culture therefore changes meaning
depending on where the process is running:

```csharp
// Wrong: culture-dependent, and allocates two strings per comparison.
bool same = left.ToLower() == right.ToLower();
```

`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` maps only the ASCII and Unicode-simple case
pairs and never consults the culture, which is what you want for identifiers.

## Hint 3

Sanity-check your hash independently of the dictionary: two keys that compare
equal must return the same `GetHashCode()`. If you can write a pair of codes
where equality says yes and the hashes differ, the dictionary is already
broken, and it will fail silently rather than throw.

Left to you: whether `SkuIndex` exposes the key type at all. Keeping `SkuKey`
internal to the index and taking `string` at the boundary is a defensible API
choice, and it is the one this signature makes.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two things are fighting. `with` calls the copy constructor, which copies every
field verbatim — including a cached hash that was computed for the *old*
lines. And a record's generated equality reads every field, including that
cache.

Both problems go away if you take control of the two members that touch fields:
write `Equals` and `GetHashCode` yourself, and make sure every construction
path runs the constructor that computes the cache.

## Hint 2

`ImmutableArray<T>` does not give you structural equality — its `Equals`
compares the wrapped array reference, exactly like a plain array:

```csharp
ImmutableArray<int> a = [1, 2];
ImmutableArray<int> b = [1, 2];
Console.WriteLine(a == b);                       // False
Console.WriteLine(a.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(b));  // True
```

Its mutation methods return new arrays:
`Lines.Add(line)`, `Lines.RemoveAt(index)`, `Lines.SetItem(index, line)`.
Each copies, so each is O(n) — honest, and worth knowing before you call one in
a loop.

## Hint 3

Give `Lines` an explicit `init` accessor that assigns the field *and*
recomputes the cache. That is the one change that makes `with` correct, because
`with` goes through `init` for every member it sets — and it means `Add` can be
`this with { Lines = Lines.Add(line) }` and stay honest.

Left to you: whether `Equals` compares the cached hashes first as a fast reject
before the element loop. It is a legitimate optimisation with one subtlety —
equal hashes do not imply equal values, so it can only ever be used to say
"definitely not equal".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from what goes wrong if you do nothing. Suppose you leave the generated
members in place and add `private readonly int _hash;`:

```csharp
Basket one = new Basket([lineA]);
Basket two = one.Add(lineB).RemoveAt(1);   // same lines as `one`
```

Are they equal? Only if `_hash` happens to match, because the generated
`Equals` compares every field and `_hash` is a field. You have made equality
depend on construction history. That is the bug the exercise exists to make you
feel.

## Hint 2

Think about where "compute once" can honestly happen in an immutable type.
There are exactly two moments: the constructor, and an `init` accessor. Nothing
else runs before the value is handed out, and nothing may run after — a lazy
`_hash ??= Compute()` writes to a field after publication, which breaks the
value semantics and is not thread-safe without more machinery than this is
worth.

Eager is not merely simpler here; it is the only version that is correct.

## Hint 3

Watch for the ordering trap in the constructor: you must assign `Lines` before
you compute the hash from it, and if you compute the hash inside the `init`
accessor, that ordering takes care of itself.

Left to you: what `RemoveAt` does with an out-of-range index. `ImmutableArray`
will throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for you; decide whether you want that
raw or wrapped in something that names the basket.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — replaying changes

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Challenge.cs`.

```csharp
public readonly record struct Change(string Field, string Value);

public record Snapshot
{
    public static Snapshot Empty { get; }
    public Snapshot Apply(Change change);
    public Snapshot ApplyAll(IEnumerable<Change> changes);
    public int AppliedCount { get; }
}
```

`ApplyAll` walks the sequence in order and applies each change, except that a
change **identical to one already applied** is skipped entirely — same field,
same value, seen before, ignored. A change to a field that was already set with
a *different* value overwrites it and counts.

Worked example. Given, in order:

```
("city", "berlin"), ("tier", "gold"), ("city", "berlin"), ("city", "lisbon"), ("tier", "gold")
```

- `AppliedCount` -> `3`
- `ToString()` -> `Snapshot { city = lisbon, tier = gold }`

The printed form is sorted by field name, ordinal, and produced by overriding
`PrintMembers` — the type name and braces must still come from the generated
`ToString`. An empty snapshot prints `Snapshot { }`.

Three sector ideas meet here: value equality does the deduplication (a
`HashSet<Change>` only works because `Change` is a record), `with` does the
application, and `PrintMembers` does the printing. The snapshot must stay
immutable throughout: `Empty` is asserted to be unchanged after a hundred
applications.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state have to travel with each snapshot: the field values, and
the set of changes already seen. The second one is what makes deduplication
possible without rescanning the input, and it is also the thing people forget
to copy.

Both are collections, and this is a record, so pick collection types whose
"add" gives you a new collection rather than mutating the one your predecessor
is still holding.

## Hint 2

`ImmutableDictionary` and `ImmutableHashSet` both hand you a new instance:

```csharp
ImmutableDictionary<string, string> next = current.SetItem("city", "lisbon");
ImmutableHashSet<Change> seen = applied.Add(change);
```

`ImmutableHashSet<Change>.Contains` is what turns record equality into
deduplication: it hashes the `Change` and compares candidates, and both of
those come from the generated members on the record struct.

## Hint 3

`Apply` is: if `seen` already contains the change, return `this` unchanged;
otherwise return `this with { ... }` setting both collections and incrementing
the count. `ApplyAll` is a fold — `changes.Aggregate(this, (s, c) => s.Apply(c))`
or a plain `foreach` over a local.

For `PrintMembers`, order the pairs with `OrderBy(pair => pair.Key,
StringComparer.Ordinal)` and join with `", "`. Left to you: whether `Empty` is a
static property returning a cached instance or a fresh one each time. One of
those makes the "unchanged after a hundred applications" assertion mean
something.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Attack the specification first; the code is short once the rules are exact.
Write out what happens to `AppliedCount` and to the field values for each of
the five changes in the worked example, one line each. Two of the five are
skipped, and they are skipped for the same reason — the exact pair has been
seen — not because the field has been seen.

If your reading of the rule ever says "skip because the field already has a
value", the fourth change would be dropped and the answer would be `berlin`.

## Hint 2

There is a tempting shortcut that fails: deduplicating the input with
`changes.Distinct()` before folding.

```csharp
foreach (Change change in changes.Distinct()) { ... }   // wrong count
```

`Distinct` removes duplicates from *this* call's sequence. The specification is
about changes this snapshot has ever applied, which includes ones from an
earlier `ApplyAll` on the same lineage. Keeping `seen` on the snapshot is what
makes the two behave differently, and the gate applies changes in two batches
to catch exactly this.

## Hint 3

A stable `ToString` is a testability property, not an aesthetic one. Any type
that prints a dictionary in enumeration order has an untestable `ToString`,
because hash order is not contractual and can change between runtimes. Sorting
is the fix and it costs nothing at these sizes.

Left to you: whether `PrintMembers` returns `false` for an empty snapshot. Look
at what `ToString` does with the return value before you decide - the printed
form for the empty case is specified, so try both and keep the one that matches.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the field that does not identify

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA01_Records/Review1.cs`.

```csharp
public record Measurement(string Sensor, double Celsius, DateTimeOffset CapturedAt)
{
    public virtual bool Equals(Measurement? other);
    public override int GetHashCode();
    public Measurement Recapture(DateTimeOffset at);
}
```

Two measurements are the same value when the sensor and the temperature match.
`CapturedAt` is real business data — it goes in the database, it appears in
reports — and it plays no part in equality, because the pipeline deduplicates
repeated readings from a chattery sensor.

- `new Measurement("s3", 20.5, t1) == new Measurement("s3", 20.5, t2)` -> `true`
- `new Measurement("s3", 20.5, t1) == new Measurement("s4", 20.5, t1)` -> `false`
- `new Measurement("s3", 20.6, t1) == new Measurement("s3", 20.5, t1)` -> `false`
- a `HashSet<Measurement>` fed five readings from one sensor at one temperature
  with five different timestamps holds `1` item
- `ToString()` still prints all three members, including the timestamp

`Recapture(at)` returns the same reading stamped at a new time, via `with`.

The sensor name is compared ordinally and case-sensitively. The temperature is
a `double`: compare it with `Equals` rather than `==` and say in a comment why
those two differ for one specific value.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca01_records_value_equality review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is ex8's cached-field problem wearing different clothes. There, a field
had to be excluded because it was an implementation detail. Here, a field has
to be excluded because the *domain* says it does not identify the reading.

The mechanism is identical: the generated members read every field, so if you
want a field left out, you write those members yourself.

## Hint 2

Two members, both short:

```csharp
public virtual bool Equals(Measurement? other) =>
    other is not null
    && EqualityContract == other.EqualityContract
    && /* the two members that matter */;

public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(/* the same two */);
```

The rule that keeps you honest: whatever appears in `Equals` appears in
`GetHashCode`, and nothing else does. Include the timestamp in the hash but not
in `Equals` and your `HashSet` will hold five items while `==` insists they are
one — the worst kind of inconsistency, because both halves look right in
isolation.

## Hint 3

For the `double`: `double.NaN == double.NaN` is `false`, but
`double.NaN.Equals(double.NaN)` is `true`. `Equals` is the one that gives a
sane hash-container experience, which is why `EqualityComparer<double>.Default`
uses it and why the generated record equality would have used it too.

Left to you: whether comparing temperatures for exact equality is defensible at
all. It is here, because the readings arrive as identical doubles from one
sensor; write the comment that says so, because the next reader will ask.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the pipeline, not the type. A sensor reports every 200 ms; the store
wants one row per distinct reading; the report wants to know when the reading
was first seen. That is three requirements, and only the second one is about
equality.

Once you phrase it that way, "which fields identify a measurement?" has an
obvious answer, and the timestamp is not in it.

## Hint 2

The wrong fix, seen often: dropping `CapturedAt` from the record and passing it
around separately.

```csharp
public record Measurement(string Sensor, double Celsius);   // timestamp elsewhere
```

Now every caller carries two things that belong together, and the first one to
forget produces an unlabelled reading. Excluding a field from *equality* is not
the same as excluding it from the *type*, and records let you do the first
without the second — that is exactly what writing the two members buys.

## Hint 3

Check your work against the contract rather than the gate: pick three
measurements, at least two of which are equal under your rule, and verify
reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity by hand. Excluding a field cannot break
any of them, which is why this is a safe kind of custom equality — unlike
"equal if within 0.1 degrees", which breaks transitivity and would quietly
corrupt a hash set.

Left to you: whether `Recapture` should refuse a timestamp earlier than the
current one. The gate does not ask; a real ingestion pipeline would have an
opinion.

lessons.title: V3·A2 — Pattern matching end to end
lessons.summary: Patterns stopped being a nicer `if` several versions ago. This sector covers the whole vocabulary — relational, logical, property, positional, list and slice — plus what the compiler builds from them, why `when` guards defeat exhaustiveness, and when a type switch is a missing virtual method.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A2 — Pattern matching end to end

You have used `is` for a null check and a `switch` for a handful of constants.
That is about 20% of the feature. Since C# 9 the pattern language has grown a
grammar of its own — patterns compose, nest, negate and combine — and the
switch *expression* turned "map an input to an output" from a page of
statements into something you can read in one pass.

The reason to learn the whole vocabulary is not brevity. It is that the
compiler understands patterns. It can tell you an arm is unreachable, warn you
that your arms do not cover every input, and compile twelve type tests into a
decision tree that does far fewer than twelve tests. An `if`/`else` chain gets
none of that; it is opaque code the compiler must run exactly as written.

`04_inheritance_polymorphism` told you to let the object decide instead of
asking what kind it is. That advice still stands, and this sector is where you
learn the cases it does not cover: input you do not own, shapes rather than
types, and closed sets that will never grow.

## Concept — the pattern grammar

```csharp
string Describe(object value) => value switch
{
    null                            => "nothing",            // constant
    int n when n < 0                => "negative",           // guard
    int and > 100                   => "big number",         // type + relational
    int or long                     => "an integer",         // logical or
    string { Length: 0 }            => "empty text",         // type + property
    string { Length: > 100 } s      => $"long text ({s.Length})",
    Point (0, 0)                    => "origin",             // positional
    Point { X: var x, Y: var y }    => $"({x}, {y})",         // property + var
    int[] []                        => "no numbers",         // list, empty
    int[] [var only]                => $"just {only}",       // list, one element
    int[] [var first, .., var last] => $"{first}..{last}",   // slice
    not null                        => "something else",     // negation
};
```

Eight kinds of pattern appear there, and every one of them composes with every
other. The pieces worth naming:

- **Constant** — `null`, `42`, `"gold"`, an `enum` member, a `const` field.
- **Type** — `int`, `string s` (declaration pattern, binds a variable).
- **Relational** — `> 100`, `<= 0`. Only against constants, only for types with
  the built-in comparison operators.
- **Logical** — `and`, `or`, `not`, with `not` binding tightest and `or`
  loosest. `is not null` is this.
- **Property** — `{ Length: > 3 }`, nested `{ Address: { City: "Berlin" } }`,
  or the flattened form `{ Address.City: "Berlin" }` from C# 10.
- **Positional** — `(0, 0)`, which calls `Deconstruct`. Records get one free;
  lesson 1 generated it for you.
- **List and slice** — `[]`, `[1, 2, 3]`, `[var head, .. var tail]`. The type
  needs a `Length`/`Count` and an indexer, and a `Slice` method for `..` to
  bind.
- **`var`** — always matches, binds the value. Useful for capturing an
  intermediate in the middle of a bigger pattern.

## Concept — what the compiler does with them

**Arms are tested in order,** top to bottom. Put a broad pattern above a narrow
one and the narrow one can never run; for the cases it can prove, the compiler
raises CS8510 ("the pattern is already handled by a previous arm") as an
*error*, not a warning. Add a `when` guard and it stops being able to prove
anything, so a guarded arm silently shadows nothing and is silently shadowed by
nothing.

**Exhaustiveness is checked, and it usually fails.** A switch expression whose
arms do not provably cover the input type produces CS8509 — a warning — and if
you reach the end at runtime you get `SwitchExpressionException`. For an
`enum`, "provably" is achievable and still not enough (any `int` can be cast to
any enum). For a class hierarchy it is not achievable at all, unless the
hierarchy is closed: an `abstract` base with a private constructor and a fixed
set of nested records is the C# approximation of a discriminated union.

**The lowering is a decision DAG, not a chain of `if`s.** Given several arms
testing the same value, the compiler emits each test once and shares the
branches. Twelve arms distinguishing eight types does not perform twelve type
tests; it performs a tree of them. Constant switches over integers and strings
additionally get jump tables and hash-based dispatch. This is the practical
argument for using the feature rather than hand-rolled `if`s.

## Exercise 1 — from `if`/`else` to a switch expression

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex1.cs`. `HttpFacts.Category(int code)`
is written as an `if`/`else` ladder. Rewrite it as a switch expression using
relational and logical patterns: `< 100` and `>= 600` are `"invalid"`,
`>= 200 and < 300` is `"success"`, and so on.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — property patterns, nested and guarded

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex2.cs`. `Shipping.Quote(Order order)`
prices an order from its total, its destination country and whether the
customer is a member. One arm must use a nested property pattern, one must use

wrong — the compiler will tell you which.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — positional and tuple patterns

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex3.cs`. Two jobs. `Move.Beats` uses a
tuple pattern to switch on two values at once — the whole rock/paper/scissors
table in six arms plus a default. `Traffic.Next` uses a positional pattern over

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — list and slice patterns

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex4.cs`. `Cli.Parse(string[] args)`
classifies a command line: empty, `["help"]`, `["add", var name]`, anything
ending in `"--verbose"`, and a general `[var head, .. var rest]` fallback that
reports the head and the count of the rest.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — exhaustiveness over a closed hierarchy

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex5.cs`. `Payment` is an abstract
record with three nested subtypes and a private constructor, so nothing outside
the file can add a fourth. Write `Fees.For(Payment payment)` as a switch
expression with **no** discard arm, then add the fourth subtype the gate
expects and watch what the compiler says before you handle it.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — `is not null` versus `!= null`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex6.cs`. `Sneaky` overloads
`operator ==` so that comparing anything to `null` returns `false`. Write
