sequence that contains real nulls and `Sneaky` instances.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — a recursive evaluator

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex7.cs`. `Expr` is a small tree of
records — `Num`, `Add`, `Mul`, `Neg`. Write `Evaluator.Eval` as one switch
expression whose arms match on the *children*, so `Add(Num(0), x)` folds to
`x` without evaluating twice, and `Mul(Num(0), _)` is `0` without evaluating
the right side at all.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — a rules engine

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex8.cs`. `RiskRules.Assess(Applicant)`
returns a `(string Rule, int Score)` for the first matching rule, over an
applicant with optional members. Rules are ordered most specific first, several
use guards, and the method must return the *name* of the rule that fired so the
decision is explainable.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex8
```

## Challenge — a routing table

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Challenge.cs`. `Router.Route` takes an
HTTP method and a path already split into segments, and returns a route name
plus any captured parameters. List patterns match the shape, property patterns
match the method, guards handle the numeric-id case, and the fallback is a
404 route.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching challenge
```

## Review

`review1` classifies a window of sensor readings using slice patterns and
relational patterns — the ex4 and ex1 machinery in a domain where the *shape*
of the sequence, not its contents, is the thing being matched.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/v3ca02_pattern_matching

## Notes

**A pattern is a question, an expression is an answer.** The switch
*statement* executes; the switch *expression* evaluates. That difference drives
everything else: an expression must produce a value on every path, which is why
exhaustiveness matters, why every arm must be an expression, and why you cannot
`break`, `return` or `goto` out of one. When the branches need statements, you
still want a statement switch — and modern statement switches accept the same
patterns, so nothing is lost.

**Precedence in the logical patterns.** `not` binds tightest, then `and`, then
`or`. So `not 1 or 2` is `(not 1) or 2`, which is true for everything, and is
almost never what the author meant. When you write a compound pattern with more
than two operands, parenthesise it even though the compiler does not require
it.

**Relational patterns only compare against constants.** `> length` where
`length` is a local does not compile; that is a job for a `when` guard. The
restriction exists so the compiler can reason about coverage — constants form
intervals it can merge, arbitrary expressions do not.

**Property patterns read members, and read them once per test.** A property
pattern like `{ Count: > 0 }` calls the getter. If the getter is expensive or
side-effecting, a pattern that mentions it twice may call it twice. The
compiler shares evaluations where it can prove the value cannot change, which
for a property it generally cannot.

**`when` is not part of the pattern.** It is a boolean expression evaluated
*after* a successful match. That makes it powerful — anything you can write is
allowed — and makes the compiler blind: a guarded arm never counts towards
coverage, and never subsumes a later arm. Two consequences worth internalising:
a switch expression whose only "catch-all" is `_ when x` still warns CS8509,
and reordering guarded arms can change behaviour with no diagnostic at all.

**List patterns need a shape, not an interface.** The type must have a
`Length` or `Count` property and an indexer taking `int`; for a slice pattern to
bind it also needs a `Slice(int, int)` method or a range indexer. Arrays,
`List<T>`, `string`, `Span<T>` and `ImmutableArray<T>` all qualify. A plain
`IEnumerable<T>` does not, and that is deliberate: matching a shape against a
sequence you can only walk once would have to buffer.

**`is null` never calls your operator.** The null constant pattern lowers to a
reference comparison against `null`, so a type with a lying `operator ==`
cannot subvert it. `x != null` does call the operator. This is why the
guidance for library code is `is not null`, and why analysers now nudge you
there.

## ex1

The rewrite is mechanical, and it exists so the relational-and-logical syntax
becomes muscle memory before anything harder arrives. The one thing to notice
is that the arms became *intervals* — `>= 200 and < 300` says the range out
loud, where the `if` ladder said it implicitly by being ordered. The compiler
can merge intervals and tell you when they overlap; it cannot do that for an
`if` ladder.

## ex2

Nested property patterns are the feature that removes the "check for null, then
check the child" dance: `{ Destination: { Country: "GB" } }` matches only when
`Destination` is non-null, because a property pattern implies a null check on
the thing you are reading through.

The unreachable arm is the point. Putting `{ Total: > 0 }` above
`{ Total: > 100 }` makes the second dead, and the compiler says so as an error
because it can prove the intervals overlap. Add a guard to either and the error
disappears while the dead code remains — which is the price of guards, paid in
silence.

## ex3

Tuple patterns give you a genuine truth table. Nine rock/paper/scissors
combinations collapse into three winning arms, one draw arm and a default,
which is both shorter and easier to audit than nested `if`s, because every arm
is a row of the table.

The positional pattern over the record is the same mechanism reaching a
different `Deconstruct`. Note that a positional pattern is matched against the
*generated* deconstructor from lesson 1, so a record you defined without
positional parameters has none and the pattern will not compile.

## ex4

Slice patterns are where list patterns stop being a novelty. `[var head, ..
var rest]` binds two things and asserts a length constraint in one expression,
and `[.., "--verbose"]` says "ends with" without an index calculation, which is
the arithmetic people get wrong.

The `[]` arm matters more than it looks: it is the empty-input case that an
index-based implementation forgets, and it reads as a shape rather than as
`args.Length == 0`.

## ex5

A closed hierarchy — abstract base, private constructor, nested subtypes — is
as near as C# gets to a discriminated union today. Because the compiler can see
every subtype in the file and knows nothing outside can add one, the switch
expression over them is provably exhaustive and the CS8509 warning disappears.

Then you add a case and the warning comes back, in the right file, at the right
moment. That is the payoff for omitting the `_` arm: a discard arm turns "you
forgot a case" into "the default silently handled it", and the bug ships.

## ex6

`is not null` lowers to `ldnull; ceq; not`, roughly — a reference comparison
that no user code can intercept. `!= null` compiles to a call to your
`operator !=` if you defined one. The exercise makes a type that lies, which is
artificial, but the real version is not: a type deriving from
`UnityEngine.Object`, or a mocking proxy, or any class whose author decided
`==` should mean something domain-specific.

The habit worth taking is unconditional. In library code, use `is null` and
`is not null` for null checks. There is no case where the operator version is
better and several where it is worse.

## ex7

Matching on children is the thing that makes pattern matching feel like a
different language. `Add(Num(0), var right) => Eval(right)` is a rewriting rule
written as a pattern, and the `Mul(Num(0), _) => 0` arm is a *short-circuit*
that never touches the right subtree — which you can observe, because the gate
passes an expression whose right side would throw.

Order matters here for correctness, not just speed: the specific folding arms
must sit above the general `Add(var l, var r)` arm, or they never run.

## ex8

Explainability is the real requirement. A rules engine that returns a number
and no reason is unusable in production, because the first question anyone
asks is "why did this application score 40?". Returning the rule name costs one
tuple member and makes the whole thing auditable.

The ordering discipline is the other half: most specific first, guards for
anything that needs a computed comparison, and a final unguarded arm so the
expression is exhaustive without a discard doing the work invisibly.

## challenge

Routing is the canonical shape-matching problem, which is why every web
framework has a routing DSL. Writing one with list patterns shows what those
DSLs are hiding, and the `["orders", var id] when int.TryParse(id, out _)` arm
is where you feel the limits — a guard can validate but cannot *bind* the
parsed value, so you parse twice or restructure. Both answers are defensible;
knowing why you had to choose is the lesson.

## review1

The readings exercise is deliberately about shape rather than type: every
element is a `double`, and the classification comes from the arrangement.
Slice patterns with relational sub-patterns — `[< 0, ..]`, `[.., > 100]` — say
"starts below zero", "ends above a hundred" directly, and the alternative is
index arithmetic that is correct until someone passes an empty array.

# V3·A2 — Pattern matching end to end (archive)

## The vocabulary, with the rule for each

| Pattern | Example | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Constant | `42`, `"gold"`, `null`, `Status.Open` | compile-time constants only |
| Type | `string` | tests the runtime type |
| Declaration | `string s` | type test plus binding |
| `var` | `var x` | always matches, binds |
| Discard | `_` | always matches, binds nothing |
| Relational | `> 100`, `<= 0` | constant right-hand side only |
| Logical | `and`, `or`, `not` | `not` > `and` > `or` |
| Property | `{ Length: > 3 }` | implies a null check on the receiver |
| Extended property | `{ Address.City: "Berlin" }` | C# 10, same as nesting |
| Positional | `(0, 0)` | needs `Deconstruct` |
| List | `[1, 2]`, `[]` | needs `Length`/`Count` and an indexer |
| Slice | `[first, .., last]` | additionally needs `Slice` or a range indexer |

## Worked example — the same logic three ways

```csharp
// 1. if ladder: opaque to the compiler
if (o != null && o.Total > 100 && o.Customer != null && o.Customer.IsMember)
    return 0m;

// 2. patterns in an if: null checks folded in
if (o is { Total: > 100, Customer.IsMember: true })
    return 0m;

// 3. a switch expression: exhaustive, ordered, and one value out
return o switch
{
    { Total: > 100, Customer.IsMember: true } => 0m,
    { Total: > 100 }                          => 4.99m,
    { Customer.IsMember: true }               => 2.99m,
    _                                         => 6.99m,
};
```

Version 2 is not just shorter — `{ Customer.IsMember: true }` cannot throw a
`NullReferenceException`, because a property pattern fails to match rather than
dereferencing null. That single property removes an entire bug class from this
kind of code.

## Worked example — a closed hierarchy

```csharp
public abstract record Payment
{
    private Payment() { }                       // nothing outside can derive

    public sealed record Card(string Last4, decimal Amount) : Payment;
    public sealed record Cash(decimal Amount) : Payment;
    public sealed record Voucher(string Code) : Payment;
}

static decimal Fee(Payment p) => p switch
{
    Payment.Card c    => c.Amount * 0.014m,
    Payment.Cash      => 0m,
    Payment.Voucher   => 0.25m,
};                                              // no discard arm, and no warning
```

The private constructor is what makes the omitted `_` safe: the compiler can
enumerate the subtypes and prove coverage. Add a fourth nested record and this
method stops compiling cleanly, which is exactly the behaviour you want from a
type that gained a case.

## Worked example — guards and what they cost

```csharp
static string Size(int n) => n switch
{
    < 10        => "small",
    _ when Log(n) => "never",     // guard: not analysable
    < 100       => "medium",      // NOT flagged as unreachable, and unreachable
    _           => "large",
};
```

The third arm can never run, and the compiler cannot say so, because it does
not know what `Log` returns. Every guard you add is a piece of the switch the
compiler stops checking for you.

## Worked example — list patterns versus index arithmetic

```csharp
// Index arithmetic: correct, and wrong for empty input.
if (args.Length >= 1 && args[args.Length - 1] == "--verbose") { ... }

// Shape: says the same thing, and the length constraint is part of the pattern.
if (args is [.., "--verbose"]) { ... }
```

The first version has three places to make a mistake — the bound, the
subtraction, and the order of the `&&`. The second has none, because the
pattern only matches arrangements that exist. Extend both to "starts with
`add`, ends with `--force`, and has at least one thing in between":

```csharp
if (args is ["add", _, .., "--force"]) { ... }
```

The index version of that is four conditions and an off-by-one waiting to
happen. This is the practical argument for list patterns: they are not shorter
by much, they are shorter in the parts where bugs live.

## Worked example — patterns over a nullable value type

```csharp
static string Band(decimal? income) => income switch
{
    null            => "unknown",
    < 20_000m       => "low",
    < 80_000m       => "middle",
    _               => "high",
};
```

A relational pattern against a `decimal?` matches only when the value is
present, so the `null` arm is the only place null is handled and the remaining
arms need no `.HasValue` anywhere. Get this wrong the old way — `income <
20_000m` in an `if` — and null quietly evaluates to `false` on both sides of
every comparison, so a missing income silently lands in "high".

## Common mistakes

1. **`_` as a default in a switch over a closed set.** It converts "you forgot
   a case" into silence.
2. **Assuming `or`/`and` bind like `||`/`&&`.** `not a or b` is `(not a) or b`.
3. **Relational pattern against a variable.** Only constants; use a guard.
4. **Expecting a list pattern on `IEnumerable<T>`.** It needs indexed access.
5. **Forgetting that positional patterns need `Deconstruct`.** A non-positional
   record has none.
6. **Using `!= null` on a type with a custom `==`.** Use `is not null`.
7. **Matching on type where a virtual method belongs.** If you own the
   hierarchy and it is open, the switch is a maintenance liability.
8. **Guarding an arm and then reordering arms.** No diagnostic, changed
   behaviour.
9. **Assuming the arms are tested one by one.** They are compiled to a shared
   decision tree, so side effects in property getters are not ordered the way
   the source reads.
10. **Using a switch expression when the branches need statements.** A
    statement switch takes the same patterns.

## In an interview

*"When would you use a switch expression over polymorphism?"* — When you do not
own the types (matching on `JsonElement`, `Exception`, a third-party model),
when the set is genuinely closed and the operations keep growing, or when the
logic belongs to the caller rather than the data. When you own an open
hierarchy and the *types* keep growing, a virtual method wins, because adding a
type then means adding one file rather than editing N switches.

*"How does the compiler execute a switch expression?"* — It builds a decision
DAG over the tests, sharing common subtests, and emits jump tables for dense
integer cases and hashing for string cases. It is not a sequential chain of
`if`s, though the observable semantics are as if the arms were tried in order.

*"What is the difference between `is null` and `== null`?"* — `is null` is a
pattern; it always performs a reference comparison and never calls a
user-defined operator. `== null` calls `operator ==` when one is defined.

## Check yourself

1. Write a pattern matching a string of length between 3 and 10 inclusive.
2. Why does `{ Customer.IsMember: true }` not throw when `Customer` is null?
3. What does the compiler do when two unguarded arms overlap? What if one is
   guarded?
4. Which members must a type have for `[a, .., b]` to compile against it?
5. Give a switch expression that is exhaustive with no `_` arm, and explain
   what makes it provable.
6. What exception does a switch expression throw when nothing matches?
7. Rewrite `not 1 or 2` with parentheses showing the actual precedence.
8. Why can a relational pattern not use a local variable?
9. When does a `when` guard run relative to the pattern test?
10. What is the type of `x` in `case var x when x is not null:`?
11. Show two ways to bind the last element of an array in a pattern.
12. Why is a list pattern unavailable on `IEnumerable<T>`?
13. Name a case where a type switch is better design than a virtual method.

# Long read — the pattern language, and what it compiles to

## Five versions of growth

C# 7 (2017) introduced patterns as a small addition to `is` and `switch`: type
patterns with a binding, constant patterns, and `when` clauses on `case`
labels. The motivation was pragmatic — the "cast twice" idiom, where you write
`if (o is Foo) { var f = (Foo)o; ... }` and pay for two type tests — and the
feature was scoped tightly.

C# 8 (2019) added the switch *expression*, property patterns, positional
patterns and the discard. This is the release where the feature became a way of
writing programs rather than a way of shortening casts, and it borrowed heavily
from F#, where the same constructs had been carrying pipelines for a decade.

C# 9 (2020) filled in the grammar: relational patterns, `and`/`or`/`not`, and
type patterns without a designation (`case Payment.Cash:` with no variable).
C# 10 added extended property patterns (`{ A.B.C: 1 }`), which are pure
syntactic sugar for nesting. C# 11 (2022) added list and slice patterns.

The through-line is that patterns became *compositional*. Each release added
operators over patterns rather than special cases, which is why the vocabulary
is now small enough to memorise and large enough to express most classification
logic.

## What the compiler builds

A switch expression is not lowered to a chain of tests in source order. Roslyn
builds a *decision DAG*: a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are individual
tests (is it null? is it a `Card`? is `Length` greater than 3?) and whose edges
are the true/false outcomes. Common tests are shared, so a switch with ten arms
that all begin `string s` performs one type test, not ten.

That representation is also what powers the diagnostics. Subsumption (CS8510)
is the compiler noticing that an arm's node is unreachable in the DAG.
Exhaustiveness (CS8509) is it noticing that some path reaches the end without
producing a value. Both are graph properties, which is why adding a `when`
guard destroys them: a guard is an opaque edge whose outcome the graph cannot
predict, so every path through it must be assumed to fail.

For constant patterns over integers the DAG's leaves get the classic switch
optimisations: a dense set of cases becomes a jump table (one bounds check and
an indirect branch), a sparse set becomes a binary search. For `string` cases,
Roslyn emits a computed hash of the input and switches on that, falling back to
a string comparison only within a bucket. Both of these predate patterns — they
are the same optimisations C# 1 applied to `switch` — but they still apply
underneath the newer syntax.

List patterns lower to a length check plus indexer calls, and slice patterns to
a length check plus a `Slice` call or a range indexer. There is no hidden
enumeration and no allocation: `[var first, .., var last]` on an `int[]` is a
length comparison and two array loads.

## Performance

The honest summary is that pattern matching costs what the tests cost, and the
compiler removes the redundancy you would have left in by hand. A switch
expression over types is a sequence of `isinst` instructions arranged in a
tree; each is a cheap runtime type check against a method table pointer.

Two things do cost. First, property patterns call getters, and a getter that
computes is a getter that computes once per test that mentions it. Second,
patterns on interfaces are more expensive than patterns on classes, because
interface type tests can require a walk of the interface map rather than a
single pointer comparison. Neither matters outside a hot loop, and in a hot
loop the answer is usually to hoist the classification out entirely.

The `SwitchExpressionException` path is worth one sentence: it is thrown by a
generated `throw` at the end of the DAG, so a non-exhaustive switch costs
nothing extra until it fails.

## The two diagnostics, and how to keep them

CS8510 and CS8509 are the reason this feature is worth more than its syntax,
and both are fragile in the same way.

CS8510 — "the pattern is unreachable" — is an *error*, not a warning, and it
fires when the compiler can prove an arm's tests are already satisfied by an
earlier arm. It catches the classic ordering inversion where a broad interval
sits above a narrow one. It cannot fire once either arm carries a guard,
because a guard is an opaque edge in the DAG.

CS8509 — "the switch expression does not handle all possible values" — is a
warning, and the fix people reach for is a discard arm, which is precisely the
wrong fix when the input set is closed. The right response is to ask *why* the
compiler cannot prove coverage. Three answers come up: the type is an open
hierarchy (close it, or accept the discard); the input is a nullable reference
(handle null explicitly); the arms are all guarded (add one unguarded arm that
is genuinely the fallback).

The discipline that follows is short. Treat CS8509 as a design question rather
than a diagnostic to silence, and treat every `when` you write as a small
withdrawal from the compiler's ability to check your work. A switch with no
guards at all is fully analysed; one with a guard on every arm is an `if`
ladder with better formatting.

## Discriminated unions, and the gap

Every example in this sector that uses a closed hierarchy is working around a
missing feature. F# has discriminated unions; C# does not, and the standard
approximation — abstract record, private constructor, nested sealed records — is
verbose and gives up exhaustiveness the moment the hierarchy leaves one file.

The C# language design team has an active proposal for unions; until it ships,
the pattern to know is the one in ex5, and the discipline to keep is: **omit the
discard arm on a closed set**. That single choice is what converts "someone
added a case" from a runtime surprise into a build failure.

## When not to use it

**When you own an open hierarchy.** If new types keep arriving and the set of
operations is stable, a virtual method is the correct tool, because adding a
type touches one file. A switch on type means every new type is a hunt for
switches to update, and the compiler helps you with none of them. This is the
open/closed principle stated in terms of what the compiler can check.

**When the switch is a missing domain concept.** Five arms that all compute a
discount are a `Discount` policy that has not been written yet. The tell is a
switch that appears in more than one place with the same arms.

**When the branches want statements.** A switch expression forces every arm to
be a single expression, which encourages people to cram side effects into
expression bodies. Use a switch statement; it takes every pattern in this
sector.

**When a guard would do all the work.** `_ when a && b` arms in sequence are an
`if`/`else` chain wearing a costume, with worse formatting and no diagnostics.

## Further reading

- [Patterns (C# reference)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/patterns)
  — the normative grammar, including the exact requirements for list and slice
  patterns.
- [`switch` expression](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/switch-expression)
  — arm ordering, exhaustiveness and `SwitchExpressionException`.
- [Pattern matching — C# design notes](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/main/proposals/csharp-9.0/patterns3.md)
  — the C# 9 proposal, where subsumption and the decision DAG are specified.
- [Tutorial: use pattern matching to build type-driven algorithms](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/tutorials/pattern-matching)
  — Microsoft's worked example of the "types you do not own" case.
- [Discriminated unions proposal](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/main/proposals/TypeUnions.md)
  — what the closed-hierarchy workaround is standing in for.

## Exercise 1 — from `if`/`else` to a switch expression

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex1.cs`.

```csharp
public static class HttpFacts
{
    public static string Category(int code);
    public static bool IsRetryable(int code);
}
```

`Category` maps a status code to one word, using relational and logical
patterns only — no `if`, no comparison operators, no `when`:

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `99`, `600`, `-1` | `"invalid"` |
| `100`..`199` | `"informational"` |
| `200`..`299` | `"success"` |
| `300`..`399` | `"redirect"` |
| `400`..`499` | `"client error"` |
| `500`..`599` | `"server error"` |

`IsRetryable` is `true` for exactly `408`, `429`, and anything in `500..599`
except `501`. Write it as a single switch expression using `or` and `and not`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A relational pattern compares the switched value against a constant, so you
never repeat the variable name. `code switch { < 100 => ... }` already knows
what it is comparing.

Because the arms are tried in order, an ordered ladder needs only one bound per
arm — but that is the version that reads like the `if` chain you are replacing.
Writing both bounds says the interval out loud and lets the compiler check the
intervals for overlaps. Prefer the second.

## Hint 2

Combining a lower and an upper bound:

```csharp
string Band(int age) => age switch
{
    < 0            => "impossible",
    >= 0 and < 18  => "minor",
    >= 18 and < 65 => "adult",
    _              => "senior",
};
```

Note the final `_`: without it the compiler cannot prove every `int` is covered
and will warn. With explicit intervals you will need it even though you know
the ranges are complete.

## Hint 3

`IsRetryable` wants a set union with a hole in it. The two shapes available
are `408 or 429 or (>= 500 and < 600 and not 501)` in one arm returning `true`
with a `_ => false`, or one arm per group.

Left to you: which reads better to someone auditing retry policy at 3am. The
one-arm version is compact; the multi-arm version puts each rule on its own
line where a reviewer can comment on it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look at what the `if` ladder in the file is hiding. Each branch tests only an
upper bound, because the earlier branches already excluded everything below.
That is correct and it is invisible: delete or reorder one line and the
remaining ones silently change meaning.

Your rewrite should make each arm independently true — a reader should be able
to check one line without reading the others.

## Hint 2

The `-1` case is the one that catches people. A naive rewrite tests `< 100` for
"informational", so `-1` becomes informational instead of invalid. Enumerate
your test inputs before you write: `-1`, `99`, `100`, `199`, `200`, `599`,
`600`. Six of those are boundaries, and boundaries are where classification
code goes wrong.

## Hint 3

For `IsRetryable`, work from the semantics rather than the numbers. 408 is
"request timeout", 429 is "too many requests", 5xx is "the server had a
problem" — except 501, "not implemented", which will still not be implemented
if you ask again. Retrying anything else is either useless or actively harmful.

Left to you: whether to name the constants. `429` is famous enough to leave
bare; a project with more of these would put them in a `static class Status`.

## Exercise 2 — property patterns, nested and guarded

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex2.cs`.

```csharp
public record Customer(string Name, bool IsMember, int OrdersThisYear);
public record Address(string Country, string PostCode);
public record Order(decimal Total, Address? Destination, Customer? Customer);

public static class Shipping
{
    public static decimal Quote(Order order);
}
```

Rules, in the order they must be evaluated:

1. destination is `null` -> `-1m` (cannot quote)
2. total over 100 **and** the customer is a member -> `0m`
3. destination country is `"GB"` **and** the customer has placed more than 12
   orders this year -> `0m` (a guard is required here: the comparison is
   against a value the rules can change, so it arrives as the `frequentAt`
   parameter of a private constant)
4. destination country is `"GB"` -> `4.99m`
5. total over 100 -> `7.99m`
6. anything else -> `12.99m`

Worked examples:

- `new Order(150m, new Address("DE", "10115"), new Customer("ada", true, 1))` -> `0m`
- `new Order(20m, new Address("GB", "SW1A"), new Customer("bo", false, 30))` -> `0m`
- `new Order(20m, new Address("GB", "SW1A"), new Customer("bo", false, 3))` -> `4.99m`
- `new Order(150m, null, null)` -> `-1m`
- `new Order(150m, new Address("FR", "75001"), null)` -> `7.99m`

At least one arm must use a nested property pattern reaching through
`Destination` without a null check of your own. The gate also passes an order
whose `Customer` is `null` and whose total is over 100, which is where a naive
`order.Customer.IsMember` would throw.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A property pattern implies a null test on whatever it reads through. That is
the feature doing the defensive work for you: `{ Customer.IsMember: true }`
fails to match a null customer rather than dereferencing it.

So rule 2 does not need a null check, and rule 1 is not there to protect the
later rules — it is there because a missing destination is a distinct answer.

## Hint 2

Nested and flattened forms are the same thing:

```csharp
order is { Destination: { Country: "GB" } }   // nested
order is { Destination.Country: "GB" }        // extended, C# 10 and later
```

Use the flattened form when you are testing one leaf and the nested form when
you are testing several members of the same child, which keeps the child's name
from repeating.

## Hint 3

Rule 3 needs a guard because it compares against a value that is not a
compile-time constant from the pattern's point of view. The shape is:

```csharp
{ Destination.Country: "GB", Customer: { OrdersThisYear: var orders } }
    when orders > FrequentThreshold => 0m,
```

Left to you: whether to bind with `var orders` and guard, or to bind the whole
customer and guard on a property. The first is narrower; the second reads
better when the guard needs two members.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the arms in the wrong order first, on purpose. Put rule 4 (`"GB"` ->
4.99) above rule 3 (`"GB"` plus frequent -> 0) and compile.

You will get no error, because rule 3 is guarded and the compiler stops
reasoning about guarded arms. You will get a wrong answer for the frequent GB
customer. That silence is the single most important thing to learn about
guards, and it is cheaper to learn it here than in a pricing bug.

## Hint 2

Now try the unguarded version of the same mistake: put `{ Total: > 0 }` above
`{ Total: > 100 }`. This time the compiler refuses:

```
error CS8510: The pattern is unreachable. It has already been handled by a
previous arm of the switch expression.
```

Two arms, one diagnostic, and the difference between them is a `when`. That
comparison is the exercise.

## Hint 3

Check the null cases deliberately rather than trusting the pattern. Three
orders will exercise them: destination null, customer null with a high total,
and both null. A single `order.Customer.IsMember` anywhere in your solution
turns the second of those into a `NullReferenceException`.

Left to you: whether `-1m` is a good way to say "cannot quote". It is what the
gate wants; in real code you would reach for `decimal?` or a result type, and
saying so in a comment is not wasted.

## Exercise 3 — positional and tuple patterns

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex3.cs`. Two independent jobs.

**Tuple pattern.** Implement

```csharp
public static class Rules
{
    public static string Beats(Move left, Move right);
}
```

`Move` is an enum with `Rock`, `Paper`, `Scissors`. Return `"left"`, `"right"`
or `"draw"`. Write it as one switch expression over the tuple `(left, right)` —
three winning arms, one draw arm, one fallback. No `if`, no nested switch.

- `Beats(Move.Rock, Move.Scissors)` -> `"left"`
- `Beats(Move.Rock, Move.Paper)` -> `"right"`
- `Beats(Move.Paper, Move.Paper)` -> `"draw"`

**Positional pattern.** `Light` is
`record Light(string Colour, int SecondsLeft)`. Implement

```csharp
public static Light Next(Light light);
```

using positional patterns against the record's generated `Deconstruct`:

- `("green", 0)` -> `("amber", 4)`
- `("amber", 0)` -> `("red", 30)`
- `("red", 0)` -> `("green", 25)`
- any light with `SecondsLeft > 0` -> same colour, one second fewer
- any other colour at zero -> `("red", 30)` (fail safe)


exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A tuple pattern is a positional pattern over a `ValueTuple`, and you get it for
free because tuples deconstruct. So `(left, right) switch { (Move.Rock,
Move.Scissors) => ... }` needs no supporting code at all.

Nine combinations exist. Three of them are wins for the left player, three are
draws, three are wins for the right. You need at most five arms — think about
which of those three groups is cheapest to describe.

## Hint 2

Two arms doing a lot of work:

```csharp
(var a, var b) when a == b => "draw",
```

and, for the state machine, a positional pattern with a relational sub-pattern:

```csharp
Light (var colour, > 0) => light with { SecondsLeft = light.SecondsLeft - 1 },
```

Positional sub-patterns are just patterns, so a relational one is allowed
wherever a constant would be.

## Hint 3

For `Beats`, put the draw arm first or last — first if you write it as
`(var a, var b) when a == b`, last if you enumerate the three drawing pairs.
Then three winning arms and a fallback.

For `Next`, the countdown arm must sit **above** the three colour-change arms,
or a green light with 12 seconds left will turn amber immediately. Left to you:
whether the fallback resets to red at 30 or preserves the seconds. The gate
wants a fresh red; a real controller would argue for the same.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Draw the truth table on paper before writing any code. Three rows by three
columns, each cell holding "left", "right" or "draw". Now look at it: the
diagonal is draws, and the three "left" cells are the classic cycle — rock beats
scissors, scissors beats paper, paper beats rock.

Every arm you write should correspond to something you can point at in that
table. If you cannot point at it, the arm is wrong.

## Hint 2

The state machine has a trap that the table does not. Consider what the
following pair of arms does to `("green", 12)`:

```csharp
("green", _) => new Light("amber", 4),
(var colour, > 0) => light with { SecondsLeft = light.SecondsLeft - 1 },
```

The first arm matches any green light regardless of the countdown, so the
second is dead for green. The lights change instantly and the countdown is
decoration. Order is not a stylistic choice here; it is the specification.

## Hint 3

Check that `Next` never returns the receiver. Every arm produces a new `Light`,
either with `with` or with a constructor, because the record is immutable and
"advance the light" means "produce the next state".

Left to you: whether `Next` should be a method on `Light` instead of a static
helper. It would read better as `light.Next()`; the gate's signature is static
so that the positional pattern has an obvious subject.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — list and slice patterns

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex4.cs`.

```csharp
public static class Cli
{
    public static string Parse(string[] args);
}
```

Classify a command line, in this order:

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `[]` | `"usage"` |
| `["help"]` | `"help"` |
| `["add", "widget"]` | `"add widget"` |
| `["remove", "widget", "--force"]` | `"remove widget (forced)"` |
| anything whose **last** element is `"--verbose"` | `"verbose: <n> args"` where `n` is the total length |
| `["ship", "a", "b", "c"]` | `"ship + 3 more"` |

The last row is the general fallback: report the first element and how many
elements follow it.

Constraints: no `args.Length` comparisons, no indexing with `[0]` or `[^1]`,
and no `if`. Every case is a list or slice pattern. The `"--verbose"` rule must
use a slice pattern, and the general fallback must bind both the head and the
rest.

No discard arm is needed, and adding one is an error. Work out why before you
reach for it: which two arms, between them, cover every possible length?

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A list pattern describes a shape. `[]` is "no elements", `["help"]` is "exactly
one element, equal to help", `[_, _]` is "exactly two of anything". The length
constraint is part of the pattern, which is why you never write a `Length`
comparison next to one.

The slice `..` means "zero or more elements here", and it may appear at most
once in a pattern. That single restriction is what makes matching decidable
with one length check and a couple of index reads.

## Hint 2

Binding through a slice:

```csharp
string Describe(int[] values) => values switch
{
    [var only]                 => $"one: {only}",
    [var first, .. var middle] => $"{first} then {middle.Length}",
    _                          => "impossible",
};
```

`.. var middle` binds the sliced portion as its own array, so `middle.Length`
is available. Writing plain `..` discards it, which is cheaper when you do not
need it — the slice is not materialised at all.

## Hint 3

"Ends with `--verbose`" is `[.., "--verbose"]`, and it needs the total length,
so bind the whole thing: a `var` designation after a list pattern is allowed —
`[.., "--verbose"] and var all` — or capture the slice and add one.

Order matters twice here. `["help"]` must precede any one-element wildcard, and
the `--verbose` arm must precede the general fallback, because a verbose
command line also has a head and a tail.

Left to you: whether `["add", var name]` should also accept extra arguments.
The table says exactly two; a real CLI would probably disagree.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by writing the six inputs from the table as literal arrays in a scratch
file, then, for each one, say which patterns it matches — not which arm wins,
but every pattern it satisfies. You will find that `["ship", "a", "b", "c"]`
matches four of your six patterns, and the arm that wins is decided purely by
position.

Classification code is mostly the discipline of ordering overlapping rules.
Patterns make the overlaps visible; they do not remove them.

## Hint 2

There is a wrong version worth ruling out. This compiles and is subtly
different:

```csharp
[_, .., "--verbose"] => ...,   // at least two elements
[.., "--verbose"]    => ...,   // at least one element
```

The first will not match `["--verbose"]` on its own, because it demands an
element before the slice. Decide which you want; the gate passes the
single-element case.

## Hint 3

Watch the interaction between the `"remove"` arm and the `--verbose` arm. A
command line of `["remove", "widget", "--verbose"]` matches both a
three-element list pattern and "ends with verbose". Which one should win is a
product decision, and the table's ordering answers it — read the table again
rather than guessing.

Left to you: whether an unrecognised single argument (`["frobnicate"]`) should
be an error rather than falling into the general arm. The gate only requires
the general arm to describe it.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The habit this exercise attacks is the reflexive `_ => throw new ...` at the
bottom of every switch. It feels defensive and it is the opposite: it converts
a compile-time error into a runtime one, in a codebase where the compiler was
willing to do the work.

You only get to drop the discard when the compiler can enumerate the subtypes.
Look at what makes that true here, because it is one line and it is easy to
delete by accident.

## Hint 2

Nested types are referred to through the containing type:

```csharp
static string Name(Payment p) => p switch
{
    Payment.Card    => "card",
    Payment.Cash    => "cash",
    Payment.Voucher => "voucher",
    Payment.BankTransfer => "transfer",
};
```

Note the type patterns have no variable designation, because these arms need no
data. Add one — `Payment.Card c` — only where you use it.

## Hint 3

For the card fee, `Math.Round(amount * 0.014m, 2, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero)`
is the shape. Rounding money to the cent with bankers' rounding, which is the
`Math.Round` default, is the wrong choice here — 0.125 becomes 0.12 rather than
0.13, and finance teams notice.

Left to you: whether to bind with a property pattern (`Payment.Card { Amount:
var amount }`) or a declaration pattern (`Payment.Card card`). The first binds
only what you need; the second reads better when you need two members.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Do step 1 of the prompt before you write anything else. Comment out one arm,
build, and read the whole message rather than the squiggle:

```
warning CS8509: The switch expression does not handle all possible values of
type 'Payment' (it is not exhaustive). For example, the pattern
'Payment.BankTransfer' is not covered.
```

It named the missing case. That is only possible because the hierarchy is
closed, and it is the entire argument for closing hierarchies.

## Hint 2

Now try the experiment that shows what closure buys. Temporarily make the
`Payment` constructor `protected` instead of `private` and rebuild with all four
arms present. The warning appears again, with different wording, because a type
in another assembly could now derive from `Payment` and the compiler can no
longer promise anything.

Change it back. The one-word difference between `private` and `protected` is the
difference between a checked switch and an unchecked one.

## Hint 3

Think about what `SwitchExpressionException` means as a design signal. It is
thrown from a generated `throw` at the end of the decision tree — the case the
compiler warned you about, arriving at runtime, in production, with a message
that names a type rather than a business rule.

Left to you: whether you would still add a discard arm for defence in depth in
a codebase where the hierarchy is closed but a colleague might open it. There is
a real argument both ways; write down which one you find persuasive.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two completely different mechanisms with nearly identical syntax.
One is an operator call — ordinary method dispatch, resolved by the compiler
from the operand types, overridable by any type author. The other is a pattern,
lowered to a comparison against the null reference, with no call site anyone
can intervene in.

Only one of them is safe in library code, and it is the one that cannot be
overridden.

## Hint 2

You can see the difference in the generated code. Roughly:

```csharp
bool a = x != null;          // call Sneaky.op_Inequality(x, null)
bool b = x is not null;      // ldarg; ldnull; ceq; ldc.i4.0; ceq
```

The second has no `call` instruction in it at all. That is why a type cannot
subvert it, and why analysers such as CA2225 and the Roslyn nullability
analysis reason about `is null` but not about `!= null` on a type with custom
operators.

## Hint 3

`IsMissing` is one expression using a pattern. The generic constraint
`where T : class` is what allows the null test at all — an unconstrained `T`
could be an `int`, and lesson 3 covers what that would mean.

`CountMissing` is a single LINQ `Count` with a predicate, or a `foreach` with a
counter. Left to you: whether to write it as `values.Count(v => v is null)` or
a loop. The LINQ version reads better; lesson 5 has opinions about when that
stops being true.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Answer the prompt's question first, on paper. Given `Sneaky? s = null;`:

- `s != null` calls `operator !=(null, null)`, which returns the hard-coded
  `true`. So the code believes a null reference is not null.
- `s is not null` compares the reference to null and returns `false`.

The operator is wrong. It is *allowed* to be wrong, because C# lets a type
define what `==` means, and nothing constrains that definition to agree with
reference identity.

## Hint 2

`Sneaky` is artificial; the real cases are not. Three you will meet:

- Unity's `UnityEngine.Object` overloads `==` so a destroyed native object
  compares equal to null while the managed reference is very much alive.
- Mocking and proxy frameworks generate types whose equality is delegated
  somewhere unexpected.
- Any value-semantics type where the author overloaded `==` and forgot to
  special-case a null operand, which throws instead of returning `false`.

In all three, `is null` behaves and `== null` does not.

## Hint 3

Consider what happens if you write `IsMissing` as `value == null`. With
`T : class` and an unconstrained generic, the compiler resolves `==` for `T`
as a *reference* comparison — generics do not dispatch to a type's operators —
so it would actually be correct here, by accident, for the wrong reason.

That accident is worth understanding and worth not relying on: change the
method to take `Sneaky?` instead of `T?` and the same source text silently
starts calling the lying operator. Left to you: whether you find that a
convincing argument for `is null` everywhere. It is the one that convinced the
BCL team.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A pattern can look inside a child, and then inside that child's children, as
deeply as you like. `Neg(Neg(var x))` is one pattern, not two matches, and it
binds the grandchild directly.

Once you accept that, the simplification rules stop being code and become a
list of shapes. Each rule is one arm, and the arm reads almost exactly like the
mathematical identity it encodes.

## Hint 2

Positional patterns nest:

```csharp
static string Describe(Expr e) => e switch
{
    Expr.Add(Expr.Num(0), var other) => $"zero plus {Describe(other)}",
    Expr.Add(var l, var r)           => $"{Describe(l)} plus {Describe(r)}",
    _                                => "something",
};
```

The first arm reaches two levels down and binds one thing. The second is the
general case and must sit below it, or the specific rule never fires.

## Hint 3

Short-circuiting is not something you write; it is something the arm's *shape*
gives you. `Expr.Mul(Expr.Num(0), _)` matches without binding the right side,
and the arm's body is the constant `0`, so nothing recurses. The discard is
doing the work.

For `EvalCount`, increment a static field at the top of `Eval` — which means
`Eval` cannot be a pure expression-bodied method any more. Left to you: whether
the counter lives in a `[ThreadStatic]` field. It matters for a test runner
executing in parallel, and the gate is single-threaded.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The counter is the specification, not decoration. Before writing an arm, ask:
"how many times should `Eval` be entered for this input?" Write the numbers
down for the three worked examples in the prompt. `Neg(Neg(Num(7)))` is the
interesting one — the naive implementation enters four times, the
double-negation rule makes it two.

If your implementation is correct but the counts are wrong, your rules are
firing in the wrong order.

## Hint 2

There is a wrong way to short-circuit that looks right:

```csharp
Expr.Mul(var l, var r) when Eval(l) == 0 => 0,
```

This *is* zero when the left side is zero, and it evaluates the left side to
find out, then evaluates it again in the general arm for other inputs — and
guards run after the pattern matched, so you have moved work into a place where
it may be repeated. Match on the shape (`Expr.Num(0)`) rather than on a
computed value, and the work disappears rather than moving.

## Hint 3

Order the arms in three groups and keep the groups visually separate: the
absorbing rules (times zero), the identity rules (plus zero, times one), the
involution rule (double negation), then the general cases. A reader should be
able to delete the first three groups and still have a correct — merely
slower — evaluator.

Left to you: whether to add `Add(Num(a), Num(b)) => a + b` as a constant-folding
arm. It is not required, it is correct, and it changes the counts, so check the
gate's expectations before you commit to it.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — a rules engine

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Ex8.cs`.

```csharp
public record Applicant(
    int Age,
    decimal? AnnualIncome,
    string? Employer,
    int MissedPayments,
    string Country);

public static class RiskRules
{
    public static (string Rule, int Score) Assess(Applicant applicant);
}
```

Rules, most specific first. The first match wins, and the returned `Rule` is
the name in the left column so the decision is explainable:

| Rule | Condition | Score |
|---|---|---|
| `"underage"` | age below 18 | `0` |
| `"unverified"` | income is null **or** employer is null | `20` |
| `"delinquent"` | three or more missed payments | `10` |
| `"watchlist"` | one or two missed payments and income below 20000 | `30` |
| `"prime"` | income at or above 80000, no missed payments, employer known | `95` |
| `"foreign-prime"` | income at or above 80000 and country is not `"GB"` | `70` |
| `"standard"` | anything else | `50` |

Worked examples:

- `new Applicant(17, 200_000m, "Acme", 0, "GB")` -> `("underage", 0)`
- `new Applicant(30, null, "Acme", 0, "GB")` -> `("unverified", 20)`
- `new Applicant(30, 15_000m, "Acme", 1, "GB")` -> `("watchlist", 30)`
- `new Applicant(30, 90_000m, "Acme", 0, "GB")` -> `("prime", 95)`
- `new Applicant(30, 90_000m, "Acme", 0, "DE")` -> `("foreign-prime", 70)`
- `new Applicant(30, 30_000m, "Acme", 0, "GB")` -> `("standard", 50)`

Constraints: one switch expression, no `if`, no early returns. `decimal?`
income means at least one arm needs a nullable-aware pattern, and at least two
arms need guards because the thresholds live in `const` fields.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate problems live in this exercise, and it helps to solve them one at
a time.

The first is *ordering*: the rules overlap heavily — a 17-year-old with no
employer matches three of them — and the table's order is the specification.
Transcribe the table top to bottom and resist the urge to rearrange.

The second is *nullability*: `AnnualIncome` is `decimal?`, and a relational
pattern on a nullable value type matches only when it has a value.

## Hint 2

Patterns over a nullable value type:

```csharp
{ AnnualIncome: null }            // no value at all
{ AnnualIncome: > 1000m }         // has a value, and it is over 1000
{ AnnualIncome: not null and var income } when income > Threshold
```

The middle one is the useful surprise: a relational pattern against `decimal?`
does *not* match null, so you never need a separate null check beside it.

## Hint 3

The name-plus-score return means every arm produces a tuple:
`=> ("watchlist", 30)`. That is what turns the switch into an audit trail —
the caller can log the rule name next to the score, and a disputed decision has
an answer.

The `"prime"` versus `"foreign-prime"` pair is the ordering trap: they overlap
on income, and only the country separates them. Left to you: whether
`"foreign-prime"` should also require no missed payments. The table does not say
so; decide whether that is an omission or a rule, and comment on it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the test matrix before the code. Take the six worked examples and, for
each, list *every* rule whose condition it satisfies. The 30-year-old on 90,000
in Germany satisfies both `"prime"` and `"foreign-prime"` — no, look again:
`"prime"` requires no missed payments and a known employer, which it has. Both
match. Order decides.

Any rules engine you write for real will have this property, and the reason
they end up unmaintainable is that nobody wrote the matrix down.

## Hint 2

Consider what the alternative implementation costs. As an `if` ladder:

```csharp
if (applicant.Age < 18) return ("underage", 0);
if (applicant.AnnualIncome is null || applicant.Employer is null) return ("unverified", 20);
// ...
```

It works. It is also seven return statements the compiler will not check
against each other, in a method where a stray `else` or an early `return`
changes the semantics silently. A switch expression is one expression: there is
nowhere to put a stray statement, and every arm must produce the same type.

## Hint 3

Watch the `"delinquent"` and `"watchlist"` pair. Three or more missed payments
is delinquent regardless of income; one or two is only a watchlist entry when
income is low. Put watchlist above delinquent and a customer with four missed
payments and a low income gets the *softer* score, which is exactly the kind of
inversion that survives review because the individual lines both look right.

Left to you: whether the score for `"unverified"` should really be lower than
`"standard"`. It is what the table says. Whether that is what the business
meant is a question worth asking out loud.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a routing table

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Challenge.cs`.

```csharp
public readonly record struct Route(string Name, string? Parameter);

public static class Router
{
    public static Route Match(string method, string[] segments);
}
```

`segments` is a URL path already split on `/` with empty entries removed, so
`/orders/42/items` arrives as `["orders", "42", "items"]`. Match the following
table, in order:

| method | segments | result |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `[]` | `("home", null)` |
| `GET` | `["health"]` | `("health", null)` |
| `GET` | `["orders"]` | `("orders.index", null)` |
| `POST` | `["orders"]` | `("orders.create", null)` |
| `GET` | `["orders", <all digits>]` | `("orders.show", "<that id>")` |
| `GET` | `["orders", <not digits>]` | `("orders.by-reference", "<that value>")` |
| `DELETE` | `["orders", <all digits>]` | `("orders.destroy", "<that id>")` |
| `GET` | `["orders", <all digits>, "items"]` | `("orders.items", "<that id>")` |
| any | anything ending in `"debug"` | `("debug", "<the method>")` |
| any | anything else | `("not-found", null)` |

Worked examples:

- `Match("GET", ["orders", "42"])` -> `("orders.show", "42")`
- `Match("GET", ["orders", "ABC-9"])` -> `("orders.by-reference", "ABC-9")`
- `Match("GET", ["orders", "42", "items"])` -> `("orders.items", "42")`
- `Match("PATCH", ["anything", "debug"])` -> `("debug", "PATCH")`
- `Match("PUT", ["orders"])` -> `("not-found", null)`

Requirements: one switch expression over the tuple `(method, segments)`, list
patterns for the shapes, and a guard for the "all digits" test. Method matching
is case-sensitive.

The guard is where the design tension lives: a guard can test the segment but
cannot bind anything new, so you either validate in the guard and use the raw
string, or restructure. Pick one and say why in a comment.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Switch on the pair, not on the method and then the path. `(method, segments)
switch { ("GET", []) => ..., }` puts the whole route on one line, which is
what makes the table auditable — a reviewer can read each arm against the
specification row without holding state in their head.

The debug rule is the one that does not fit the tuple neatly, because it
ignores the method for matching and then reports it. Bind it.

## Hint 2

A guard beside a list pattern:

```csharp
("GET", ["orders", var id]) when id.All(char.IsAsciiDigit) =>
    new Route("orders.show", id),
```

`char.IsAsciiDigit` (.NET 7 and later) is the right predicate here rather than
`char.IsDigit`, which accepts every Unicode decimal digit — including Arabic-
Indic and Devanagari digits, which `int.Parse` will happily accept and your
database key will not.

## Hint 3

The by-reference arm must sit directly below the numeric one and needs no guard
at all: anything that reached it is a two-segment orders path that failed the
digit test. That is arm ordering doing work that a condition would otherwise
have to repeat as a negation.

Left to you: whether to write a small `private static bool IsId(string s)`
helper. Three arms need the same test, and a named helper makes the guards read
like the table.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the failure mode this exercise is really about. Routing tables go
wrong when two rules overlap and the more general one is written first —
`["orders", var anything]` above `["orders", var id] when IsId(id)` makes the
numeric route dead, and no compiler diagnostic appears because the second arm
is guarded.

Write the overlapping pairs down first: there are three. Then order them.

## Hint 2

The prompt mentions a design tension; here it is concretely. You want the id as
an `int` for the handler, but a guard cannot introduce a binding:

```csharp
("GET", ["orders", var id]) when int.TryParse(id, out int parsed) =>
    new Route("orders.show", parsed.ToString()),   // parsed IS in scope here
```

That actually works — an `out` variable declared in a guard is in scope in the
arm — and it is one of the less-known corners of the language. It also parses
and re-formats, which changes `"007"` into `"7"`. The gate wants the original
text, so this is a trap dressed as a shortcut.

## Hint 3

Test the empty path deliberately. `Match("GET", [])` must be `("home", null)`,
and a `[.., "debug"]` arm placed too high would not match it — but a `[..]`
arm would match everything including it. The empty case is where shape-matching
code is usually wrong, and a list pattern makes it a visible arm rather than an
implicit consequence.

Left to you: whether `Route.Parameter` should be `string?` at all, or whether
two route types would model this better. The nullable member is the pragmatic
answer; lesson 4 argues about the honest one.

exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — classifying a window of readings

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA02_PatternMatching/Review1.cs`.

```csharp
public static class Readings
{
    public static string Classify(double[] window);
}
```

Every element is a temperature. The classification comes from the *shape* of
the window, not from the type of anything in it. Rules, in order:

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `[]` | `"no data"` |
| exactly one reading | `"single: <value>"` formatted with one decimal place, invariant culture |
| first reading below `-40` | `"cold start"` |
| last reading above `100` | `"overheating"` |
| exactly two readings, the second at least 20 higher than the first | `"spike"` |
| first and last equal, three or more readings | `"stable"` |
| anything else | `"n readings"` where n is the length |

Worked examples:

- `Classify([])` -> `"no data"`
- `Classify([21.5])` -> `"single: 21.5"`
- `Classify([-50.0, 3.0])` -> `"cold start"`
- `Classify([3.0, 250.0])` -> `"overheating"`
- `Classify([10.0, 35.0])` -> `"spike"`
- `Classify([10.0, 35.0, 10.0])` -> `"stable"`
- `Classify([10.0, 35.0, 12.0])` -> `"3 readings"`

Constraints: no indexing, no `Length` comparisons, no `if`. Slice patterns with
relational sub-patterns do the first four rules; two of the later rules need
guards, because they compare two elements to each other rather than to a
constant.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca02_pattern_matching review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A relational pattern can sit inside a list pattern anywhere a constant could.
`[< -40, ..]` reads as "starts below minus forty" and asserts a length of at
least one at the same time — which is why the empty case never reaches it.

That combination is the point of the exercise: shape and value in one pattern,
with the boundary conditions handled by the shape rather than by arithmetic.

## Hint 2

Two useful forms side by side:

```csharp
[.., > 100]              // last element over 100, at least one element
[var first, .., var last] // binds both ends, at least two elements
```

Note the second demands two elements, not one, because `first` and `last` are
separate positions. If you want "first and last of a possibly single-element
array", that is a different pattern.

## Hint 3

The `"spike"` and `"stable"` rules compare two elements to each other, which a
relational pattern cannot do — those need bindings plus a guard.

For the formatting, `value.ToString("0.0", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)` gives
`"21.5"` on every machine; plain interpolation gives `"21,5"` in half of
Europe, and the gate runs under a culture chosen to catch that.

Left to you: whether `"stable"` should use exact `double` equality. The gate's
data makes it safe. Whether you would ever write that in a real sensor pipeline
is a question worth answering in a comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Take the seven worked examples and, for each one, write down which rules match
before ordering decides. `[10.0, 35.0]` matches `"spike"` and the fallback.
`[-50.0, 200.0]` matches both `"cold start"` and `"overheating"` — and the
table says cold start wins, which is a decision someone made and you are
implementing.

If you find yourself wanting to reorder for elegance, remember that the table
is a specification written by someone who knows what the sensor does.

## Hint 2

The single-element rule and the two-element rules interact in a way worth
seeing explicitly. Consider:

```csharp
[var first, .., var last] when first == last => "stable",
```

For a one-element array this does not match at all — `first` and `last` are
distinct positions, so the pattern requires two elements. Many people expect
`..` to be able to match "nothing between, and also the same element twice". It
cannot, and that is why the prompt's `"stable"` rule says three or more.

## Hint 3

Check the culture assertion by reasoning rather than by running. Under `de-DE`,
`21.5.ToString()` produces `"21,5"` — a comma. Any format string without an
explicit `IFormatProvider` picks up `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, which in a web
application is whatever the request thread was set to.

Left to you: whether to pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` at the call site or
to reach for the `System.Globalization` invariant-mode switch project-wide. The
first is local and explicit; the second is a project decision with consequences
far beyond this method.

# V3·A3 — Generics, constraints and generic math

`07_generics` gave you type parameters, `where T : IComparable<T>` and
`where T : new()`. That is enough to write a container. It is not enough to
write a *library*, because the interesting questions in generic code are all
about the edges: what does "nothing" mean for a `T` that might be an `int` or
might be a `string`? Why does `==` not compile on a `T` that you know is a
number? How do you write `Sum` once instead of six times?

The through-line for this sector is a single idea: **a type parameter is opaque
until a constraint opens a window in it**. Each constraint opens exactly one
window, and knowing which window you need is most of generic design.

## Concept — the constraints, and what each one buys

```csharp
where T : struct        // T is a non-nullable value type
where T : class         // T is a reference type; `class?` allows a nullable one
where T : notnull       // T is non-nullable, value or reference
where T : unmanaged     // T is a struct containing no references, at any depth
where T : new()         // T has a public parameterless constructor
where T : SomeBase      // T derives from SomeBase
where T : ISomething    // T implements ISomething
where T : U             // T derives from or implements another type parameter
where T : default       // "this override does not add a class/struct constraint"
```

They combine, with an ordering rule: `class`/`struct`/`notnull`/`unmanaged`
first, then a base class, then interfaces, then `new()` last. The compiler
error when you get the order wrong names the rule, which is unusually kind.

What each buys, concretely:

- **`struct`** lets you write `T?` meaning `Nullable<T>`, guarantees `default(T)`
  is not null, and — the underrated part — lets the JIT specialise your code
  for that struct, which usually devirtualises and inlines any interface calls.
- **`class`** lets you compare with `null`, assign `null`, and use `T?` meaning
  "a possibly-null reference".
- **`notnull`** is the one you want on a dictionary key. It bans `T?` as an
  argument and produces a warning when a caller supplies a nullable type.
- **`unmanaged`** lets you take a pointer or a `Span<byte>` over the value; it
  is how `MemoryMarshal` methods are declared.
- **`new()`** lets you write `new T()`. It is far less useful than it looks —
  it cannot express a constructor with parameters, and the lowering calls
  `Activator.CreateInstance` for reference types.
- **An interface constraint** lets you call that interface's members without a
  cast, and, since C# 11, its `static abstract` members through `T.Member`.

## Concept — "nothing" is not one thing

```csharp
static T Find<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, bool> match)
{
    foreach (T item in items) if (match(item)) return item;
    return default;              // null for a class, 0 for an int, warning either way
}
```

`default(T)` is whatever "all zero bits" means for `T`, and for an unconstrained
`T` the compiler cannot tell you whether that is a valid value. This is why the
BCL's answer is uniform: return `bool` and hand the value back through an
`out T?` parameter, so the caller is forced to look at the flag. `TryGetValue`,
`TryParse`, `TryDequeue`, `TryPop` — all the same shape, for this reason.

## Concept — one `Sum` for every number

Before .NET 7, `static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T>)` was impossible: `+` is not on
any interface, so there was nothing to constrain to. Teams shipped six
overloads, or a `dynamic` version that was 50 times slower, or an
`Expression`-compiled trick.

C# 11 added **static abstract interface members**, and the BCL used them to
build the generic math hierarchy:

```csharp
static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>
{
    T total = T.Zero;                      // a static abstract property
    foreach (T value in values) total += value;   // IAdditionOperators<T, T, T>
    return total;
}
```

`INumber<T>` is an interface whose members include `static abstract T Zero`,
`static abstract T operator +(T, T)`, and the parsing and comparison members. It
is declared with the *curiously recurring* shape — `INumber<TSelf> where TSelf :
INumber<TSelf>` — because a static member has no `this` and therefore needs the
implementing type named in the interface itself.

`where T : INumber<T>, IMinMaxValue<T>`, returning count, min, max and sum in a

```

```

`review1` is a generic `Range<T>` constrained on `IComparable<T>` for

# Reading - csharp/v3ca03_generics_constraints

## Notes

**Generics are a runtime feature, not a compiler trick.** Unlike Java's erased
generics, `List<int>` is a real type at runtime with its own method table.
That has two consequences you can feel: no boxing when you store an `int`, and
`typeof(T)` works inside a generic method.

**Reference instantiations share code; value instantiations do not.** The JIT
compiles one body for all reference types — every `T` becomes a pointer-shaped
`__Canon` — and a separate specialised body for each value type. So
`List<string>`, `List<Uri>` and `List<Stream>` share machine code, while
`List<int>` and `List<double>` each get their own. The upside is that a
`struct` constraint lets the JIT see the concrete type and inline through
interface calls; the downside is code size when you instantiate a generic over
dozens of structs.

**`default(T)` is zero bits, and that is the whole definition.** For a
reference type it is `null`; for a numeric it is `0`; for a struct it is the
struct with every field zeroed, which may violate every invariant the type
thinks it has. `default!` silences the nullability warning without changing the
value, and it is a promise you are making, not a check.

**`T?` means two different things.** With `where T : struct`, `T?` is
`Nullable<T>` — a real, different type with `HasValue`. With `where T : class`
or no constraint, `T?` is the same type with a nullability annotation, which
exists only at compile time. A generic method declaring `out T? value` with no
constraint therefore does the right thing for both, which is why the BCL writes
it that way.

**`==` is not available on an unconstrained `T`.** It would have to mean either
reference equality or a user-defined operator, and the compiler cannot know
which without a constraint. `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` is the answer: it
resolves once, statically caches an instance, and dispatches to `IEquatable<T>`
when the type implements it. For a struct implementing `IEquatable<T>` this
means no boxing at all — the single most common reason to implement that
interface.

**Variance is about safety, not convenience.** `out T` means `T` appears only
in output positions, so an `IEnumerable<Dog>` can be handed to something
expecting `IEnumerable<Animal>` — every dog it yields is an animal. `in T`
means input positions only. `IList<T>` can be neither: it both returns and
accepts `T`, and allowing covariance would let you put a cat into a list of
dogs. Arrays *are* covariant, from C# 1, and pay for it with a runtime check on
every store — which is exactly the `ArrayTypeMismatchException` ex5 makes you
trigger.

**Static abstract members close the last gap.** Before C# 11 an interface could
only describe instance members, so "types that can be added" or "types that can
parse themselves" were inexpressible. `static abstract` members are dispatched
through the type argument at the call site — `T.Zero` compiles to a direct call
into the concrete type once the JIT specialises — so generic math costs nothing
compared to hand-written numeric code, for value types.

## ex1

The whole exercise is the `out T?` declaration and the absence of `!`. Write
`out T` instead and the compiler warns on `found = default;`, correctly: for a
reference type that is a null you promised not to produce. Write `out T?` and
the warning goes away *and* the caller is told to check the flag before using
the value.

The `Func<T, bool>` parameter is there to keep the method honest — a `TryFirst`
that takes no predicate is `FirstOrDefault`, and lesson 5 has opinions about
that one.

## ex2

Five constraints, five unlocked operations: `new T()` needs `new()`, comparing
to `null` needs `class`, `Nullable<T>` needs `struct`, calling a member needs an
interface constraint, and using `T` as a dictionary key without a warning needs
`notnull`.

Writing the comment matters more than adding the keyword. A constraint that
nobody can explain is a constraint that will be widened by the next person who
hits it, and widening a constraint is a silent API break for anyone who
implemented against the narrower one.

## ex3

`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` is the correct answer to "how do I compare two
`T`s" roughly always. It handles null on both sides, uses `IEquatable<T>` when
available, and is a singleton, so the property access is free after the first
call.

The comparer overload matters because the *caller* often knows better than the
type does: case-insensitive strings, tolerance-based numbers, comparing entities
by id. Every BCL collection takes one for this reason, and a generic helper of
yours that does not is a helper someone will have to wrap.

## ex4

`new()` is a constraint people reach for and then regret. It cannot express
"has a constructor taking a connection string", it forces every value to have a
public parameterless constructor, and for reference types the lowering is an
`Activator.CreateInstance` call rather than a `newobj`, which is measurably
slower in a loop.

The factory overload has none of those problems and is strictly more
expressive: `new()` is the special case where the factory happens to be
`static () => new T()`. The gate's struct with no parameterless constructor is
the case that decides it.

## ex5

The variance annotation is one keyword and the compiler does the rest — it
checks that `T` really does appear only in output positions and refuses the
declaration otherwise. Try adding a `void Put(T item)` to your interface and
read the error; it is one of the clearest in the compiler.

`ArrayCovariance.Demonstrate` is the historical counterexample. `Dog[]` is a
`Animal[]` because C# 1 needed it for `Array.Sort`, and the cost is a type check
on every array store in every .NET program ever run. Generics were designed with
variance opt-in precisely so this could not happen again.

## ex6

`INumber<T>` is a big interface, and the point of the exercise is that you do
not need to know it — you need `T.Zero` and the operators, and the compiler
tells you when you reach for something the constraint does not provide.

`SumChecked` is where the numeric conversion API shows up. A `checked` context
inside a generic method still uses the type's `checked` operator, and
`INumber<T>` requires those, so `checked { total += value; }` throws for `int`
and behaves for `double` — which cannot overflow, it goes to infinity.

## ex7

`static abstract` plus the curiously recurring constraint is the shape every
BCL parsing interface uses. `IParsable<TSelf>`, `ISpanParsable<TSelf>`,
`IUtf8SpanParsable<TSelf>` are all declared this way, and once you have written
one of your own their signatures stop looking strange.

The payoff is that `RowReader.ReadAll<T>` needs no reflection, no delegate
parameter and no factory registration. The type argument carries the
construction logic, and the JIT resolves the call at specialisation time.

## ex8

Two constraints working together: `INumber<T>` for the arithmetic,
`IMinMaxValue<T>` for the seeds. Seeding `min` with `T.MaxValue` and `max` with
`T.MinValue` is the trick that makes a single pass possible without a "first
element" flag — and it is also the reason the empty sequence needs a documented
answer, because those seeds would otherwise leak out as the result.

"No boxing" is not a slogan here: everything in the method is a call on a
constrained type parameter, which for a value type instantiation the JIT
compiles to direct calls on the concrete struct.

## challenge

`Result<TValue, TError>` is the standard exercise for a reason: it forces you to
think about which type parameters are covariant, what `Map` does to the error
side, and how `Bind` differs from `Map` — the second one is where people
discover they have written `Result<Result<T, E>, E>`.

The short-circuiting `Sum` ties it to generic math: the value side is
constrained `INumber<TValue>`, so the accumulator can start at `TValue.Zero`,
and the first error stops the fold.

## review1

`Range<T>` is a small type with a large constraint list, which makes it a good
place to notice that constraints are API. Adding `INumber<T>` so that `Length`
can exist excludes `DateTime` — which is comparable but not a number — and
whether you want that exclusion is a design decision, not a technicality. The
alternative, two types or an interface with a `Subtract`, is the conversation
every library author has once.
