# V3·A3 — Generics, constraints and generic math (archive)

## The constraint table

| Constraint | Unlocks | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `struct` | `T?` as `Nullable<T>`; JIT specialisation | implies `notnull` |
| `class` | `null` comparison and assignment | `class?` allows a nullable reference type |
| `notnull` | use as a dictionary key with no warning | value or reference |
| `unmanaged` | pointers, `Span<byte>` reinterpretation | implies `struct` |
| `new()` | `new T()` | must be last; `Activator` for reference types |
| base class | members of that class | one only |
| interface | that interface's members, including `static abstract` | many |
| `T : U` | treat `T` as a `U` | ties two parameters together |

Order: `class`/`struct`/`notnull`/`unmanaged`, then base class, then
interfaces, then `new()`.

## Worked example — the `Try` shape, done properly

```csharp
public static bool TryFirst<T>(
    IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, bool> match, out T? found)
{
    foreach (T item in items)
    {
        if (match(item))
        {
            found = item;
            return true;
        }
    }

    found = default;
    return false;
}
```

`out T?` with no constraint is doing real work: for `int` it is `int` (a value
type's `T?` without a `struct` constraint stays `T`, annotated), for `string`
it is `string?`, and the nullable analysis in the caller is correct for both.
This is the exact signature `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>.TryGetValue` uses.

## Worked example — comparing two `T`s

```csharp
public static int IndexOf<T>(IReadOnlyList<T> items, T value) =>
    IndexOf(items, value, EqualityComparer<T>.Default);

public static int IndexOf<T>(IReadOnlyList<T> items, T value, IEqualityComparer<T> comparer)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++)
        if (comparer.Equals(items[i], value)) return i;
    return -1;
}
```

`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` is created once per closed generic type and
cached in a static field. For a `T` implementing `IEquatable<T>` it returns a
`GenericEqualityComparer<T>` whose `Equals` calls the typed method directly — so
a struct key never boxes.

## Worked example — generic math

```csharp
public static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>
{
    T total = T.Zero;
    foreach (T value in values) total += value;
    return total;
}

public static T Mean<T>(IReadOnlyCollection<T> values) where T : INumber<T> =>
    values.Count == 0
        ? throw new InvalidOperationException("The sequence is empty.")
        : Sum(values) / T.CreateChecked(values.Count);
```

`T.CreateChecked(int)` is the sanctioned way to get a `T` from another numeric
type. Three variants exist and the difference matters:

- `CreateChecked` throws `OverflowException` when the value does not fit.
- `CreateSaturating` clamps to `T.MinValue`/`T.MaxValue`.
- `CreateTruncating` keeps the low bits — the behaviour of an `unchecked` cast.

## Worked example — a static abstract member

```csharp
public interface IFromRow<TSelf> where TSelf : IFromRow<TSelf>
{
    static abstract TSelf FromRow(string[] cells);
}

public sealed record User(int Id, string Name) : IFromRow<User>
{
    public static User FromRow(string[] cells) => new(int.Parse(cells[0]), cells[1]);
}

public static List<T> ReadAll<T>(IEnumerable<string[]> rows) where T : IFromRow<T> =>
    rows.Select(T.FromRow).ToList();
```

`where TSelf : IFromRow<TSelf>` is the curiously recurring template pattern. It
is not decoration: without it, `TSelf` is unconstrained inside the interface and
`T.FromRow` at the call site has nothing to dispatch to.

## Worked example — variance, and the array it replaced

```csharp
public interface IReadOnlyBox<out T> { T Item { get; } }

IReadOnlyBox<Dog> dogs = new Box<Dog>(rex);
IReadOnlyBox<Animal> animals = dogs;        // safe: nothing can be put in
```

Add `void Put(T item);` to the interface and the *declaration* stops compiling
with CS1961 — the compiler checks the annotation against every member, so an
unsafe variant interface cannot be written. Contrast that with arrays, which
have been covariant with no such check since C# 1:

```csharp
Dog[] dogs = [rex];
Animal[] animals = dogs;       // legal
animals[0] = new Cat("mog");   // ArrayTypeMismatchException, at run time
```

The array version pushes the check to run time, and pays for it on *every*
store into a reference-type array in every .NET program. That cost is the
reason generic variance was made opt-in and verified.

Two limits worth remembering: variance applies only to interfaces and
delegates, never to classes, and only for reference type arguments — an
`IEnumerable<int>` is not an `IEnumerable<object>`, because boxing changes the
representation and a variant conversion must be free.

## Common mistakes

1. **Returning `default` from an unconstrained generic and treating it as
   "not found".** `0` is a perfectly good `int`. Return `bool` plus `out`.
2. **Using `!` to silence a nullability warning on `default`.** Sometimes
   right, usually a sign the signature should say `T?`.
3. **`where T : new()` when a factory delegate would do.** Less expressive and
   slower for reference types.
4. **Expecting `==` to work on `T`.** Use `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`.
5. **Widening a constraint to fix a caller.** It is a source-breaking change for
   implementers of your interface.
6. **Forgetting `notnull` on a dictionary key parameter.** The warning arrives
   at the caller and is confusing there.
7. **Assuming variance works for classes.** Only interfaces and delegates can
   be variant.
8. **Instantiating a large generic over many structs.** Each one gets its own
   JIT'd code; this is a real cause of startup cost.
9. **Using `dynamic` for arithmetic over an unknown numeric type.** `INumber<T>`
   exists now, and `dynamic` is roughly two orders of magnitude slower.
10. **Constraining to a concrete type.** `where T : Order` with one
    implementation means you did not want a generic.

## Worked example — a cache without `new()`

```csharp
public sealed class Cache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull
{
    private readonly Dictionary<TKey, TValue> _entries = new();

    public TValue GetOrAdd(TKey key, Func<TKey, TValue> factory)
    {
        if (_entries.TryGetValue(key, out TValue? existing)) return existing;
        TValue created = factory(key);
        _entries[key] = created;
        return created;
    }
}
```

`notnull` rather than `class` is the deliberate choice: a key may be an `int`,
a `DateOnly` or a record struct, and the constraint should say "a real value",
not "a reference". A `Func<TKey, TValue>` rather than `new()` is the other:
`new()` cannot express a constructor with arguments, silently accepts any
struct (handing back the all-zero value the type's real constructor would have
rejected), and lowers to `Activator.CreateInstance<T>()` for reference types.

If you do want the convenience, put the constraint on an extension method so it
applies to that one call rather than to every use of the type:

```csharp
public static TValue GetOrAddNew<TKey, TValue>(this Cache<TKey, TValue> cache, TKey key)
    where TKey : notnull where TValue : new() =>
    cache.GetOrAdd(key, _ => new TValue());
```

A constraint on a class's type parameter applies everywhere that class is
mentioned. That is the general rule worth taking away: push constraints as far
down as they will go.

## In an interview

*"How are C# generics implemented?"* — Reified, not erased. The runtime creates
a distinct type for each instantiation; reference-type instantiations share a
single JIT'd body through `__Canon`, value-type instantiations get specialised
code. That is why there is no boxing in `List<int>` and why `typeof(T)` works.

*"Why can't you use `+` on a type parameter?"* — Historically because operators
are static members and interfaces could not declare them. Since C# 11 they can,
via `static abstract`, and `where T : INumber<T>` gives you arithmetic.

*"What does `where T : notnull` do that `where T : class` does not?"* — It
permits value types too. It is the right constraint for a key: "must be a real
value", not "must be a reference".

## Check yourself

1. What does `default(T)` produce for an unconstrained `T`? What is the type of
   `T?` in that case?
2. Give the constraint that makes `T?` mean `Nullable<T>`.
3. Why does `List<string>` share JIT'd code with `List<Uri>` but not with
   `List<int>`?
4. Write `IndexOf<T>` without using `==`.
5. Why can `IList<T>` not be covariant? Give the code that would break.
6. Name the three `Create*` conversion methods on `INumber<T>` and how they
   differ.
7. What does the constraint `where TSelf : IShape<TSelf>` accomplish?
8. When is `where T : new()` the wrong tool, and what replaces it?
9. What runtime exception does array covariance produce, and on which
   operation?
10. What must be true of `T` for `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` to avoid boxing?
11. In what order must constraints be written?
12. Why does a `struct` constraint often make interface calls faster?
13. What is the difference between `where T : class` and `where T : class?`?

# Long read — how generics run, and the road to generic math

## Reified, and why it mattered

When generics shipped in .NET 2.0 (2005), the decision that shaped everything
afterwards was reification: the CLR itself understands type parameters, so
`List<int>` is a real runtime type rather than a `List<object>` with casts. Java
had gone the other way a year earlier with erasure, for backwards-compatibility
reasons, and pays for it to this day — `List<int>` is impossible there, and
every element boxes.

The cost of reification is in the JIT. When you write `List<T>`, the runtime
must produce machine code for each instantiation. It does this in two modes.
For every reference type argument, the code is identical — a pointer is a
pointer — so the runtime compiles one body against a placeholder type called
`__Canon` and shares it. For each value type argument it compiles a separate
body, because the size, the field layout and the copy semantics all differ.

The observable consequences: no boxing for value types in generic collections;
`typeof(T)` and `default(T)` work; and instantiating a big generic over twenty
different structs produces twenty copies of the code, which shows up as JIT
time at startup and as instruction-cache pressure later. This is a real
consideration in AOT-compiled and mobile workloads, and the mitigation is
usually to move the type-specific part behind a small interface.

## Constraints as a compiler contract

A constraint is not an optimisation hint; it is the compiler's entire knowledge
of `T`. Inside `Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>`, you may call
`CompareTo` and nothing else beyond `object`'s members. That is by design:
generic code must compile once against the constraint, so anything not in the
constraint cannot be there.

Two constraints do more than open a window. `struct` tells the JIT the concrete
type at specialisation time, so a call to an interface member on `T` becomes a
`constrained callvirt` that resolves to a direct call — usually inlined, with no
boxing. This is why `where T : struct, IEquatable<T>` appears throughout
high-performance BCL code. And `unmanaged` guarantees the value contains no
references anywhere in its field graph, which is what makes
`MemoryMarshal.AsBytes` and pointer arithmetic legal.

`new()` is the odd one out. For a value type the compiler emits `initobj`,
which is free. For a reference type it emits a call to
`Activator.CreateInstance<T>()`, which — despite years of optimisation — is
still a reflective path. In a hot factory, a `Func<T>` parameter is both faster
and more flexible.

## Variance, and the array mistake

C# 1 made arrays covariant: `Dog[]` is assignable to `Animal[]`. The motivation
was that without generics, a method taking `object[]` was the only way to write
a general-purpose sort. The cost is a runtime type check on *every* store into
an array of reference types, and an `ArrayTypeMismatchException` when it fails —
a check the JIT can sometimes eliminate and often cannot.

When generics arrived, variance was made explicit and opt-in, and C# 4 (2010)
added the `out` and `in` keywords for interfaces and delegates. The compiler
verifies the annotation: a type parameter marked `out` may appear only in
output positions, so no method can accept one, and the unsafe store becomes
impossible to express. `IEnumerable<out T>`, `IReadOnlyList<out T>`,
`Func<in T, out TResult>` and `IComparer<in T>` are the ones you use daily.

Variance applies only to interfaces and delegates, and only for reference type
arguments — `IEnumerable<int>` is not an `IEnumerable<object>`, because the
representations differ and a variant conversion must be free at runtime.

## The road to `INumber<T>`

"Write `Sum` once" was one of the longest-standing requests in C#. The obstacle
was structural: operators are static, interfaces could only declare instance
members, so no constraint could promise `+`.

The workarounds were all bad. Six overloads is the honest one. `dynamic` costs
a call-site cache lookup and roughly 100x the time of a direct add.
`Expression.Compile` builds a delegate at runtime, which is fast afterwards and
costs milliseconds up front and does not work under AOT. A `IArithmetic<T>`
helper object passed alongside the values works and is the pattern F# uses,
with an extra indirection per operation.

C# 11 and .NET 7 (2022) shipped `static abstract` interface members and the
generic math interfaces built on them: `IAdditionOperators<TSelf, TOther,
TResult>`, `IComparisonOperators<,,>`, `IAdditiveIdentity<,>`,
`IMinMaxValue<T>`, and the aggregate `INumber<T>` that pulls them together. The
call `T.Zero` is dispatched through the type argument: for a value type
instantiation the JIT knows the concrete type and emits a direct call, so
`Sum<int>` compiles to the same loop you would write by hand.

The design cost is the curiously recurring constraint. `INumber<TSelf> where
TSelf : INumber<TSelf>` looks like a mistake the first ten times you read it. It
is what lets the interface mention its own implementing type — a static member
has no `this`, so the interface has to name the type some other way.

## Where `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` comes from

This one static property is doing more than it looks, and it is the answer to
"how do I compare two `T`s" often enough to be worth understanding.

`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` is a lazily initialised static field on a closed
generic type, so there is exactly one instance per `T` and reading it after the
first time is a field load. The instance it holds is chosen by the runtime
based on `T`: a `GenericEqualityComparer<T>` when `T` implements
`IEquatable<T>`, a `NullableEqualityComparer<T>` for `Nullable<T>`, an
`EnumEqualityComparer<T>` for enums (which exists purely to avoid boxing in the
`Enum.Equals` path), and an `ObjectEqualityComparer<T>` for everything else.

The consequence that matters: for a struct implementing `IEquatable<T>`, the
comparison reaches a typed `Equals(T)` with no boxing, and for a struct that
does not, every comparison boxes both operands and lands in
`ValueType.Equals`, which walks fields reflectively. That single difference is
the reason `IEquatable<T>` exists at all, and lesson 8 shows how to implement
it properly.

The same story repeats for `Comparer<T>.Default` and `IComparable<T>`, and for
`EqualityComparer<T>.Default.GetHashCode`. A dictionary keyed on a struct that
implements neither interface is one of the more common quiet performance
problems in .NET code.

## Performance notes

Generic code over value types is as fast as hand-written code, because it *is*
hand-written code after specialisation. Generic code over reference types costs
one shared body and, where a `T` is used through an interface, a virtual call
the JIT usually cannot devirtualise.

The three things that actually cost:

- **`Activator.CreateInstance<T>()` from `new()`** in a loop.
- **Boxing through an unconstrained `T`.** Calling `ToString()` or `Equals` on
  an unconstrained `T` that turns out to be a struct boxes it, unless the call
  goes through `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`.
- **Instantiation explosion.** Twenty struct arguments to a large generic
  produce twenty bodies. Under Native AOT this is a binary-size question.

## When not to be generic

When the type parameter appears exactly once in the signature, it is a cast in
disguise. When there is one caller and one type argument, a concrete method is
clearer. When the constraint list grows past three, ask whether you are
describing an interface that should exist as a named abstraction. And when you
find yourself adding a constraint purely so the body compiles, check whether
the body wants to be a delegate parameter instead — `Func<T, TResult>` composes
where a constraint restricts.

## Further reading

- [Generics in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/)
  — reification, sharing, and why `List<int>` does not box.
- [Constraints on type parameters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters)
  — the normative list, the ordering rule, and `notnull` / `unmanaged`.
- [Generic math](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/math)
  — the interface hierarchy, and the `CreateChecked`/`Saturating`/`Truncating`
  distinction spelled out with examples.
- [Static abstract members in interfaces](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/whats-new/tutorials/static-virtual-interface-members)
  — the tutorial that makes the curiously recurring constraint make sense.
- [Covariance and contravariance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/concepts/covariance-contravariance/)
  — including the array-covariance history and why generics opted out of it.

## Exercise 1 — `TryFirst`, and what "nothing" means

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA03_GenericsConstraints/Ex1.cs`.

```csharp
public static class Sequences
{
    public static bool TryFirst<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, bool> match, out T? found);
    public static T FirstOr<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, bool> match, T fallback);
}
```

`TryFirst` returns `true` and sets `found` to the first matching element, or
returns `false` and sets `found` to `default`. `FirstOr` returns the fallback
instead.

- `TryFirst([1, 2, 3], x => x > 1, out int? n)` -> `true`, `n` is `2`
- `TryFirst([1, 2, 3], x => x > 9, out int? n)` -> `false`, `n` is `0`
- `TryFirst(["a"], s => s == "b", out string? s)` -> `false`, `s` is `null`
- `FirstOr([0, 0], x => x != 0, -1)` -> `-1`

Rules: no constraints on `T` at all, no `!` anywhere, and the file must compile
with zero warnings under `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`.

The gate calls `TryFirst<int>` and asserts that a `false` result yields `0` — a
perfectly valid `int`, which is exactly why the method returns a `bool` instead
of just handing you the value.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca03_generics_constraints ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are a `foreach` with an early return. The difficulty is entirely in
the signature, specifically in one character.

Ask what the compiler is allowed to assume about `T` when you write
`found = default;`. If `T` is `string`, `default` is `null` — so a signature
promising a non-null `T` would be lying, and the compiler says so.

## Hint 2

The two candidate signatures, and what each means:

```csharp
static bool TryGet<T>(out T value);    // "on any path, value is a valid non-null T"
static bool TryGet<T>(out T? value);   // "value may be null or default; check the bool"
```

`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>.TryGetValue` uses the second. So does
`Queue<T>.TryDequeue`, `ConcurrentDictionary.TryRemove`, and every other `Try`
method in the BCL. That consistency is not an accident.

## Hint 3

For an unconstrained `T`, `T?` is not `Nullable<T>` — it is `T` with a
nullability annotation, which for `int` is just `int`. That is why the gate can
declare `out int? n` and get `0` rather than a `Nullable<int>` with no value.

`FirstOr` needs no `?` at all, because the caller supplied a real `T`.

Left to you: whether `FirstOr` should call `TryFirst` or repeat the loop.
Calling it is less code and one more branch; both are defensible for a method
this small.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the caller's problem. Someone writes:

```csharp
int found = Find(numbers, x => x > 100);
if (found == 0) { /* not found? or found a zero? */ }
```

There is no answer. `0` is a legitimate element. Every sentinel value has this
defect for some `T`, which is why the BCL stopped inventing sentinels and
started returning `bool`.

That is the design being drilled; the code is three lines.

## Hint 2

Try the version the compiler rejects, so you have seen the diagnostic:

```csharp
public static bool TryFirst<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, bool> match, out T found)
{
    // ...
    found = default;   // warning CS8601: Possible null reference assignment.
    return false;
}
```

Now try silencing it with `default!`. It compiles, and it is a lie: a caller
who writes `string name = ...; TryFirst(..., out name); name.Length` gets a
`NullReferenceException` with no warning anywhere. The `?` moves the obligation
to the caller, where it belongs.

## Hint 3

Verify the `int` case by reasoning about what `T?` becomes. With no constraint,
the annotation applies only if `T` is a reference type; for `T = int` the
parameter is plain `int` and `default` is `0`. The gate's assertion that a
failed lookup yields `0` is checking that you did *not* add a `where T : class`
or a `where T : struct` to make the warning go away.

Left to you: whether `TryFirst` should throw for a null `items`. The gate does
not test it; a public API in a library would, and lesson 4 says with what.

Work method by method and ask one question each time: what operation is the

## Exercise 3 — equality without `==`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA03_GenericsConstraints/Ex3.cs`.

```csharp
public static class Search
{
    public static int IndexOf<T>(IReadOnlyList<T> items, T value);
    public static int IndexOf<T>(IReadOnlyList<T> items, T value, IEqualityComparer<T> comparer);
    public static int BoxCount { get; }
}
```

`T` is unconstrained, so `==` will not compile. Use
`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` in the two-argument overload and forward to the
three-argument one.

- `IndexOf([1, 2, 3], 2)` -> `1`
- `IndexOf(["a", "b"], "c")` -> `-1`
- `IndexOf([new Tag("x")], new Tag("x"))` -> `0` where `Tag` is a record
- `IndexOf(["A", "b"], "a", StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` -> `0`

`BoxCount` is incremented by a counting struct the gate supplies: it implements
`IEquatable<CountingKey>` and bumps a counter in its `Equals(object?)`
override. After a search over `CountingKey` values, `BoxCount` must be `0` —
proving the comparer took the typed path and never boxed.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca03_generics_constraints ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`==` on an unconstrained `T` has no meaning the compiler can choose: reference
equality and a user-defined operator are both plausible, and it refuses to
guess. `object.Equals(a, b)` would work and would box every value type.

`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` is the third option, and it is the one the entire
BCL uses.

## Hint 2

The shape:

```csharp
public static bool Contains<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, T value)
{
    IEqualityComparer<T> comparer = EqualityComparer<T>.Default;
    foreach (T item in items)
        if (comparer.Equals(item, value)) return true;
    return false;
}
```

Hoist the comparer into a local rather than calling the property in the loop.
The property is a cached static field read, so it is nearly free, but the local
also documents that one comparer is used for the whole search.

## Hint 3

Write the three-argument overload first, then make the two-argument one a
single-line forward. That way there is one loop in the file and one place for a
bug.

`IReadOnlyList<T>` gives you `Count` and an indexer, so a `for` loop with an
index is natural and returns the index directly.

Left to you: whether to guard against a null `comparer` argument. It is a public
API taking a required collaborator; ex4 and lesson 4 both have opinions.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the boxing assertion, because it is what makes this more than a
loop. `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` is not one class — it is a factory. For a
`T` implementing `IEquatable<T>` it returns a `GenericEqualityComparer<T>`
whose `Equals` calls `x.Equals(y)` on the *typed* overload. For everything else
it returns an `ObjectEqualityComparer<T>` that calls `object.Equals`, boxing
value types on the way.

So `BoxCount == 0` is not testing your loop; it is testing that you went
through the default comparer instead of `object.Equals`.

## Hint 2

Contrast the three candidate implementations:

```csharp
if (item.Equals(value))              // boxes: object.Equals on an unconstrained T
if (object.Equals(item, value))      // boxes, and handles nulls
if (comparer.Equals(item, value))    // typed path when T : IEquatable<T>
```

The first also throws for a null `item`. The second is correct and slow. Only
the third is both.

## Hint 3

Think about why the comparer overload exists at all. The type author decided
what equality means; the *caller* frequently disagrees — case-insensitive
strings, entities compared by id, numbers compared with a tolerance. A generic
helper without a comparer overload is one somebody will end up wrapping.

Left to you: whether the two-argument overload should be an optional parameter
(`IEqualityComparer<T>? comparer = null`) instead of a separate method. The BCL
uses separate overloads; consider what a default parameter does to binary
compatibility before you copy the shorter form.

## Exercise 4 — a cache, and the trouble with `new()`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA03_GenericsConstraints/Ex4.cs`.

```csharp
public sealed class Cache<TKey, TValue>
    where TKey : notnull
{
    public int Count { get; }
    public TValue GetOrAdd(TKey key) /* where TValue : new() — see below */;
    public TValue GetOrAdd(TKey key, Func<TKey, TValue> factory);
    public bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue? value);
}
```

The parameterless `GetOrAdd` needs a `new()` constraint on `TValue` — but a
constraint on the *class* would infect both overloads and the whole type. Move
it: make the parameterless one a generic *method* with its own type parameter,
or make it an extension method on `Cache<TKey, TValue>` constrained separately.
Either is acceptable; say which you chose and why in a comment.

Behaviour:

- `GetOrAdd("a", k => k.Length)` twice -> the factory runs **once**, `Count` is `1`
- `TryGet("missing", out int? v)` -> `false`, `v` is `0`
- the factory must not be invoked when the key is already present

The gate then uses `Point3` — a struct with only a three-argument constructor —
as `TValue` and asserts that the factory overload compiles and works while the
`new()` one is not even applicable. That contrast is the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca03_generics_constraints ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Constraints on a type parameter of the *class* apply everywhere the class is
used. If `Cache<TKey, TValue>` demanded `TValue : new()`, then no caller could
ever cache a `string`, an `ImmutableArray<T>`, or any struct with only a
parameterised constructor — regardless of which `GetOrAdd` they intended to
call.

So the constraint has to live on something narrower than the class.

## Hint 2

A generic method can introduce its own constrained parameter:

```csharp
public TResult GetOrAddNew<TResult>(TKey key)
    where TResult : TValue, new() => GetOrAdd(key, _ => new TResult());
```

The `where TResult : TValue` part is a type-parameter constraint — one
parameter constrained by another — and it is what keeps the method type-safe:
whatever you construct must be storable as a `TValue`.

## Hint 3

`GetOrAdd` with a factory is four lines: try the dictionary, return on a hit,
otherwise call the factory, store, return. Do not use
`dictionary.TryGetValue` and then `dictionary[key] = ...` in a way that hashes
the key three times — `CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault` exists for
exactly that, and lesson 7 uses it.

Left to you: whether the cache should be thread-safe. It is not, the gate does
not require it, and saying so in the XML doc is what separates a helper from a
trap.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failure the gate demonstrates. `Point3` looks like this:

```csharp
public readonly struct Point3
{
    public Point3(int x, int y, int z) { ... }
}
```

Every struct has an implicit parameterless "constructor" that zeroes the
fields, so `where TValue : new()` actually *does* accept `Point3` — and the
value you get back is `(0, 0, 0)`, which the type's real constructor would
never have produced.

That is worse than a compile error. Sit with it for a moment before writing the
factory overload; it is the strongest argument against `new()` there is.

## Hint 2

Now consider the reference-type side. For `TValue : new()` with a class, the
compiler emits:

```
call !!0 System.Activator::CreateInstance<TValue>()
```

not a plain `newobj`. `Activator.CreateInstance<T>()` has been optimised hard
over the years and is still a reflective path with a cache lookup. In a cache
that constructs on miss, in a loop, this is measurable.

A `Func<TKey, TValue>` is a delegate invocation: one indirect call, no
reflection, and it can pass arguments.

## Hint 3

Check the "factory runs once" requirement by counting rather than by trusting.
The gate uses a closure incrementing a local, and the classic bug it catches is
calling the factory before checking the dictionary:

```csharp
TValue candidate = factory(key);       // always runs
return dictionary.TryAdd(key, candidate) ? candidate : dictionary[key];
```

That is correct and wasteful, and if the factory opens a database connection it
is a bug rather than an inefficiency.

Left to you: whether `TryGet`'s `out TValue?` should be `out TValue` given the
class has no constraint on `TValue`. Reread ex1 before deciding.

## Exercise 5 — variance

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA03_GenericsConstraints/Ex5.cs`.

```csharp
public sealed class Box<T> : IReadOnlyBox<T> { ... }

public static class Zoo
{

    public static string ArrayCovariance();
}
```

`Animal` and `Dog : Animal` are declared for you. Add the variance annotation
so this compiles:

```csharp
IReadOnlyBox<Dog> dogBox = new Box<Dog>(new Dog("rex"));
string name = Zoo.NameOf(dogBox);        // "rex"
```

Then, in the same file, add a commented-out method `Put(T item)` to

compiler refuses the declaration, which is the safety the annotation buys.

`ArrayCovariance()` demonstrates what C# 1 allowed instead. It must:

1. create a `Dog[]`
2. assign it to an `Animal[]` variable — legal since C# 1
3. store a non-`Dog` `Animal` into it inside a `try`
4. catch `ArrayTypeMismatchException` and return its type name

- `Zoo.ArrayCovariance()` -> `"ArrayTypeMismatchException"`


exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Covariance is safe when the type parameter is only ever handed *out*. A box you
can only read from will only ever give you a `Dog`, and every `Dog` is an
`Animal`, so treating the box as a box of animals cannot go wrong.

The moment the interface can accept a `T`, that reasoning collapses — a box of
animals accepts a cat, and the box was really a box of dogs.

## Hint 2

The annotation and the check:

```csharp
public interface IProducer<out T> { T Get(); }        // fine
public interface IConsumer<in T> { void Put(T item); } // fine
public interface IBoth<out T> { void Put(T item); }    // error CS1961
```

The compiler verifies the annotation against every member. That verification is
the feature: you cannot write an unsafe variant interface, so a variant
conversion never needs a runtime check.

## Hint 3

For the array demonstration, the store is where the exception comes from — not
the assignment. `Animal[] animals = dogs;` succeeds; `animals[0] = new Cat();`
throws, because the runtime checks the element type on every store into an
array of references.

Left to you: whether to return `ex.GetType().Name` or a hard-coded string. The
first proves you actually caught the exception rather than predicting it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it from the cost side. Array covariance is not free: because
`Animal[] animals = dogs` is legal, *every* store into a reference-type array
in .NET carries a type check. Not just this one — all of them, in every program
ever run, because the JIT can only sometimes prove the array's element type.

Generic variance has no such cost, because the compiler made the unsafe case
inexpressible. That is the trade being demonstrated: a keyword at declaration
time instead of a check at every write.

## Hint 2

Try to break your own interface once it compiles. Add each of these and read
the error:

```csharp
void Put(T item);            // T in an input position
T[] GetAll();                // fine - still output
void Sort(IComparer<T> c);   // T is in an input position of an input... allowed?
```

The third is the interesting one: `IComparer<in T>` is contravariant, so
`IComparer<T>` in an input position puts `T` back in an *output* position by
double negation. The compiler works this out; most people cannot on first
reading, and that is fine — the point is that it is checked.

## Hint 3

Note what variance does *not* do: `IReadOnlyBox<int>` is not an
`IReadOnlyBox<object>`. Variant conversions must be representation-preserving,
and boxing an `int` changes the representation. Only reference type arguments
participate.

Left to you: whether `Box<T>` should be `sealed`. It is in the gate's file, and
the reason is lesson 4's: a sealed class is one the JIT can devirtualise.

## Exercise 6 — generic math

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA03_GenericsConstraints/Ex6.cs`.

```csharp
public static class Maths
{
    public static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>;
    public static T Mean<T>(IReadOnlyCollection<T> values) where T : INumber<T>;
    public static T SumChecked<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>;
}
```

One implementation each, working unchanged for `int`, `double` and `decimal`:

- `Sum([1, 2, 3])` -> `6`
- `Sum(new[] { 1.5, 2.5 })` -> `4.0`
- `Sum(new[] { 0.1m, 0.2m })` -> `0.3m`
- `Sum(Array.Empty<int>())` -> `0`
- `Mean([1, 2, 3, 4])` -> `2` for `int` (integer division — say so in a comment)
- `Mean(new[] { 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 })` -> `2.5`
- `Mean(Array.Empty<int>())` -> throws `InvalidOperationException`

`SumChecked` must throw `OverflowException` when the running total overflows:

- `SumChecked([int.MaxValue, 1])` -> `OverflowException`
- `Sum([int.MaxValue, 1])` -> `int.MinValue` (wraps, no exception)
- `SumChecked(new[] { double.MaxValue, double.MaxValue })` -> `double.PositiveInfinity`,
  because IEEE 754 does not overflow

Use `T.Zero` for the seed and `T.CreateChecked` to turn the `int` count into a
`T` in `Mean`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca03_generics_constraints ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The constraint is doing all of the work. `where T : INumber<T>` gives you the
arithmetic operators, the comparison operators, `T.Zero`, `T.One`, and the
conversion helpers — everything the body needs and nothing else.

You do not have to learn the interface. Write the loop you would write for
`int`, replace `0` with `T.Zero`, and let the compiler tell you about anything
else.

## Hint 2

Converting between numeric types inside a generic method:

```csharp
T count = T.CreateChecked(values.Count);   // throws if the count does not fit
T clamped = T.CreateSaturating(veryBig);   // clamps to T.MinValue / T.MaxValue
T wrapped = T.CreateTruncating(veryBig);   // keeps the low bits, like an unchecked cast
```

`CreateChecked` is the right default: a silently wrong number is worse than an
exception, and for `Mean` the count is an `int` that always fits anyway.

## Hint 3

For `SumChecked`, a `checked` block inside the loop is enough — the checked
operators are part of `INumber<T>`, so `checked { total += value; }` dispatches
to the type's checked addition.

That is also why the `double` case does not throw: IEEE 754 addition has no
overflow, it saturates to infinity, and the checked operator for `double` is
the same operator.

Left to you: what `Mean` should throw for an empty collection.
`InvalidOperationException` is what the gate wants and what LINQ's `Average`
does; `DivideByZeroException` would leak an implementation detail.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look at the `decimal` assertion first, because it explains why this feature
exists. `Sum(new[] { 0.1m, 0.2m })` is exactly `0.3m`, while the `double`
version of the same sum is `0.30000000000000004`. One method, correct for both,
with the type deciding the arithmetic.

Before .NET 7, giving both answers meant two methods. The alternative that
teams reached for — `dynamic` — is about a hundred times slower per operation
and defers every error to runtime.

## Hint 2

The `Mean` for `int` returning `2` for `[1, 2, 3, 4]` is not a bug you should
fix. `10 / 4` in integer arithmetic is `2`, and `INumber<T>`'s division is the
type's own division. Writing a mean that promotes to `double` internally would
be a different method with a different signature:

```csharp
static double MeanAsDouble<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T> =>
    double.CreateChecked(Sum(values)) / values.Count();
```

Choosing between them is a domain question. Documenting which one you wrote is
not optional.

## Hint 3

Verify the overflow behaviour by reasoning about where `checked` applies.
`checked` is an *expression* context in C#, not a runtime mode: it selects the
checked operator at compile time. Inside a generic method over `INumber<T>` the
checked operator is `IAdditionOperators<T, T, T>.op_CheckedAddition`, which
`int` implements as an overflow-throwing add and `double` implements as the
ordinary one.

Left to you: whether `Sum` should be checked by default. The BCL's
`Enumerable.Sum` is checked for `int` and unchecked for `long` in some
overloads — a historical inconsistency worth knowing about before you pick a
side.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An instance member is found through an object. A static member has no object,
so an interface declaring one has to name the implementing type some other way
— which is what the `TSelf` parameter is for, and why it must be constrained to
the interface itself.

Once the constraint is in place, `T.FromRow(cells)` inside a generic method is
an ordinary call, resolved at the call site from the type argument.

## Hint 2

Implementing a static abstract member looks exactly like an ordinary static
member:

```csharp
public sealed record Point(int X, int Y) : IFromRow<Point>
{
    public static Point FromRow(string[] cells) =>
        new(int.Parse(cells[0]), int.Parse(cells[1]));

    public static int ExpectedColumns => 2;
}
```

No `override`, no `virtual`. The interface says the type must have it; the type
has it.

## Hint 3

`ReadAll` is a `foreach` with a length check and a `Skipped` counter. Reset the
counter at the top, because the gate calls the method twice and asserts the
second call's count independently.

For `Reading`, parse the double with
`double.Parse(cells[1], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`. Left to you: whether

## Hint 1

Do the deletion experiment the prompt asks for first, because it makes the
constraint concrete. Remove `where TSelf : IFromRow<TSelf>` from the interface

`T.FromRow(...)` inside `ReadAll`, because `T` is constrained to
`IFromRow<T>` and the interface can no longer promise that `TSelf` has the
member.

The curiously recurring constraint is the language's way of saying "the
implementing type is itself".

## Hint 2

Compare what you have written with the three alternatives that predate it:

```csharp
static List<T> ReadAll<T>(rows, Func<string[], T> factory)   // caller supplies it
static List<T> ReadAll<T>(rows) where T : new()              // then set properties
static List<T> ReadAll<T>(rows)                              // Activator + reflection
```

The first works and pushes the knowledge to every call site. The second cannot
construct a record with a primary constructor. The third is slow and fails at
runtime. The static abstract version puts the knowledge on the type, once, and
is checked at compile time.

## Hint 3

Notice where the dispatch happens. `T.FromRow` in the JIT-specialised body for

Left to you: whether `ExpectedColumns` belongs on the interface at all. It

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — a one-pass statistics accumulator

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA03_GenericsConstraints/Ex8.cs`.

```csharp
public readonly record struct Summary<T>(int Count, T Min, T Max, T Sum)
    where T : INumber<T>;

public static class Stats
{
    public static Summary<T> Describe<T>(IEnumerable<T> values)
        where T : INumber<T>, IMinMaxValue<T>;
}
```

One pass over the sequence — the gate wraps the input in a counting enumerable
and asserts it was enumerated exactly once. Seed `min` with `T.MaxValue` and
`max` with `T.MinValue`, which is what makes a single pass possible without a
"have I seen anything yet" flag.

- `Describe([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])` -> `Count 5, Min 1, Max 5, Sum 14`
- `Describe(new[] { 2.5, -1.0 })` -> `Count 2, Min -1.0, Max 2.5, Sum 1.5`
- `Describe(Array.Empty<int>())` -> `Count 0, Min 0, Max 0, Sum 0`

The empty case is the design decision. Leaking the seeds — `Min = int.MaxValue`
— is the bug this exercise exists to prevent, and returning `T.Zero` for all
three is the documented answer. Write the sentence that says so.

The gate also asserts that no boxing occurs: the element type is a struct
implementing `INumber<T>` whose `Equals(object?)` increments a counter, and that
counter must stay at zero.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca03_generics_constraints ex8
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the "one pass" requirement, because it constrains the shape more
than the arithmetic does. Any implementation calling `values.Count()`,
`values.Min()` or `values.Any()` alongside the loop enumerates twice — and for
an `IEnumerable<T>` backed by a file, a database cursor or a random generator,
the second pass produces different data or throws.

That is lesson 5's territory and it starts here: an `IEnumerable<T>` parameter
is a promise you may enumerate it once.

## Hint 2

Think about what the boxing assertion is really watching. Every operation in
your loop must go through the type parameter, not through `object` or a
non-generic interface. These two lines look equivalent and are not:

```csharp
if (value < min) { ... }                          // constrained call: no box
if (((IComparable)value).CompareTo(min) < 0) { }  // boxes on every element
```

The first compiles to a `constrained callvirt` that the JIT resolves to the
struct's own operator. The second casts to a non-generic interface, which for a
value type means an allocation per element.

## Hint 3

Sanity-check the seeds against a sequence that contains only negative numbers,
and again against one containing only `T.MaxValue`. The second is the edge case
that catches a flag-based implementation with an inverted condition, and it
costs nothing to add to your own scratch tests.

Left to you: whether `Summary<T>` should also carry the mean. It would need a
conversion from `int` to `T` and a division, both of which you have from ex6 —
and it would make the empty case harder to answer honestly.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three fields carry the whole type: the value, the error, and a flag saying
which one is meaningful. The two static factories are the only constructors,
which is what stops anyone building a result that is neither.

`Match` being the only reader is the design decision that makes the type worth
having. A public `Value` property would be readable without checking `IsOk`,
and every caller who skipped the check would get `default` instead of an error.

## Hint 2

`Map` and `Bind` differ by one word, and the difference is worth writing out:

```csharp
public Result<TNext, TError> Map<TNext>(Func<TValue, TNext> project) =>
    IsOk ? Result<TNext, TError>.Ok(project(_value)) : Result<TNext, TError>.Fail(_error);

public Result<TNext, TError> Bind<TNext>(Func<TValue, Result<TNext, TError>> project) =>
    IsOk ? project(_value) : Result<TNext, TError>.Fail(_error);
```

`Map` wraps the projection's output. `Bind` does not, because the projection
already returned a wrapped value. Use `Map` when the step cannot fail and
`Bind` when it can.

## Hint 3

`SumOf` is a `foreach` with an early return, not a LINQ `Aggregate` —
`Aggregate` has no way to stop early, so it would evaluate every element
including the ones after the error.

Left to you: whether `SumOf` on an empty sequence is `Ok(T.Zero)` or an error.
Zero is the additive identity and the gate expects it; a sum of nothing being
an error is a defensible rule in some domains, and if you pick it, say so.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the type parameters and ask which of them could be variant. `TValue`
appears as an input to `Map`'s delegate and as an output of `Match` — so the
struct itself cannot be variant, and in any case only interfaces and delegates
can be.

That is worth noticing rather than skipping: a `Result` type in a language with
variance would want `Result<out TValue, out TError>`, and C# cannot express it
for a struct. If you need the covariant view, it is a separate read-only
interface, exactly as in ex5.

## Hint 2

The short-circuit assertion is the one to design for. Here is the version that
fails it:

```csharp
public static Result<T, TError> SumOf<T, TError>(IEnumerable<Result<T, TError>> results)
    where T : INumber<T>
{
    var materialised = results.ToList();                       // enumerates everything
    var firstError = materialised.FirstOrDefault(r => !r.IsOk); // second pass
    ...
}
```

Two passes, and the first one has already evaluated the element that throws.
The fold has to look at each result and decide immediately.

## Hint 3

Watch what `Bind` does to the error type. `Bind<TNext>` maps
`Result<TValue, TError>` to `Result<TNext, TError>` — the error type is fixed
across the chain, which is what makes chaining possible and also what makes a
`Result` with a rich error type awkward when two steps fail differently.

Left to you: whether to add a `MapError` for that case. It is four lines, it is
the symmetric operation, and the gate does not ask for it — but a `Result` type
without one tends to grow a cast somewhere instead.

## Review 1 — a generic range

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA03_GenericsConstraints/Review1.cs`.

```csharp
public readonly record struct Range<T>(T Start, T End)
    where T : IComparable<T>
{
    public bool Contains(T value);
    public bool Overlaps(Range<T> other);
    public Range<T>? Intersect(Range<T> other);
}

public static class Ranges
{
    public static TNumber Length<TNumber>(Range<TNumber> range)
        where TNumber : INumber<TNumber>, IComparable<TNumber>;
}
```

Ranges are half-open: `Start` inclusive, `End` exclusive, so
`Range(1, 5).Contains(5)` is `false`. A range whose `End` is not greater than
its `Start` is empty and contains nothing.

- `new Range<int>(1, 5).Contains(3)` -> `true`
- `new Range<int>(1, 5).Contains(5)` -> `false`
- `new Range<int>(1, 5).Overlaps(new Range<int>(5, 9))` -> `false` (touching, not overlapping)
- `new Range<int>(1, 5).Intersect(new Range<int>(3, 9))` -> `Range(3, 5)`
- `new Range<int>(1, 2).Intersect(new Range<int>(8, 9))` -> `null`
- `new Range<DateOnly>(jan1, feb1).Contains(jan15)` -> `true`
- `Ranges.Length(new Range<int>(3, 10))` -> `7`

Note where the two constraints live. `Range<T>` needs only `IComparable<T>`, so
it works for `DateOnly`, `string` and anything else ordered. `Length` needs
subtraction, so it sits outside the type with an extra constraint — putting
`INumber<T>` on the struct would make a range of dates impossible.

Say in a comment why `Intersect` returns `Range<T>?` rather than an empty
range, and what `Range<T>?` means for a struct.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca03_generics_constraints review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every method here is `CompareTo` and nothing else. `a.CompareTo(b) < 0` means
"a sorts before b" — write a tiny private helper if the comparisons start to
read badly, because a range type is mostly four comparisons wearing different
names.

The interesting decision is not the code. It is which constraint goes on the
type and which goes on the one method that needs more.

## Hint 2

Overlap, stated once and reused:

```csharp
public bool Overlaps(Range<T> other) =>
    Start.CompareTo(other.End) < 0 && other.Start.CompareTo(End) < 0;
```

Two comparisons, and both are strict, which is what makes touching ranges
(`[1,5)` and `[5,9)`) report `false`. Getting this wrong by one `<=` is the
classic interval bug, and it shows up as double-counting in reports.

`Intersect` is then the larger start and the smaller end, returning `null` when
that is not a real range.

## Hint 3

`Range<T>?` on a struct is `Nullable<Range<T>>` — a genuine "no value" state,
distinct from an empty range, which is a real range that happens to contain
nothing. Returning `null` says "these do not meet"; returning `Range(5, 5)`
would say "they meet in a zero-width interval", and the caller would have to
know which one you meant.

Left to you: whether `Length` should throw for an inverted range or return
zero. `Range(10, 3)` is empty by the type's own rule; make `Length` agree with
`Contains`, whatever you choose.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the constraint split, because it is what this review is testing.
Write down which operations each member needs:

- `Contains`, `Overlaps`, `Intersect` — ordering only.
- `Length` — subtraction, and therefore arithmetic.

`DateOnly` and `string` are ordered and are not numbers. If `INumber<T>` sat on
the struct, `Range<DateOnly>` would not compile, and the gate constructs one.
Constraints are API: this one decides which types your users may have.

## Hint 2

There is a tempting alternative worth rejecting explicitly: making `Length`
return `TimeSpan` for dates by adding an overload. That way lies a method per
element type, which is exactly what generic math exists to avoid. The honest
answer is that "length" is a numeric concept, so it lives with the numeric
constraint, and a `Range<DateOnly>` simply does not have one — its caller wants
`Days`, which is a different question.

## Hint 3

Test the half-open rule at every boundary before you trust it: `Contains(Start)`
is `true`, `Contains(End)` is `false`, an empty range contains nothing including
its own start, and two ranges that share only an endpoint do not overlap. Four
assertions, and they catch every off-by-one this type can have.

Left to you: whether `Range<T>` should validate that `Start <= End` in a
constructor. The half-open rule already makes an inverted range empty and
harmless; validating instead would be a different, also defensible design, and
lesson 1's ex4 shows you where the check would have to go.

lessons.title: V3·A4 — Nullable reference types and null-safety
lessons.summary: Nullable reference types are a compile-time analysis, not a runtime guarantee — `string` and `string?` are the same type at run time. This sector covers what the flow analysis actually tracks, the attributes that make an API honest, and where the annotations stop protecting you.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A4 — Nullable reference types and null-safety

`12_exceptions` taught you to fail loudly at a boundary. This sector is about
the failure that does not throw an exception you wrote — the
`NullReferenceException`, which arrives with no message, no argument name, and a
stack trace pointing at the line that dereferenced rather than the line that
supplied the null.

C# 8 added nullable reference types to attack this at compile time. The feature
is genuinely good and it is routinely misunderstood in one specific way, so
start with the sentence that prevents the misunderstanding:

**`string` and `string?` are the same type at run time.** The annotation is
metadata. Nothing in the runtime checks it, nothing prevents a caller from
passing null, and `typeof(string?)` does not compile because there is nothing
to name. What you get is a compiler that tracks nullability through your
method bodies and warns when the flow does not line up.

That makes NRT a *linting* feature with unusually deep integration — and it
means public API boundaries still need real, throwing argument checks.

## Concept — what the compiler tracks

The compiler assigns every expression a nullable *state*: not-null,
maybe-null, or not-tracked. State flows:

```csharp
void Use(string? name)
{
    // name: maybe-null
    Console.WriteLine(name.Length);     // warning CS8602

    if (name is null) return;
    // name: not-null from here
    Console.WriteLine(name.Length);     // fine

    name = MightReturnNull();
    // name: maybe-null again
}
```

Three things reset or confuse the state, and they are where most confusion
lives:

- **Assignment** sets the state from the right-hand side.
- **A method call** may invalidate what the compiler knew about *fields*,
  because the method could have written to them.
- **A property** is re-evaluated on every access. `if (x.Name is not null)`
  narrows `x.Name` for a while, but the compiler will drop that knowledge
  readily — copying to a local is the fix, and the local is also faster.

## Concept — the attributes that make an API honest

Flow analysis stops at method boundaries. Attributes from
`System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis` carry the missing information across:

```csharp
bool TryParse(string s, [NotNullWhen(true)] out Thing? value);   // the Try shape
T? FirstOrNull<T>([MaybeNullWhen(false)] out T value);
[return: NotNullIfNotNull(nameof(input))] string? Trim(string? input);
[MemberNotNull(nameof(_buffer))] void Initialise();
[DoesNotReturn] static void Throw(string message);
[AllowNull] public string Name { get; set; }                     // set null, get non-null
```

Each one answers a question the compiler cannot: "if this returns true, the out
parameter is not null"; "this member is assigned by the time this returns";
"control never comes back from here". Without them you end up writing `!` at
every call site, which is the smell this sector is really about.

## Concept — `!` and `required`

`!` — the null-forgiving operator — erases a warning and generates no code. It
is a promise, and like all promises it is only as good as its author. The
legitimate uses are narrow: a fact the compiler cannot see, a field the
framework assigns by reflection, and test code. Everything else is a signature
that should have said `?`.

`required` (C# 11) fixed the most common reason people reached for `!`: a
property that must be set but cannot be a constructor parameter. `required
string Name { get; init; }` makes the object initialiser mandatory, checked at
compile time, with no `= null!;` anywhere.

## Notes

**The annotations are metadata, and metadata can be absent.** Annotations
compile to `[Nullable]` and `[NullableContext]` attributes on the member.
Assemblies compiled before C# 8, or with the feature off, carry none — the
compiler calls that state *oblivious* and warns about nothing when you use
them. So a third-party library's `string` parameter tells you nothing about
whether it accepts null, and its return value tells you nothing about whether
it produces one.

**Three project settings, not one.** `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` turns on
both annotations and warnings. `annotations` lets you annotate your API
without being told about your own bodies — the right first step for a large
migration. `warnings` warns but treats every unannotated reference as
oblivious. Per-file `#nullable enable` exists for incremental work, and
`#nullable disable warnings` for the file you will get to later.

**The warnings are warnings.** CS8600 through CS8655 do not stop a build. A
codebase that is serious about this sets `<WarningsAsErrors>Nullable
</WarningsAsErrors>`, or at least treats the specific codes as errors, because
a warning nobody fixes is a comment.

**Generics have their own rules.** For an unconstrained `T`, `T?` means "T,
which may be null if it is a reference type" and disappears entirely when `T`
is a value type. `default(T)` warns for the same reason. `where T : notnull`
bans nullable arguments; `where T : class?` permits them explicitly. Lesson 3
covered the constraint side of this.

**`Nullable<T>` is a different feature with colliding syntax.** `int?` is a
real struct with `HasValue` and `Value`, boxing to `null` when empty, with
lifted operators — `null + 1` is `null`, and comparisons involving null are
false, including `<` *and* `>=` at the same time. `string?` is `string` with a
compiler note attached. The two share a `?` and share nothing else.

**Where the analysis stops.** Deserialisers, reflection, EF Core materialisation
and `Array.CreateInstance` all produce objects the compiler never saw
constructed. A JSON payload missing a field gives you `null` in a
non-nullable `string`, with no warning anywhere, and the exception arrives three
layers later. Annotations describe intent inside your compilation; they do not
validate data crossing into it.

## ex1

Fixing signatures rather than bodies is the discipline the exercise enforces. A
warning is nearly always the compiler telling you the *signature* is wrong: a
method that can return null should say so, and once it does, the callers'
warnings are correct and useful rather than noise.

The rule of thumb worth carrying: when a warning appears, the first question is
"is the annotation wrong?", not "how do I silence this?".

## ex2

`[NotNullWhen(true)]` is the single highest-value attribute in the set, because
the `Try` shape is everywhere. Without it, every caller writes:

```csharp
if (config.TryGet("host", out string? host) && host is not null)
```

That second check is dead code, and the fact that people write it anyway is
evidence the API failed to communicate. With the attribute, the first check
narrows `host` for the rest of the block, and the redundant test produces its
own warning.

## ex3

The mechanism is worth stating precisely: the compiler tracks state for
*expressions* it can prove are stable. A local variable is stable. A property
is a method call, and the compiler assumes a second call may return something
different — which is not paranoia, since a property backed by a dictionary
lookup or a lazily rebuilt cache really can.

Copying to a local is therefore not a workaround. It is the fix, and it is also
one fewer call.

## ex4

`[MemberNotNull]` exists because the constructor's flow analysis stops at the
call. It sees `Reset();` and has no idea what happened inside. The attribute
says "when this method returns normally, these fields are not null", and the
compiler both *believes* it in the constructor and *checks* it inside `Reset`.

That second half is what makes it different from `!`: the promise is verified
where it is made.

## ex5

Two attributes for two asymmetries. `[NotNullIfNotNull]` links a return value
to a parameter, so `Clean("x")` is known non-null while `Clean(null)` is not —
without it, every caller with a non-null argument has to explain themselves.

`[AllowNull]` describes a property whose setter is more permissive than its
getter. `Theme = null` means "back to default", and the getter never returns
null. Before the attribute, this shape forced the property to be `string?`,
which lied to every reader.

## ex6

`[DoesNotReturn]` on a throw helper is what lets you extract guard clauses
without losing analysis. Without it, the compiler treats `Guard.Missing(name)`
as an ordinary call and still considers the value maybe-null on the next line.

`[DoesNotReturnIf(true)]` is the conditional version, and it is how
`Debug.Assert` teaches the compiler in .NET 5 and later. Note that
`Debug.Assert` is compiled out in release builds while its *annotation* is not,
which is a subtlety worth knowing before you rely on it for safety rather than
for analysis.

## ex7

The point of the shim is to show that annotations protect your compilation and
nothing else. A caller in an oblivious assembly, a caller using `!`, a
deserialiser, or reflection can all hand you a null through a parameter typed
`string`.

`ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` is the cheap, correct boundary check: one
line, the parameter name captured automatically by
`CallerArgumentExpression`, and a throw the caller can act on. Keep the
annotation as well — it tells honest callers what you expect, and the check
handles the rest.

## ex8

`required` removes the last common excuse for `= null!`. Before it, a
non-nullable property that could not be a constructor parameter had to be
initialised to a lie. Now the compiler demands the object initialiser supply
it, at every construction site.

`[SetsRequiredMembers]` is the escape hatch for a constructor that assigns them
all, and it is exactly as trustworthy as you make it: the compiler stops
checking, so an added member with no assignment is a silent hole.

## challenge

The interesting requirement is "report everything". A binder that throws on the
first missing key makes configuration debugging into a loop of restarts, one
per mistake. Collecting errors and failing once is a small amount of extra code
and a large amount of saved time.

Nullability drives the shape: the input dictionary is `string?`-valued, the
output record is fully non-null, and the only way to get from one to the other
without `!` is to funnel every read through a helper the compiler believes.

## review1

The final case is the one people forget after a sector like this: sometimes
null is the right answer. A terminating `Next` in a chain, a parent link at the
root, an optional middle name. Annotating those as `?` is not a compromise; it
is the annotation being accurate, and the value of the feature is that the
compiler then makes every consumer handle the case.

# V3·A4 — Nullable reference types and null-safety (archive)

## The one-sentence model

Nullable reference types are a compile-time flow analysis plus metadata. There
is no runtime component, no new type, and no enforcement at an assembly
boundary. `string?` and `string` are `System.String` in both cases.

## The attribute set, with the question each answers

| Attribute | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| `[NotNullWhen(true/false)]` | "if the method returns this, the out/parameter is not null" |
| `[MaybeNullWhen(false)]` | "if the method returns false, the out may be null" |
| `[NotNullIfNotNull(nameof(x))]` | "the return is not null when `x` was not null" |
| `[MemberNotNull(...)]` | "these fields are assigned when this returns" |
| `[MemberNotNullWhen(true, ...)]` | the conditional version, for `IsInitialised` |
| `[DoesNotReturn]` | "control never comes back" |
| `[DoesNotReturnIf(true)]` | "control does not come back if this argument is true" |
| `[AllowNull]` | "the setter takes null even though the type says otherwise" |
| `[DisallowNull]` | "the setter refuses null even though the type is `T?`" |
| `[NotNull]` | "after this call, the argument is not null" (the `ThrowIfNull` shape) |

## Worked example — the `Try` pattern

```csharp
public bool TryGet(string key, [NotNullWhen(true)] out string? value)
{
    value = _entries.TryGetValue(key, out string? found) ? found : null;
    return value is not null;
}

// caller
if (config.TryGet("host", out string? host))
{
    Console.WriteLine(host.Length);   // no warning, no second null check
}
```

Without the attribute the caller must check twice, and the second check is
dead code the compiler cannot prove is dead.

## Worked example — `[MemberNotNull]`

```csharp
public sealed class Buffer
{
    private char[] _data;

    public Buffer(int size) => Reset(size);      // compiler cannot see inside

    [MemberNotNull(nameof(_data))]
    private void Reset(int size) => _data = new char[size];
}
```

The attribute is checked where it is written: if `Reset` had a path that left
`_data` unassigned, the attribute itself would produce a warning. That is the
difference between an attribute and a `!` — one is verified, the other is
asserted.

## Worked example — a guard that ends analysis

```csharp
public static class Guard
{
    [DoesNotReturn]
    public static void Missing(string name) =>
        throw new InvalidOperationException($"{name} is required.");
}

string Ship(string? address)
{
    if (address is null) Guard.Missing(nameof(address));
    return address.Trim();       // no warning: the call above cannot return
}
```

Remove the attribute and the last line warns, correctly — the compiler has no
other way to know `Guard.Missing` always throws.

## Worked example — the boundary

```csharp
public string Render(Invoice invoice, string culture)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(invoice);
    ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(culture);
    ...
}
```

Both parameters are non-nullable and both are checked. That is not
belt-and-braces: the annotation is for callers you compile with, the check is
for everyone else — reflection, deserialisers, older assemblies, and anyone who
wrote `!`.

## Worked example — `required` instead of `= null!`

```csharp
// Before C# 11: a lie that compiles.
public sealed class Profile
{
    public string DisplayName { get; init; } = null!;
}

// C# 11 and later: a demand the compiler enforces at every construction site.
public sealed class Profile
{
    public required string DisplayName { get; init; }
}
```

`= null!` leaves a genuine null in the field until someone assigns it, and
nothing checks that anyone does. `required` makes
`new Profile { }` a compile error naming the missing member. The escape hatch,
`[SetsRequiredMembers]` on a constructor that assigns them all, is exactly as
trustworthy as you keep it: add a fourth required member later and every object
initialiser fails to compile — which is the point — while that constructor
keeps compiling and silently leaves the new member unset.

## Worked example — proving a merge is complete

```csharp
if ((primary.Name ?? fallback.Name) is { } name
    && (primary.Email ?? fallback.Email) is { } email)
{
    return new Profile(name, email);      // no `!`, no runtime check
}
```

`is { }` is a property pattern with no members: it matches any non-null value
and binds it to a non-nullable local. Three of these joined by `&&` give the
compiler everything it needs to accept the constructor call. Move the same test
into a helper method — `if (AnyNull(name, email))` — and the analysis stops at
the call, because no attribute can say "if this returns false, these several
unrelated arguments are all non-null". `[NotNullWhen]` speaks about one
parameter at a time.

## Common mistakes

1. **Believing the annotation is enforced.** It is not. Public APIs still need
   `ThrowIfNull`.
2. **Silencing with `!`.** Each one is an unverified promise. Grep for them
   periodically; a growing count is a design signal.
3. **`= null!` on a property.** Use `required` instead, or a constructor
   parameter.
4. **Checking a property instead of a local.** The compiler discards property
   state readily; a local is stable and cheaper.
5. **Assuming a `?` on a `T` in a generic means `Nullable<T>`.** Only with a
   `struct` constraint.
6. **Trusting a deserialised object's annotations.** JSON has no idea what your
   attributes say.
7. **Enabling `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` across a large codebase at once.**
   Start with `annotations`, or file by file.
8. **Leaving the warnings as warnings.** Set `WarningsAsErrors` for the
   nullable codes or they become background noise.
9. **Writing `x != null` on a type with a custom `==`.** Lesson 2's ex6; use
   `is not null`.
10. **Annotating a parameter `?` to silence a warning inside the body.** That
    changes your contract for every caller, to fix your own code.
11. **Treating `[SetsRequiredMembers]` as free.** It switches off the check for
    that constructor permanently, including for members added later.
12. **Reading a nullable property twice after checking it once.** The state does
    not survive; copy to a local, which is also one fewer call.

## In an interview

*"Do nullable reference types prevent NullReferenceException?"* — No. They are a
compile-time analysis; the annotations are metadata and the runtime ignores
them. They prevent a large class of mistakes *within* code you compile with
them enabled, and they do nothing about reflection, deserialisation, oblivious
assemblies or `!`.

*"What is the null-forgiving operator and when is it acceptable?"* — `!`
suppresses a nullability warning and emits no code. It is acceptable when you
know something the compiler cannot — a field assigned by a framework, a value
validated by a helper the compiler cannot see through, or a test asserting a
value is present. In production logic it usually means the signature is wrong.

*"What does `[NotNullWhen(true)]` do?"* — It tells the compiler that when the
method returns `true`, the annotated parameter is not null, so a caller's `if`
narrows the state and needs no second check.

## Check yourself

1. What is the runtime type of `string?`?
2. Name three ways a null can reach a non-nullable parameter.
3. Which attribute makes `TryGetValue`-style APIs pleasant to call?
4. Why does copying a nullable property to a local change what the compiler
   knows?
5. What does `[MemberNotNull]` promise, and where is that promise checked?
6. Give the difference between `[AllowNull]` and `[DisallowNull]`.
7. What is the difference between `<Nullable>annotations</Nullable>` and
   `warnings`?
8. In a generic method with no constraints, what does `T?` mean?
9. What does `int? x = null; Console.WriteLine(x >= 0);` print, and why?
10. When is `= null!` justified, and what feature replaced most of its uses?
11. What is an "oblivious" nullability context?
12. Why do you still write `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` in an annotated
    public API?

# Long read — how the analysis works, and where it ends

## Why the feature had to be a compile-time one

Tony Hoare called the null reference his billion-dollar mistake, and by 2018
the .NET team had two decades of code depending on it. Any fix had to be
backwards compatible in the strictest sense: existing assemblies must keep
working, existing source must keep compiling, and `null` must remain assignable
to a reference at run time.

That ruled out a runtime change. `string` cannot become a type that rejects
null, because a thousand existing libraries pass null to a thousand existing
methods and expect it to work. What remained was to add information the
compiler could reason about, and to warn — never error — when the reasoning
failed.

The result shipped in C# 8 (2019). `string?` compiles to `System.String` with a
`[Nullable]` attribute on the parameter, field, or return. Generic and array
cases get a byte array in that attribute describing each position — so
`Dictionary<string, List<string?>>?` is encoded as a sequence of flags. If you
have ever decompiled an annotated assembly and seen `[Nullable(new byte[] { 2,
1, 2 })]`, that is what you were looking at.

## The flow analysis

The compiler runs a dataflow pass over each method body, assigning every
expression a *nullable state*: not-null, maybe-null, or oblivious. Assignments,
comparisons, patterns, `??`, `?.`, `throw` expressions and `[DoesNotReturn]`
calls all update it.

Two properties of the analysis explain most of its surprising behaviour.

First, it is **per-expression, and only for expressions it considers stable**.
Locals and parameters are stable. Fields are stable until something might have
written to them. Properties are never stable across a call, because a property
is a method and the compiler will not assume purity. This is why

```csharp
if (order.Customer is not null) Use(order.Customer.Name);
```

can warn while the version with a local never does. It is also why the local is
the better code independently of the warning: one property call instead of
three.

Second, it is **not a proof system**. It does not track relationships between
variables, so this warns:

```csharp
bool hasName = name is not null;
if (hasName) Console.WriteLine(name.Length);   // CS8602
```

The compiler does not connect `hasName` to `name`. Attributes exist precisely
to carry those relationships across boundaries the analysis cannot see — which
is what `[NotNullWhen]` is doing for `TryGetValue`.

## Where the guarantees stop

**At the assembly boundary.** An assembly compiled without the feature is
*oblivious*: its `string` means "no information". The compiler warns about
nothing when you use it, which is the right default and also means an
unannotated dependency is a silent hole in your analysis.

**At the serialisation boundary.** `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Person>` uses
reflection and setters; a payload missing `"name"` produces a `Person` whose
non-nullable `Name` is null. `System.Text.Json` added
`JsonSerializerOptions.RespectNullableAnnotations` in .NET 9 to close some of
this, and it is off by default for compatibility. EF Core has its own story:
it uses annotations to infer column nullability, and then materialises entities
by reflection anyway.

**At `!`.** Every null-forgiving operator is an assertion with no verification.
They are load-bearing in test code and in a handful of framework patterns; in
business logic they are the thing to count during review.

**At `default!`.** `private string _name = default!;` compiles, runs, and gives
you a null in a field the compiler now believes is non-null. `required`
replaced most legitimate uses of this in C# 11.

## The attributes, and why there are so many

The attribute set looks sprawling until you notice it is answering one question
in several grammatical moods: *what does this member guarantee that its
signature cannot say?*

`[NotNullWhen]` and `[MaybeNullWhen]` relate a return value to a parameter.
They exist because the `Try` shape puts the interesting information in the
`bool` and the value in the `out`, and the type system has no way to connect
two parameters. Roughly every `Try` method in the BCL carries one.

`[NotNullIfNotNull]` relates a return value to an argument, which is the
`Path.GetDirectoryName`/`string.Concat` shape: null in, null out; text in, text
out. Without it, callers who know they passed a real string still have to
handle a null they can prove will not arrive.

`[MemberNotNull]` and `[MemberNotNullWhen]` relate *fields* to a method's
completion. They exist because constructor flow analysis stops at a call. Both
are verified where they are written: give the annotated method a path that
leaves the field unassigned and the warning lands on the attribute, not on some
distant caller. That verification is what separates them from `!`.

`[DoesNotReturn]` and `[DoesNotReturnIf]` describe control flow rather than
nullability, and they exist so that a guard clause can be extracted into a
helper without the analysis forgetting what the helper did. `Debug.Assert`
carries `[DoesNotReturnIf(false)]`, with the wrinkle that the call disappears
in release builds while its effect on compile-time analysis does not.

`[AllowNull]` and `[DisallowNull]` describe a property whose getter and setter
disagree — "assign null to reset", or "may read as null, may never be set to
null". Both were previously inexpressible without lying in one direction.

`[NotNull]` is the `ThrowIfNull` shape: the parameter accepts null and, if the
method returns at all, it was not null. It is why
`ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(x)` narrows `x` for the rest of your method.

## `Nullable<T>` is a different animal

The syntax collision is unfortunate. `int?` is `System.Nullable<int>`: a real
struct with `HasValue` and `Value`, its own boxing behaviour (boxing an empty
`int?` produces a null reference, not a boxed struct), and *lifted* operators.
Lifting is where it surprises people:

```csharp
int? a = null;
Console.WriteLine(a > 0);    // False
Console.WriteLine(a <= 0);   // False - both are false at once
Console.WriteLine(a + 1);    // (blank) - null
```

Every comparison involving a null operand is false, so `>` and `<=` are not
complements. Arithmetic propagates null. None of this applies to `string?`,
which has no runtime existence at all.

## Migration, in practice

The order that works, roughly: turn on `<Nullable>annotations</Nullable>` for
the project, annotate the public API top-down, then switch to `enable` file by
file with `#nullable enable`, fixing the body warnings as you go. Set
`<WarningsAsErrors>Nullable</WarningsAsErrors>` the day a project is clean, or
the count only goes up.

The trap is annotating to silence rather than to describe. A parameter changed
to `string?` because the body warned is a contract change affecting every
caller, made for the convenience of one method. The question to ask at each
warning is "which of these two is lying — the annotation, or the code?"

## When not to reach for it

There is no good reason to leave the feature off in new code. There are good
reasons to keep expectations calibrated:

- It will not protect a public library from its callers. Keep the argument
  checks.
- It will not validate data arriving from outside the process. Validate at the
  boundary, with a real validator.
- It is not worth a big-bang migration of a legacy codebase mid-project. The
  file-by-file route delivers most of the value with none of the merge pain.
- `!` and `= null!` scattered to make a build clean produce a codebase that
  claims safety it does not have, which is worse than one that claims nothing.

## Further reading

- [Nullable reference types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references)
  — the feature overview, including the four project settings and what each
  changes.
- [Attributes for null-state static analysis](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/attributes/nullable-analysis)
  — every attribute with a worked example; the reference to keep open.
- [Nullable reference types specification](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/main/proposals/csharp-8.0/nullable-reference-types-specification.md)
  — how the flow states are computed, for when the compiler's answer surprises
  you.
- [`required` members](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/required)
  — and `[SetsRequiredMembers]`, which is the part that needs care.
- [Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types)
  — lifted operators and boxing, for the feature that merely shares the `?`.
