## Hint 1

Read each warning as a sentence about the *signature*, not about the line it
points at. "Possible null reference return" means the method's return type
claims something the body cannot deliver.

There is exactly one edit per warning and every one of them is a `?`. The
skill being drilled is resisting the urge to change the body instead.

## Hint 2

The four shapes you will need:

```csharp
public string? MayReturnNull();          // return can be null
public void Accepts(string? maybe);      // parameter may be null
public string? Property { get; set; }    // property may hold null
public string NeverNull(string input);   // no change needed
```

Note the third one: a property that starts life as null is a `string?`, even if
it is non-null for most of the object's life. "Usually set" is not a thing the
compiler can express — `required` (ex8) is the tool for "must be set".

## Hint 3

`Format` is the one people get wrong. Its body handles a null name, so the
parameter should be `string?`; its return is always a real string, so the return
type stays `string`. Two different answers in one signature.

Left to you: whether `Find` returning `null` is the right design at all. `null`
for "absent" is defensible for a lookup; `TryFind` is what ex2 does, and it
tells the caller more.

## Hint 1

Start by asking what each member promises to a caller who cannot see the body.
Write the promise as a sentence for each of the four:

- "Give me a name and I will give you a number." Is that true when the name is
  unknown?
- "Give me a name and a number and I will store them." Can either be null?
- "Give me a name — possibly none — and I will give you a display string."
- "Ask me what I last looked up." What is the answer before anything happened?

Two of those sentences are lies as currently typed. The `?` characters go where
the lies are.

## Hint 2

A useful diagnostic habit: temporarily add `!` to make a warning disappear,
then ask what you just promised. For `Find`, `return null!;` compiles and
promises callers a non-null string. The very next caller writes
`book.Find("nobody").Length` with no warning, and gets a
`NullReferenceException`.

Then delete the `!`. Seeing the bug it would have created is the fastest way to
learn where `!` does not belong.

## Hint 3

Check the property carefully. `LastLookup` has a private setter and starts as
null, so it is `string?`. The temptation is `= string.Empty;` to make it
non-null — which is a design change, not an annotation fix, and it makes "never
looked anything up" indistinguishable from "looked up an empty string".

Left to you: which of those two designs you would actually ship. The gate wants
the annotation; the argument is worth having.

## Exercise 2 — the `Try` shape, told to the compiler

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA04_NullableReferences/Ex2.cs`.

```csharp
public sealed class Config
{
    public Config(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string?> entries);

    public bool TryGet(string key, out string? value);
    public string Describe(string key);
}
```

`TryGet` returns `true` only when the key is present **and** its value is not
null; a key present with a null value counts as missing. Annotate the `out`
parameter so a caller who checks the `bool` needs no null check of its own.

`Describe` must be written with no `is null`, no `?.`, no `??` and no `!`:

- `Describe("host")` where `host` is `"example.com"` -> `"host = example.com (12 chars)"`
- `Describe("port")` where `port` is missing -> `"port is not set"`
- `Describe("empty")` where `empty` maps to `null` -> `"empty is not set"`

The gate compiles with warnings as errors, so a missing attribute is a build
failure rather than a style note.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca04_nullable_reference_types ex2
```

## Hint 1

The `bool` and the `out` are related, and the type system cannot express the
relationship. That is the entire reason this attribute exists: the return value
carries information about a different parameter.

Once you say so, the compiler's flow analysis picks it up at every call site
for free, forever.

## Hint 2

The shape, with its `using`:

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis;

public bool TryFind(string key, [NotNullWhen(true)] out Thing? found)
```

There is a symmetric attribute, `[MaybeNullWhen(false)]`, which says the same
thing from the other side and is used when the parameter's declared type is not
nullable — `Dictionary` uses the first, `Queue<T>.TryDequeue` the second.

## Hint 3

`Describe` becomes a single `if` once the attribute is in place, because
inside the `true` branch the compiler knows `value` is a real string and
`value.Length` is legal.

Left to you: whether `TryGet` should treat a present-but-null entry as missing.
The prompt says yes, and it is the pragmatic choice for configuration — but it
means a caller cannot distinguish "unset" from "explicitly cleared", and some
config systems care.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write `Describe` first, without the attribute, and look at what the compiler
makes you add:

```csharp
if (TryGet(key, out string? value) && value is not null)
```

That `&& value is not null` is the tell. It is unreachable-when-false in
practice — `TryGet` promised — but the promise was made in prose and the
compiler cannot read prose. Every redundant check in a codebase is a place
where an attribute is missing.

## Hint 2

Consider the alternative API that needs no attribute at all:

```csharp
public string? Get(string key);          // null means absent
```

Then `Get(key) is { } value` narrows in one step and nothing needs annotating.
The `Try` shape exists for the case where the *value itself* may legitimately be

`string?`-valued configuration it does not.

Knowing when the `Try` shape is earning its keep is part of the exercise.

## Exercise 3 — why the property check did not help

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA04_NullableReferences/Ex3.cs`.

```csharp
public sealed class Order
{
    public Customer? Customer { get; set; }
    public decimal Total { get; set; }
}

public static class Receipts
{
    public static string Render(Order order);
}
```

`Render` must produce:

- with a customer named `"Ada"` and total `20m` -> `"Ada (3) owes 20"`
- with no customer -> `"guest owes 20"`

where `(3)` is the length of the name. The existing body checks
`order.Customer is not null` and then reads `order.Customer.Name` twice, and
the compiler is not satisfied.

Fix it by copying to a local, then write a comment explaining the two reasons
the local is better — one about what the compiler can prove, one about what the
machine actually does.

The gate additionally supplies an `Order` subclass whose `Customer` property
returns a **different** customer on every access, and asserts your `Render`
produces a self-consistent string. A property-based implementation fails that
assertion even when it compiles.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca04_nullable_reference_types ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The compiler treats a property access as a method call, because that is what it
is. Two calls to the same property may return two different values — nothing in
the language says otherwise — so knowing the first call returned non-null tells
it nothing about the second.

A local, once assigned, cannot change. That is why the state survives.

## Hint 2

The pattern that does both jobs in one line:

```csharp
if (order.Customer is { } customer)
{
    return $"{customer.Name} ({customer.Name.Length})";
}
```

`is { }` is a property pattern with no members — it matches any non-null value
— and the designation binds it. You get the null test and the local from one
construct.

## Hint 3

Your comment needs two distinct reasons, and "it is cleaner" is neither.

The first is about the analysis: a local has stable null state, a property does
not. The second is about the generated code: three property calls become one
field read plus two local reads, and if the property does real work — a
dictionary lookup, a lazily rebuilt cache, a database round trip in an ORM
proxy — that is three times the work.

Left to you: whether to use `is { } customer` or an explicit local assignment
followed by a null check. Both are correct; one is shorter and one is more
obvious to a reader new to patterns.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The gate's subclass is the part to think about first, because it turns a
compiler complaint into a real bug. Imagine:

```csharp
public override Customer? Customer => new Customer(_names[_index++]);
```

Nobody writes that deliberately. People do write properties backed by a
dictionary lookup, a `Lazy<T>`, an EF Core navigation that lazy-loads, or a
`DateTime.Now`-adjacent computation. The compiler's caution is not pedantry; it
is the general case of a specific bug.

## Hint 2

There is a middle option worth knowing and not using here:

```csharp
if (order.Customer is not null)
{
    return $"{order.Customer!.Name} ...";   // silences, proves nothing
}
```

The `!` makes the warning go away and does nothing about the double read. If
the property is unstable, this code is still wrong; it is merely wrong
quietly. That is the difference between fixing a warning and satisfying one.

## Hint 3

Count the property accesses in your finished version. One. If there is more
than one, you have not taken the second reason seriously — and the second
reason is the one that matters in a hot loop, where a lazily loading navigation
property has been known to turn a report into a thousand queries.

Left to you: whether `Render` should take a `Customer?` instead of an `Order`,
which would remove the question entirely. Pushing nullable state to the
boundary is usually the better design and is not always available.

## Exercise 4 — `[MemberNotNull]`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA04_NullableReferences/Ex4.cs`.

```csharp
public sealed class RingBuffer
{
    private char[] _data;
    private int _head;

    public RingBuffer(int capacity);
    public int Capacity { get; }
    public void Resize(int capacity);
    public void Write(char value);
    public string Contents { get; }
}
```

Both the constructor and `Resize` assign `_data` by calling a private
`Allocate(int capacity)`. The compiler currently reports CS8618 — "non-nullable
field must contain a non-null value when exiting constructor" — because it
cannot see inside `Allocate`.

Fix it by annotating `Allocate`. You may not:

- make `_data` nullable
- write `_data = null!;`
- inline `Allocate` into the constructor
- add a field initialiser

Behaviour: `new RingBuffer(3)`, then writing `'a'`, `'b'`, `'c'`, `'d'` leaves
`Contents` as `"dbc"` — the fourth write wrapped to index 0. `Resize` allocates
a fresh buffer and resets the head.

Then, as a second step, add a `bool IsAllocated` property and annotate it with
`[MemberNotNullWhen(true, nameof(_data))]`, and say in a comment when you would
reach for that instead.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca04_nullable_reference_types ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

CS8618 is the compiler saying "I walked every path out of your constructor and
one of them leaves this field null." It walked into the `Allocate` call and
learned nothing, because method calls are opaque to that analysis.

You need a way to tell it what `Allocate` guarantees. There is an attribute
whose entire job is that sentence.

## Hint 2

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis;

[MemberNotNull(nameof(_field))]
private void Prepare() => _field = new byte[16];
```

The attribute takes one or more member names and means "when this method
returns normally, these are not null". The compiler applies it at every call
site — and, importantly, *checks* it inside the method, so a path that leaves
the field unassigned produces a warning on the attribute itself.

## Hint 3

`[MemberNotNullWhen(true, ...)]` is for the state-check shape:
`if (buffer.IsAllocated) buffer.Write(...)` where `IsAllocated` returns a
`bool`. Reach for it when the initialisation is optional or deferred rather
than guaranteed — a `Stream` wrapper that opens lazily, for instance.

Left to you: whether `RingBuffer` should have a deferred-allocation mode at all.
The gate wants both attributes present so you have written each once; whether
both belong in one real type is a separate question.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand what the attribute is *not*. Compare these two ways of silencing
CS8618:

```csharp
private char[] _data = null!;              // a lie, unchecked
[MemberNotNull(nameof(_data))] void Alloc() => _data = new char[n];   // a claim, checked
```

The first compiles and leaves a real null in the field until something assigns
it; any path that forgets is a `NullReferenceException`. The second is verified
where it is written: give `Allocate` an early return that skips the assignment
and the compiler complains about the attribute.

Verified claims are worth writing. Unverified ones are comments with syntax.

## Hint 2

Try the experiment that shows the checking. Temporarily write:

```csharp
[MemberNotNull(nameof(_data))]
private void Allocate(int capacity)
{
    if (capacity == 0) return;          // leaves _data unassigned
    _data = new char[capacity];
}
```

The warning appears on `Allocate`, naming `_data`, pointing at the method that
broke the promise rather than at some caller three files away. That is the
diagnostic quality the attribute buys.

## Hint 3

For the ring buffer itself, check the wrap arithmetic against the stated
example rather than trusting it: capacity 3, writes `a`,`b`,`c`,`d`, contents
`"dbc"`. That means the head advances after each write and wraps with `%`, and
that `Contents` reads the buffer in index order, not in write order.

Left to you: whether `Contents` should return the logical order (oldest first).
It is a more useful ring buffer and a different assertion; the gate wants index
order because it makes the wrap visible.

## Exercise 5 — conditional nullability

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA04_NullableReferences/Ex5.cs`. Two independent members.

**Return depends on the argument.**

```csharp
public static string? Clean(string? text);
```

`Clean` trims and collapses internal runs of whitespace, and returns `null`
exactly when `text` is `null`. Annotate it so a caller passing a non-null
string gets a non-null result with no warning and no `!`:

- `Clean("  a   b  ")` -> `"a b"`, and `Clean("  a   b  ").Length` compiles clean
- `Clean(null)` -> `null`
- `Clean("   ")` -> `""`

**Setter and getter disagree.**

```csharp
public sealed class Settings
{
    public string Theme { get; set; }   // set null to reset; never returns null
}
```

`Theme` accepts `null` meaning "back to the default", and its getter always
returns a real string. Annotate it so both are true, without making the
property `string?`.

- `new Settings().Theme` -> `"light"`
- `settings.Theme = "dark"; settings.Theme` -> `"dark"`
- `settings.Theme = null; settings.Theme` -> `"light"`

The gate compiles a caller that writes `settings.Theme = null;` and reads
`settings.Theme.Length` — both must be warning-free.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca04_nullable_reference_types ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both members have the same shape of problem: the type system has one slot for
nullability and the member needs two answers.

For `Clean`, the answer depends on an argument. For `Theme`, it depends on
which accessor you are looking at. Two attributes exist for exactly these two
situations, and neither changes any code — they change what the compiler
believes.

## Hint 2

```csharp
[return: NotNullIfNotNull(nameof(input))]
public static string? Echo(string? input) => input;

public sealed class Box
{
    [AllowNull]
    public string Label
    {
        get => _label;
        set => _label = value ?? "(none)";
    }

    private string _label = "(none)";
}
```

Note where `[return:]` goes — it is a return-value attribute, so the target
prefix is required — and note that `[AllowNull]` sits on the property, applying
to the setter.

## Hint 3

`Clean` itself is `text is null ? null : string.Join(' ', text.Split((char[]?)null,
StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries))`, or a `Split` on whitespace with
`RemoveEmptyEntries` and a rejoin — several routes work.

For `Theme`, the backing field is non-nullable and the setter coalesces. The
getter never sees null, which is the fact `[AllowNull]` is recording.

Left to you: the default theme string. The gate wants `"light"`; whether a
default belongs in the property or in a constant is your call.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from what the caller sees without the attributes, because that is the
cost you are removing.

For `Clean`, every caller with a non-null argument gets a `string?` back and
has to null-check a value that cannot be null. Ten call sites, ten pointless
checks — or, more likely, ten `!` operators, each of which is a promise nobody
verified.

For `Theme`, the alternative is declaring it `string?`, which makes every
*reader* handle a null the getter never produces.

## Hint 2

`[DisallowNull]` is the mirror image of `[AllowNull]` and is worth
understanding so you pick the right one:

```csharp
[AllowNull]    public string Theme { get; set; }    // set null OK, get never null
[DisallowNull] public string? Cursor { get; set; }  // get may be null, set must not be
```

`[DisallowNull]` fits a property that starts null and, once set, may never be
cleared — a token, an id assigned on first save. If you find yourself unsure
which you want, write the two sentences out; the attribute names read as the
sentence about the *setter*.

## Hint 3

Test `Clean` against the boundary the prompt gives: `"   "` returns `""`, not
`null`. That distinction matters because it says "there was text, and it was
blank" as opposed to "there was no text". Collapsing the two is a common and
lossy shortcut, and `NotNullIfNotNull` only makes sense if you keep them apart.

Left to you: whether `Clean` should also normalise non-breaking spaces and other
Unicode whitespace. `char.IsWhiteSpace` says yes; `' '` alone says no; the
choice depends on where the text came from.

## Exercise 6 — guards that end the conversation

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA04_NullableReferences/Ex6.cs`.

```csharp
public static class Guard
{
    public static void Missing(string name);        // always throws
    public static void Against(bool condition, string message);   // throws when true
}

public static class Shipping
{
    public static string Label(string? address, string? postcode);
}
```

Annotate the two guards so that after calling them the compiler knows what you
know:

- `Guard.Missing(name)` never returns — it throws
  `InvalidOperationException($"{name} is required.")`
- `Guard.Against(condition, message)` throws `InvalidOperationException(message)`
  when `condition` is `true`, and returns otherwise

Then write `Label` using only those guards — no `is null` checks of your own
after the guard, no `!`, and the body must compile clean:

```csharp
public static string Label(string? address, string? postcode)
{
    if (address is null) Guard.Missing(nameof(address));
    Guard.Against(postcode is null, "postcode is required.");
    return $"{address.Trim()} {postcode.ToUpperInvariant()}";   // must not warn
}
```

- `Label("12 High St", "sw1a 1aa")` -> `"12 High St SW1A 1AA"`
- `Label(null, "x")` -> `InvalidOperationException` with message `"address is required."`
- `Label("a", null)` -> `InvalidOperationException` with message `"postcode is required."`

The second guard is the harder one: work out which value the attribute has to
refer to.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca04_nullable_reference_types ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Extracting a guard clause into a helper normally destroys the compiler's
knowledge, because a call is opaque: it does not know the helper threw, so on
the next line the value is still maybe-null.

Two attributes restore it — one for "this never comes back", one for "this does
not come back when the argument is true".

## Hint 2

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis;

[DoesNotReturn]
public static void Fail(string why) => throw new InvalidOperationException(why);

public static void Assert([DoesNotReturnIf(false)] bool condition) { ... }
```

Read the second one carefully: the attribute goes on the *parameter*, and its
argument is the value for which the method does not return. `Debug.Assert` uses
`[DoesNotReturnIf(false)]` because it throws when the condition is false.

## Hint 3

Your `Guard.Against` throws when the condition is `true`, so the attribute
argument is `true` — the mirror image of `Debug.Assert`. The compiler then
reasons: after the call, the condition must have been `false`; the condition was
`postcode is null`; therefore `postcode` is not null.

That chain is the part worth appreciating. The attribute is on a `bool`, and the
knowledge it recovers is about a `string?`.

Left to you: whether `Guard.Missing` should take a `[CallerArgumentExpression]`
instead of a name string. It would remove the `nameof` at every call site; it
would also change the signature the gate calls.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by removing the attributes from a working version and reading both
warnings. They are different, and the difference is instructive:
`address.Trim()` warns because the compiler thinks `Guard.Missing` returned,
and `postcode.ToUpperInvariant()` warns because it has no idea what
`Guard.Against` did with its argument.

One is about control flow, the other is about a relationship between a bool and
a reference. That is why there are two attributes.

## Hint 2

There is a subtlety with `[DoesNotReturnIf]` worth knowing before you rely on
it in production: `Debug.Assert` carries it, and `Debug.Assert` is compiled
away entirely in release builds. The *annotation* still applies at compile
time, so the compiler narrows based on a call that will not exist in the
shipped binary.

That is fine for a debug assertion and dangerous if you were treating it as
validation. Your `Guard.Against` throws unconditionally in all builds, which is
why it is a guard and not an assert.

## Hint 3

Check that the guards actually improve things by asking what the alternative
looks like:

```csharp
if (address is null) throw new InvalidOperationException("address is required.");
```

That needs no attributes and repeats the throw at every call site. The helper
plus attribute is worth it when there are many guards, when the message format
should be consistent, or when the guard does more than throw.

Left to you: whether these should throw `ArgumentNullException` instead.
`InvalidOperationException` is what the gate wants; for a public API taking the
values as arguments, `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` — which carries
`[NotNull]` on its parameter and needs no wrapper — is the better answer, and
ex7 uses it.

## Exercise 7 — the boundary needs both

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA04_NullableReferences/Ex7.cs`.

```csharp
public static class Invoices
{
    public static string Render(Invoice invoice, string culture, IReadOnlyList<Line> lines);
}
```

Every parameter is non-nullable and every one of them can still arrive null,
because the gate calls `Render` from a helper compiled in a
`#nullable disable` region — simulating a caller in an older assembly, a
deserialiser, or anyone who wrote `!`.

Add the runtime checks. Keep the annotations exactly as they are.

- `Render(null!, "en-GB", lines)` -> `ArgumentNullException`, `ParamName` is `"invoice"`
- `Render(invoice, null!, lines)` -> `ArgumentException`, `ParamName` is `"culture"`
- `Render(invoice, "  ", lines)` -> `ArgumentException`, `ParamName` is `"culture"`
- `Render(invoice, "en-GB", null!)` -> `ArgumentNullException`, `ParamName` is `"lines"`
- `Render(invoice, "en-GB", [])` -> `"INV-1 (en-GB): no lines"`
- a valid call -> `"INV-1 (en-GB): 2 lines totalling 30"`

Use `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` and
`ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace`. Neither needs a parameter-name
argument — work out why, and say so in a comment.

Then write two sentences on why the annotation is still worth keeping when the
check is there anyway.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca04_nullable_reference_types ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An annotation is a message to callers the compiler can see. A check is a
message to everyone else. The set of "everyone else" is larger than it looks:
older assemblies, dynamically generated proxies, `JsonSerializer`, EF Core
materialisation, reflection, F# and VB callers, and any C# caller who typed `!`.

Both are cheap. Neither replaces the other.

## Hint 2

The .NET 6/7 guard helpers:

```csharp
ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(invoice);
ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty(name);
ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(culture);
ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative(count);
```

Each is a static method with an `[CallerArgumentExpression]` parameter that the
compiler fills in with the *source text* of the argument — so `ThrowIfNull(
invoice)` produces a `ParamName` of `"invoice"` with nothing else written.

## Hint 3

Put every guard at the top of the method, before any work. That is not
aesthetic: a method that half-executes and then throws has left the caller in a
state neither of you reasoned about.

Left to you: whether `lines` being empty is an error or a valid case. The prompt
says valid, with its own message — which is a good example of a check that is
*not* a guard and belongs in the body rather than the preamble.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look at what `[NotNull]` does in the BCL's own signature, because it is the
piece that makes these helpers pull their weight:

```csharp
public static void ThrowIfNull(
    [NotNull] object? argument,
    [CallerArgumentExpression(nameof(argument))] string? paramName = null)
```

The parameter is `object?` — it accepts a null, obviously — and `[NotNull]`
says "after this returns, the argument is not null". So a caller who passes a
`string?` and then dereferences it needs no further check. The attribute is
doing for the caller exactly what ex6's guards did by hand.

## Hint 2

Try the failure the shim simulates. In a scratch file:

```csharp
#nullable disable
static void CallIt() => Invoices.Render(null, "en-GB", null);
#nullable restore
```

No warning. That code is legal, ships, and hands your annotated method two
nulls. If `Render` has no checks, the exception surfaces somewhere inside your
formatting code with a message that names nothing useful.

That is the whole argument for keeping the checks, and it is worth writing out
rather than accepting on authority.

## Hint 3

Your two sentences about keeping the annotation should say something the check
cannot. The annotation is documentation the compiler enforces for well-behaved
callers, it makes IDE tooling correct, and it means a caller passing a
`string?` gets a warning at *their* build rather than an exception at your
runtime — a much cheaper place to find out.

Left to you: whether to check in release builds only, or to use a source
generator. Both are things teams try; both usually cost more than the two lines
they save.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The difficulty is not the merging — it is convincing the compiler. `primary.
DisplayName ?? fallback.DisplayName` is a `string?`, and three of those cannot
be handed to a constructor taking three `string`s.

You need a shape where the null test and the binding happen together, once per
member, and where the compiler can see that all three succeeded before the
construction.

## Hint 2

The `is { }` pattern binds a non-nullable local from a nullable expression:

```csharp
if (primary.Email ?? fallback.Email is { } email)     // careful with precedence
if ((primary.Email ?? fallback.Email) is { } email)   // this one
```

Three of those in one `if`, joined by `&&`, gives you three non-nullable locals
in scope in the body. The compiler is not taking your word for anything; it
walked the pattern.

## Hint 3

`required` and `[SetsRequiredMembers]` are two halves of one feature. `required`
forces every construction site to assign the member — in an object initialiser
— and `[SetsRequiredMembers]` tells the compiler "this constructor assigns them
all, so callers of *this* constructor are excused".

The cost is exactly that excusal. Add a fourth `required` member later and the
object-initialiser callers all fail to compile, which is what you want; the
`[SetsRequiredMembers]` constructor keeps compiling, silently leaving the new
member unset.

Left to you: whether to keep the parameterless constructor at all. The gate
needs it for the object-initialiser assertion.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the version that does not work, because it is the one everybody
writes:

```csharp

string? email = primary.Email ?? fallback.Email;
string? zone = primary.Timezone ?? fallback.Timezone;

if (name is null || email is null || zone is null) { merged = null; return false; }
merged = new Profile(name, email, zone);   // does this warn?
```

Try it. The compiler does narrow all three after the combined null test, so
this actually compiles clean — the `||` chain gives it what it needs. Knowing
that is worth more than the pattern version, because it tells you the analysis
is smarter than people assume; and the pattern version is shorter.

## Hint 2

Now break it deliberately to see the edge. Change the guard to a helper:

```csharp
if (AnyNull(name, email, zone)) { merged = null; return false; }
merged = new Profile(name, email, zone);   // three warnings
```

The analysis stops at the call, exactly as in ex4 and ex6, and there is no
attribute that expresses "if this returns false, all three of these unrelated
arguments are non-null". That is a real limit: `[NotNullWhen]` applies to one
parameter at a time.

## Hint 3

For the `required` half, do the experiment the gate automates: write

Left to you: whether `Profile` should be a record with a primary constructor

- `{ host: "example.com", port: "8080" }` -> succeeds, scheme `"https"`,
  timeout 30s, no errors
- `{ }` -> fails, `Errors` is exactly `["host is required", "port is required"]`
  in that order
- `{ host: "  ", port: "x", scheme: "ftp", timeout: "soon" }` -> fails with all
  four errors, in key order
- on failure, `Options` is `null` and `Succeeded` is `false`

Requirements: no `!` anywhere; `Succeeded` annotated so a caller writing
`if (result.Succeeded) Use(result.Options.Host);` compiles without a null
check; a missing key and a present-but-null value are treated identically; and
parsing uses `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca04_nullable_reference_types challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two shapes fight here. "Collect every error" wants to keep going after a
failure; "produce a fully non-null record" wants to stop at the first one.

Resolve it by separating the phases: read and validate each key into a local
that may be null, accumulating errors as you go; then, at the end, check
whether the error list is empty and only then construct. The construction sees
locals the compiler has already proven.

## Hint 2

A small private helper per key keeps the accumulation readable:

```csharp
private static string? RequireText(
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string?> source, string key, List<string> errors)
{
    if (!source.TryGetValue(key, out string? value) || string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
    {
        errors.Add($"{key} is required");
        return null;
    }

    return value;
}
```

Note that a missing key and a present-but-null value take the same branch, which
is what the prompt asked for and one line of code rather than two.

## Hint 3

`[MemberNotNullWhen(true, nameof(Options))]` on `Succeeded` is what lets the
caller skip the null check — and it must be *true* that `Options` is non-null
whenever `Succeeded` is, so make `Succeeded` be `Options is not null` rather
than `Errors.Count == 0`. Those two are equivalent in your implementation and
only one of them is something the compiler can verify.

Left to you: whether `Bind` should return `BindResult` at all, or throw an
aggregate exception. Returning it makes the caller handle failure; throwing
makes it easy to ignore. Configuration binding at start-up is one of the few
places where either is defensible.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the error ordering, because it is the requirement most likely to
fail quietly. The prompt says "in key order" — host, port, scheme, timeout —
which means you validate in that order regardless of which keys are present.
A `foreach` over the dictionary would produce hash order and pass most of your
own tests by luck.

Deterministic error output is a testability property, exactly as in lesson 1's
challenge. It is also what makes the message useful to a person.

## Hint 2

The single most useful thing about a "collect everything" binder is worth
seeing concretely. Compare the two experiences of a badly configured service:

```
Startup failed: host is required
(fix, redeploy, wait)
Startup failed: port must be an integer
(fix, redeploy, wait)
```

against one run that names all four problems. The pattern generalises to form
validation, CSV import and command-line parsing, and it is nearly always worth
the extra list.

## Hint 3

Watch the interaction between defaults and validation. `scheme` is optional, so
a missing key is *not* an error — but a present, invalid value is. That means
three branches, not two: absent (use the default), present and valid, present
and invalid. Collapsing the first and third is the bug, and it shows up as a
typo in a config file silently becoming `https`.

Left to you: whether `timeout` should accept `"30s"` or an ISO-8601 duration.
The gate wants a bare integer count of seconds; real configuration systems
usually regret picking the bare integer, and saying so in a comment is fair.

## Hint 1

All four methods are the same walk: start at the head, loop while the current
node is not null, move to `Next`. The nullable annotation on the loop variable
is what makes the loop condition legal and the body's dereference safe.

This is what the feature looks like when it is working: the `?` is not a
problem to be solved, it is the loop's termination condition made visible in
the type.

## Hint 2

The walk, with the state narrowing where you want it:

```csharp
for (Node? current = head; current is not null; current = current.Next)
{
    // current is not null in here, so current.Value needs no check
}
```

`Join` wants a `StringBuilder` or a `List<string>` plus `string.Join` — either
is fine at this size; think about which one you would defend in review.

## Hint 3

`TryFind` reuses the same loop with an early return, and the
`[NotNullWhen(true)]` you met in ex2 is what makes the caller's
`found.Value` legal.

Left to you: your answer to the sentinel question. The honest case for `Node?`
is that "no next node" is a real state with no data, and inventing a sentinel
object means every consumer must know about it and check for it — which is a
null check wearing a costume, plus an allocation.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the design question rather than the code, because it is what this
review is for. The sector's arc was "make nullability explicit and then remove
it where it does not belong" — not "remove all nulls". A linked chain
terminates; that termination is a fact about the domain, and `Node?` is the
type system stating it.

The test for whether a `?` is honest: can the value legitimately be absent in a
correct program? Here, yes, always, for the last node.

## Hint 2

Consider the alternatives you are rejecting, briefly:

- A sentinel `EndNode` singleton. Now every consumer needs
  `if (ReferenceEquals(node, Node.End))`, which is a null check with worse
  ergonomics and an allocation.
- A `bool HasNext` alongside `Node Next`. Two fields that can disagree.
- An empty chain represented by an empty `Node`. Now `Value` is meaningless
  for that instance, and something will print it.

Every one of those replaces a language feature with a convention nobody
documents.

## Hint 3

Watch for one subtle thing in `Last`: the loop must not dereference `Next` on
the final node, and the obvious `while (current.Next is not null)` version
needs `current` to be non-null before the loop even starts. Handle the empty
chain first, and the rest falls out.

Left to you: whether `Chain` should refuse a cyclic chain. Nothing in the type
prevents `a.Next = a`, and all four methods would hang. A real linked structure
either documents the assumption or spends a `HashSet` on detecting it.

lessons.summary: A LINQ query is a recipe, not a result. This sector is about which operators stream and which buffer, why `OrderBy().First()` is not O(n), what enumerating twice really costs, and how to read a chain and predict the number of times each element is touched.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A5 — LINQ: deferred execution and real cost

You have written `Where`, `Select`, `GroupBy` and `Join`, and a drill sector
made you predict when a query runs. This one asks a harder question: **what did
that chain cost?**

Not in nanoseconds — in element visits, allocations and passes over the source.
Those three numbers are predictable from the operators alone, they explain
nearly every LINQ performance surprise, and they are what an experienced
reviewer is computing in their head when they look at a query.

The one-sentence model to hold: **a LINQ query is a recipe. Nothing happens
until someone enumerates it, and everything happens again if someone
enumerates it twice.**

## Concept — streaming, buffering, and the third category

```csharp
IEnumerable<int> query = numbers.Where(n => n > 0).Select(n => n * 2);
// nothing has run
int first = query.First();
// one element has been read from `numbers`
```

Operators fall into three groups:

**Streaming** — produce each output as soon as they can, holding no more than
one element. `Where`, `Select`, `SelectMany`, `Take`, `TakeWhile`, `Skip`,
`SkipWhile`, `Zip`, `Concat`, `Cast`, `OfType`, `Chunk`. `Distinct`,
`Union`, `Intersect` and `Except` are *nearly* streaming: they yield as they go
but accumulate a growing `HashSet` of what they have seen.

**Deferred but buffering** — return immediately, then read the *entire* source
on the first `MoveNext`. `OrderBy`, `OrderByDescending`, `Reverse`, `GroupBy`,
`Join`'s inner sequence. This category is the one that surprises people:
`OrderBy` is lazy, and it is not cheap.

**Immediate** — run to completion when you call them. `ToList`, `ToArray`,
`ToDictionary`, `ToLookup`, `Count`, `Sum`, `Any`, `First`, `Aggregate`.

The practical consequence:

```csharp
Order cheapest = orders.OrderBy(o => o.Total).First();   // O(n log n), sorts everything
Order cheapest = orders.MinBy(o => o.Total);             // O(n), one pass
```

Both are one line and one of them sorts a million records to look at the first.

## Concept — the recipe runs again

```csharp
public static string Report(IEnumerable<Order> orders) =>
    $"{orders.Count()} orders totalling {orders.Sum(o => o.Total)}";
```

Two enumerations. If `orders` came from `File.ReadLines(...).Select(Parse)`,
the file is read twice. If it came from an EF Core `IQueryable`, two queries
hit the database. If it came from a generator with a side effect, the side
effect happens twice. And if it came from a one-shot iterator, the second pass
returns nothing at all.

The fix is one line — materialise once — and the discipline is: **a method
taking `IEnumerable<T>` may enumerate it exactly once, or must materialise it
first.**

## Concept — what the operators are made of

Each streaming operator is an iterator method: `yield return` compiled into a
state machine class. Calling `Where(...)` allocates that state machine plus, if
your lambda captures anything, a display class and a delegate. So

```csharp
source.Where(x => x > threshold).Select(x => x.Name)
```

allocates roughly four objects before reading a single element, and does it
again on every enumeration. In a request handler that is irrelevant; in a
per-frame loop it is the whole problem.

LINQ to Objects fights back with internal specialisations. `Where(...).Where(...)`
combines the two predicates into one iterator. `Where(...).Select(...)` becomes
a single fused iterator, with an array-specific and a list-specific variant that
avoid the enumerator entirely. `Count()` short-circuits to `ICollection<T>.Count`.
`ElementAt` and `Last` use the indexer when the source is an `IList<T>`. You can
ask about these yourself with `TryGetNonEnumeratedCount`.

# Reading - csharp/v3ca05_linq_deferred_cost

## Notes

**Deferred means the method returned without doing anything.** `Where` returns
a `WhereEnumerableIterator` holding your source and your predicate. That is
all. The predicate has not run, the source has not been touched, and any
exception your predicate would throw has not been thrown. Everything happens on
the first `MoveNext`, which is to say inside somebody's `foreach`.

**Laziness composes, and so does its cost.** `Take(3)` after a `Where` means
the `Where` sees only as many elements as it needs to produce three matches.
That is the good half. The bad half is that a buffering operator anywhere in
the chain destroys it for everything upstream: `OrderBy` must read all of the
source before it can yield one element, so `source.Where(...).OrderBy(...)
.Take(3)` reads the entire source no matter how small the `Take`.

**`OrderBy` is the most misread operator in the library.** It is deferred — the
call itself does nothing — and it is a full buffer plus an O(n log n) sort on
first use. `OrderBy(...).First()` is therefore a sort to find a minimum.
`MinBy`/`MaxBy` (.NET 6) do it in one pass. `OrderBy(...).Take(k)` is the one
case where the sort is hard to avoid, and even then a bounded heap beats it for
small `k`.

**Enumerating twice runs the whole recipe twice.** Not "reads a cached list
twice" — re-runs every predicate, every projection, every side effect and every
database round trip. `IEnumerable<T>` makes no promise of repeatability; some
sources give different data on the second pass and some give nothing.

**The allocation story.** A streaming operator allocates an iterator object per
enumeration; a capturing lambda allocates a display class and a delegate,
usually once per call rather than per element. Non-capturing lambdas are cached
in a static field by the compiler and cost nothing after the first use. The
usual guidance is right: LINQ allocates modestly, and in a hot inner loop
"modestly" times a million is the profile.

**The fast paths exist and are worth knowing.** `Count()` on an `ICollection<T>`
is a property read, not a walk. `Last()` and `ElementAt()` on an `IList<T>` use
the indexer. `Where(...).Select(...)` fuses into one iterator with
array- and list-specialised variants. `TryGetNonEnumeratedCount` (.NET 6) tells
you whether a count is available without walking — the polite way to decide
whether to materialise.

**`Single` always reads a second element.** That is its contract: it must prove
there is exactly one. `First` stops at the first. Using `Single` where `First`
would do is one extra `MoveNext` and, on a database, a different query plan.

## ex1

Counting `MoveNext` calls turns "deferred execution" from a fact you can recite
into a number you can predict. The four chains are chosen so each isolates one
rule: nothing runs until you enumerate; `Take` limits the upstream work;
`OrderBy` does not; and `Count()` on a materialised list does not walk at all.

Predict before running. A prediction you got wrong teaches more than an
assertion you watched pass.

## ex2

The three-enumeration `Report` is a real bug pattern, not a contrived one. It
appears wherever a method signature says `IEnumerable<T>` — which is good
practice — and the body treats it like a list, which is the natural thing to do.

`TryGetNonEnumeratedCount` is the piece that makes the fix polite: if the caller
handed you a `List<T>`, materialising again would copy a million elements for
no reason. Ask first, copy only if you must.

## ex3

The three implementations are the same answer with a 3-orders-of-magnitude
spread in work done at scale. Reporting the visit counts makes it concrete: the
sort touches every element several times, `MinBy` touches each once, and the
hand-written loop touches each once and allocates nothing.

`MinBy` returning `null` for an empty sequence — rather than throwing like
`Min` — is the other thing to notice, and it is a deliberate BCL choice worth
knowing before you rely on either.

## ex4

Writing the operators is what makes deferral stop being magic. `yield return`
compiles to a class with a state field and a `MoveNext` that switches on it;
your method body becomes the state machine's transitions. The "zero touches on
construction" assertion is the proof: calling an iterator method runs *none* of
its body.

`TakeWhileInclusive` is in there because it does not exist in the BCL and is
frequently wanted — take while a condition holds, plus the element that broke
it. Writing it yourself is a five-line answer to a problem people solve with a
mutable flag and a `Where`.

## ex5

The audit is a memory exercise disguised as code, and the rewrite is the real
one. Sorting three times because three parts of a method each wanted the data
in order is the single most common wasted work in LINQ-heavy code — and it
happens because each line looks fine on its own.

## ex6

`GroupBy` is deferred and buffers everything; `ToLookup` is its immediate twin
and gives you a reusable, indexable result. If you group and then enumerate the
groups twice, `ToLookup` is what you wanted. `ToDictionary` throws on a
duplicate key, loudly, which is a feature — the alternative silently loses
data.

The mutable-key trap is lesson 1's hash-container rule arriving through a
different door: group by a mutable property, mutate it, and the group's key no
longer finds its own members.

## ex7

The exception timing is a genuine trap in production code, because the `try`
looks like it wraps the risky work and does not. The two fixes are: materialise
inside the `try` (`ToList()`), or move the enumeration inside it. They have
different memory profiles, and neither is universally right — which is the point
of asking which you would ship.

## ex8

The quadratic is written the way real quadratics are written: an `Any` inside a
`Where`, each of which is fine, composing into n×m. The hash-join rewrite is
one `ToHashSet` and one `Contains`, and the visit-count assertion shows the
difference without needing a stopwatch.

This is the single most valuable LINQ review skill: noticing that a lambda body
enumerates another sequence.

## challenge

One pass, five aggregates, over a source you may only read once. LINQ cannot do
it — every aggregate operator walks the sequence — so the honest answer is a
`foreach` with five accumulators, and the exercise is admitting that.

The comparison against the multi-pass version matters: it must produce
identical output, so the refactoring is provably safe, and it is measurably
cheaper.

## review1

Cold prediction over a chain with `Distinct` (streaming with growing state),
`SelectMany` (streaming, flattening) and `Take` (streaming, limiting), sitting
on a source that counts its own reads. If you can call the numbers before
running it, the sector did its job.

# V3·A5 — LINQ: deferred execution and real cost (archive)

## The operator table

| Operator | Category | Cost note |
|---|---|---|
| `Where`, `Select`, `Cast`, `OfType` | streaming | fused when adjacent |
| `SelectMany` | streaming | one inner enumerator at a time |
| `Take`, `TakeWhile`, `Skip`, `SkipWhile` | streaming | `Take` bounds upstream work |
| `Zip`, `Concat`, `Chunk` | streaming | `Chunk` allocates per chunk |
| `Distinct`, `Union`, `Intersect`, `Except` | streaming with state | growing `HashSet` |
| `OrderBy`, `ThenBy`, `Reverse` | deferred, buffering | full read + O(n log n) |
| `GroupBy` | deferred, buffering | builds a `Lookup`, holds every element |
| `Join`, `GroupJoin` | streaming outer, buffering inner | inner becomes a lookup |
| `ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary`, `ToLookup` | immediate | one full pass |
| `Count`, `Sum`, `Min`, `Max`, `Average`, `Aggregate` | immediate | `Count` short-circuits on `ICollection<T>` |
| `Any`, `All`, `First`, `FirstOrDefault` | immediate | short-circuit |
| `Single`, `SingleOrDefault` | immediate | always reads a second element |
| `MinBy`, `MaxBy` | immediate | one pass; returns `null` when empty |

## Worked example — the cost of a chain

```csharp
var result = orders
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)     // streaming
    .OrderBy(o => o.Placed)        // BUFFERS: reads all matching orders
    .Take(10)                      // streaming, but the sort already happened
    .Select(o => o.Id)             // streaming
    .ToList();                     // immediate
```

Element visits: every order is tested by `Where`; every match is buffered and
sorted; ten survive. `Take(10)` saves ten projections and nothing else. If
`orders` is a million rows and ten are wanted, the sort dominates and the
`Take` is decoration.

The version that is actually cheap for small `k` keeps a bounded heap, and the
version that is cheap for `k == 1` is `MinBy`.

## Worked example — enumerate once, politely

```csharp
public static string Report<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, decimal> amount)
{
    if (!items.TryGetNonEnumeratedCount(out int count))
    {
        List<T> materialised = items.ToList();
        items = materialised;
        count = materialised.Count;
    }

    decimal total = 0;
    foreach (T item in items) total += amount(item);
    return $"{count} items totalling {total}";
}
```

`TryGetNonEnumeratedCount` asks the source whether it knows its own size —
`ICollection<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, and a few internal LINQ iterators do
— so a caller who handed you a `List<T>` is not punished with a copy.

## Worked example — an iterator method

```csharp
public static IEnumerable<T> TakeWhileInclusive<T>(
    this IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> predicate)
{
    foreach (T item in source)
    {
        yield return item;
        if (!predicate(item)) yield break;
    }
}
```

Calling this runs none of the body. The compiler turned it into a class with a
state field; the `foreach` at the call site drives it. That is why an argument
validated at the top of an iterator method is validated *late* — the standard
fix is a non-iterator wrapper that validates and then calls a private iterator.

## Worked example — the accidental quadratic

```csharp
// O(n * m): the lambda enumerates `active` for every order.
var flagged = orders.Where(o => active.Any(a => a.CustomerId == o.CustomerId));

// O(n + m): one pass to build the set, one to filter.
HashSet<int> activeIds = active.Select(a => a.CustomerId).ToHashSet();
var flagged = orders.Where(o => activeIds.Contains(o.CustomerId));
```

The tell is a sequence operator inside a lambda that is itself inside a
sequence operator. Once you are looking for it, you find one in most
LINQ-heavy codebases.

## Worked example — five aggregates, one pass

```csharp
// Five walks. Correct for a list; impossible for a one-shot source.
var report = new
{
    Count = lines.Count(),
    Errors = lines.Count(l => l.Level == "error"),
    Total = lines.Sum(l => (long)l.Milliseconds),
    Slowest = lines.MaxBy(l => l.Milliseconds)?.Route,
    Routes = lines.Select(l => l.Route).Distinct().Count(),
};
```

There is no LINQ operator that produces five different answers from one walk.
`Aggregate` with a tuple accumulator technically does it and becomes unreadable
by the third field, and it cannot carry the `HashSet` the distinct count needs
without mutating shared state inside a fold. The honest version is a `foreach`
with five accumulators — longer, obvious, and the only one that works when the
source is a `DbDataReader` or a network stream.

Watch the accumulator types while you are there: milliseconds arrive as `int`
and the total must be `long`, because summing into an `int` wraps silently
somewhere past 2.1 billion.

## Worked example — the buffering audit

```csharp
// Three sorts of the same data.
string top = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).First().Region;
string bottom = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).Last().Region;
var top3 = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).Take(3);
```

Naming the query does not fix it — a deferred query is a recipe, so each
consumer of the name re-reads and re-sorts. Materialising does:

```csharp
List<Sale> sorted = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).ToList();
string top = sorted[0].Region;
string bottom = sorted[^1].Region;
var top3 = sorted.Take(3);
```

One read, one sort, one buffer. This is the single most common wasted work in
LINQ-heavy code, and it survives review because every individual line is fine.

## Common mistakes

1. **Enumerating an `IEnumerable<T>` parameter more than once.**
2. **`OrderBy(...).First()`** instead of `MinBy`.
3. **`Count() > 0`** instead of `Any()` — `Count()` may walk the whole thing.
4. **`Where(p).Any()`** instead of `Any(p)` — one iterator fewer.
5. **`Single` where `First` was meant** — an extra read and a stricter contract.
6. **Building a query inside a `try` and enumerating it outside.**
7. **Calling a sequence operator inside a lambda** — the quadratic.
8. **`GroupBy` when you wanted `ToLookup`** — and then enumerating the groups
   twice.
9. **`ToDictionary` over data with duplicate keys** — it throws; decide what you
   want first.
10. **Validating arguments at the top of an iterator method** — the check does
    not run until enumeration.
11. **Assuming `Distinct` is free.** It carries a growing set.
12. **Reusing a query variable after the source has changed.** It re-reads the
    source, which is sometimes what you want and rarely what you expected.

## In an interview

*"What is deferred execution?"* — Most LINQ operators return an object
describing the query rather than a result. The work happens when something
enumerates it, which means it happens again on every enumeration, and any
exception in a predicate or projection surfaces at that point rather than at
the call.

*"Which operators break streaming?"* — Anything that must see all the input
before producing output: `OrderBy`, `Reverse`, `GroupBy`, and the inner side of
`Join`. They are still deferred; they buffer on first use.

*"How would you find the cheapest item?"* — `MinBy`, one pass. `OrderBy(...)
.First()` sorts everything to answer a question that needs a single scan.

## Check yourself

1. How many elements does `source.Where(p).Take(2).ToList()` read from

# Long read — how the operators are built, and what they really cost

## Where LINQ came from

LINQ shipped in C# 3.0 (2007), and the language features that carry it were
added *for* it: extension methods, lambda expressions, anonymous types, object
initialisers, implicit typing, and expression trees. The query syntax
(`from x in xs where ... select ...`) is a compile-time rewrite into the method
calls; no query syntax survives compilation.

Two libraries share the name. **LINQ to Objects** works over
`IEnumerable<T>` with delegates, in memory, and is what this sector is about.
**LINQ to a provider** works over `IQueryable<T>` with expression *trees*, which
the provider translates into SQL or a REST call. The methods look identical and
have completely different costs; the boundary between them is where
`AsEnumerable()`, an unsupported call, or a materialising operator drags the
whole table into memory.

## Iterators, and what `yield` compiles to

Every streaming operator is written as an iterator method. The compiler turns

```csharp
static IEnumerable<int> Positives(IEnumerable<int> source)
{
    foreach (int n in source)
        if (n > 0) yield return n;
}
```

into a generated class implementing `IEnumerable<int>` and `IEnumerator<int>`,
with an `int _state` field, a `_current` field, fields for the captured
parameters, and a `MoveNext` whose body is your loop rewritten as a switch over
`_state`. Calling `Positives(...)` allocates that object and returns; it runs
none of your code.

Two consequences follow directly. First, argument validation inside an iterator
method runs on the first `MoveNext`, not at the call — which is why BCL
operators are written as a validating wrapper around a private iterator, and why
you should copy that shape. Second, the generated class implements both
interfaces, and the first `GetEnumerator` on the same thread reuses the instance
rather than allocating a second — a small optimisation with a sharp edge: two
threads enumerating the same query get separate state, but a query enumerated
twice sequentially reuses the object.

## The specialisations

`System.Linq.Enumerable` is far less naive than its documentation suggests. The
internal `Iterator<TSource>` base class exposes overridable `Where` and
`Select`, so adjacent calls *combine* rather than nest:

- `Where(p1).Where(p2)` becomes one iterator with the predicate `x => p1(x) &&
  p2(x)`.
- `Where(p).Select(f)` becomes a single `WhereSelectEnumerableIterator`, with
  `WhereSelectArrayIterator` and `WhereSelectListIterator` variants that index
  the source directly instead of allocating an enumerator.
- `Select(f1).Select(f2)` fuses into `x => f2(f1(x))`.

Terminal operators have fast paths too. `Count()` checks for `ICollection<T>`
and reads the property. `ElementAt`, `Last` and `LastOrDefault` check for
`IList<T>` and index. `ToList` and `ToArray` check for a known count and
pre-size the buffer, which turns a series of doubling reallocations into one
allocation. `Contains` checks for `ICollection<T>` and defers to its
implementation, which for a `HashSet<T>` is O(1).

This is why "LINQ is slow" is a poor generalisation. A `Where().Select().
ToArray()` over an array is close to a hand-written loop. A `Where()` over an
`IEnumerable<T>` from a `yield` method in a per-frame loop is not.

## The three numbers to estimate

For any chain, ask:

**Passes over the source.** One, unless a buffering operator or a second
enumeration is present. Two passes over a database query is two round trips.

**Element visits.** Each streaming operator adds one visit per element that
reaches it. `Take(k)` bounds the number that reach everything upstream of it —
unless a buffering operator intervenes.

**Allocations.** One iterator per operator per enumeration, one display class
per capturing lambda per call, one delegate per lambda (cached if
non-capturing), plus whatever the buffering operators hold. `OrderBy` allocates
a key array and an index array the size of the source.

A worked estimate: `items.Where(Big).OrderBy(ByDate).Take(10).ToList()` over a
million items with 1,000 matches costs one pass (1,000,000 visits at the
`Where`), a 1,000-element buffer, a 1,000-element sort, ten projections, and
about six objects plus the sort's arrays. Replace `OrderBy(...).Take(10)` with a
bounded heap and the sort's `n log n` becomes `n log 10`.

## Performance notes worth carrying

- `Any()` short-circuits; `Count() > 0` may not. On an `ICollection<T>` they
  are both O(1); on a generator, `Count()` walks it all.
- `Any(p)` is one iterator; `Where(p).Any()` is two.
- `Distinct` allocates a `HashSet<T>` that grows to the number of distinct
  elements. Over a million unique strings, that is a real amount of memory.
- `GroupBy` holds every source element for the lifetime of the result. Grouping
  a large sequence and keeping the result is a memory decision.
- `OrderBy` is a stable sort (an introsort over an index array, comparing keys
  then original positions), while `List<T>.Sort` and `Array.Sort` are unstable.
  Swapping one for the other changes output order for equal keys.
- `SelectMany` allocates one enumerator per inner sequence.

## Two failure modes worth naming

**The accidental quadratic.** The most expensive LINQ bug is not an operator
choice; it is a nested loop hiding in a lambda.

```csharp
customers.Where(c => sales.Any(s => s.CustomerId == c.Id))
```

`Any` walks `sales` once per customer. Ten thousand customers against a hundred
thousand sales is up to a billion element visits, and the method appears in a
profile as unexplained time because every line in it is individually cheap. The
fix is a hash join — one pass to build a `HashSet` of keys, then an O(1)
`Contains` per outer element, which is precisely what a database would do with
the same query.

The review skill is mechanical: scan every lambda body for a sequence operation
(`Any`, `All`, `Contains`, `Count`, `First`, `Where`, `Sum`, or a `foreach`). If
the sequence it touches is not the one the outer operator is walking, it is a
nested loop. Note that `Contains` is a scan on a `List<T>` and a hash lookup on a
`HashSet<T>` — the same call, two complexities, decided by a type invisible at
the call site.

**The exception that misses its `catch`.** Building a query inside a `try` and
enumerating it outside means the `try` wraps the construction of a recipe while
the cooking happens elsewhere:

```csharp
try { numbers = lines.Select(int.Parse); }      // cannot throw
catch (FormatException) { return "bad input"; }
return string.Join(',', numbers);               // throws here
```

The stack trace points at `string.Join`, inside `MoveNext`, in a method that has
no idea what parsing is. Both fixes work — materialise inside the `try`, or move
the enumeration inside it — and they trade differently: the first allocates a
list, the second widens the `try` to cover the consumer as well, so an unrelated
exception of the same type gets reported as a parse failure.

## When not to use LINQ

**In a hot inner loop.** Per-frame code in a game, a tight parsing loop, an
allocation-sensitive server path: a `foreach` with explicit accumulators has no
iterator objects and no delegate calls, and lesson 6 shows the `Span` version
of the same idea.

**When one pass must produce several answers.** Five aggregates means five
walks in LINQ. A `foreach` with five accumulators is one walk, and it is not
less readable — it is just longer.

**Across the `IQueryable` boundary carelessly.** A `Where` the provider cannot
translate either throws or, worse, silently evaluates client-side after pulling
the table.

**When the query is really a loop with a name.** A chain of six operators with
three `let`s and a comment explaining the order is a method waiting to be
extracted.

## Further reading

- [Deferred execution and lazy evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/linq/deferred-execution-lazy-evaluation)
  — the categories, with examples of each.
- [Classification of standard query operators by manner of execution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/#classification-table)
  — the definitive per-operator table of deferred/immediate and
  streaming/non-streaming.
- [`Enumerable.TryGetNonEnumeratedCount`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.trygetnonenumeratedcount)
  — what it can and cannot answer without walking.
- [Iterators](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/iterators)
  — `yield`, the generated state machine, and the argument-validation wrapper
  pattern.
- [`MinBy` / `MaxBy`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.minby)
  — including the empty-sequence behaviour, which differs from `Min`.

## Hint 1

Read each chain right to left, asking "how many elements does this operator
need from its source to produce what it was asked for?"

`Sum` needs everything its source produces. `Take(2)` produces two. `Where`
produces one output per matching input, so it needs as many inputs as it takes
to find two matches. `First` needs one output — but from `OrderByDescending`,
which needs everything.

## Hint 2

The shapes, with the trap in the second one:

```csharp
IEnumerable<int> query = source.Where(...);   // Reads: 0
int total = query.Sum();                      // Reads: all
```

and

```csharp
List<int> materialised = source.ToList();     // Reads: all
int count = materialised.Count();             // Reads: 0 more - it is a List<T>
```

`Count()` on a `List<T>` short-circuits to the `Count` property, so it walks
nothing. That is the fourth row.

## Hint 3

`SortedFirst` is the row worth staring at. `OrderByDescending` is *deferred* —
building it reads nothing — and on the first `MoveNext` it reads the entire
source, sorts it, and yields the largest. So `First()` costs a full read plus a
sort, for a question a single pass answers.

Left to you: whether to call `Reset()` between chains inside one method or to
rely on the gate constructing a fresh source. Read the signature and decide;
guessing here is how the counts drift.

## Hint 1

There are two separate problems and it helps to see them apart.

The correctness problem: a one-shot source cannot be walked twice, so any
implementation that does is broken regardless of speed. The efficiency problem:
a caller who handed you a `List<T>` should not pay for a defensive copy.


without walking — arrays, `List<T>`, `ICollection<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`
and a handful of LINQ's own iterators. It returns `false` for a `yield` method,
a file reader or a `Where` over any of them.

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA05_LinqDeferredCost/Ex4.cs`.

```csharp

{
```

All three are iterator methods. `TakeWhileInclusive` yields elements while the
predicate holds **and also yields the first element that fails it**, then stops.

- `[1, 2, 3, 4].TakeWhileInclusive(n => n < 3)` -> `[1, 2, 3]`
- `[1, 2].TakeWhileInclusive(n => n < 9)` -> `[1, 2]`

1. **Deferral.** Calling any of the three on a `CountingSource` and not
   enumerating leaves `Reads` at `0`.
2. **Late validation, and the fix.** `WhereLazy(null!, p)` must throw

   explaining why the naive version validates too late.

## Hint 1

An iterator method — one containing `yield` — does not run its body when
called. The compiler rewrote it into a class; calling the method allocates that
class and returns it. Every statement you wrote, including your argument
checks, runs on the first `MoveNext`.

That is the whole of assertion 2, and the fix is structural rather than clever.

## Hint 2

The split that the BCL uses for every operator:

```csharp
public static IEnumerable<T> Filter<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> predicate)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(predicate);
    return Iterator(source, predicate);          // no yield in this method

    static IEnumerable<T> Iterator(IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> predicate)
    {
        foreach (T item in source)
            if (predicate(item)) yield return item;
    }
}
```

The outer method has no `yield`, so it runs immediately. The local function has
the `yield` and is deferred. Two methods, one public name.

## Hint 3

`TakeWhileInclusive` is four lines: for each item, yield it, then break if the
predicate failed. Note the order — yield first, test second — which is exactly
what makes it "inclusive" and is why it cannot be expressed as `TakeWhile` plus
something.

Left to you: whether the boundary element should be yielded when the sequence
ends naturally. There is nothing to include then, so the question answers
itself, but it is worth confirming against your own implementation.

## Exercise 5 — the buffering audit

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA05_LinqDeferredCost/Ex5.cs`. Two jobs.

**Classify.** Implement

```csharp
public static string Classify(string operatorName);
```

returning `"streaming"`, `"buffering"` or `"immediate"` for these names, and
`"unknown"` for anything else:

| `"Where"`, `"Select"`, `"SelectMany"`, `"Take"`, `"Skip"`, `"Zip"`, `"Concat"`, `"Distinct"` | `"streaming"` |
| `"OrderBy"`, `"OrderByDescending"`, `"Reverse"`, `"GroupBy"` | `"buffering"` |
| `"ToList"`, `"ToArray"`, `"Count"`, `"Sum"`, `"Any"`, `"First"`, `"ToDictionary"` | `"immediate"` |

Write it as a switch expression with `or` patterns. `"Distinct"` is
`"streaming"` even though it accumulates a set — say why in a comment.

**Rewrite.** `Sales.Report` currently sorts the same sequence three times:

```csharp
public static string Report(IEnumerable<Sale> sales)
{
    string top = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).First().Region;
    string bottom = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).Last().Region;
    var top3 = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).Take(3).Select(s => s.Region);
    return $"{top}/{bottom}/{string.Join('+', top3)}";
}
```

Rewrite it to sort once, enumerate the source once, and produce the same
string. The gate counts source reads and asserts exactly one pass.

- with sales `[("north", 30), ("south", 10), ("east", 20), ("west", 5)]` ->
  `"north/west/north+east+south"`

## Hint 1

Every `OrderByDescending` call in that method is a separate query object over
the same source. None of them shares work with the others: three full reads,
three buffers, three sorts.

The fix is to give the sorted result a name and reuse it — but a query variable
is still a recipe, so naming it is not enough. It has to be materialised.

## Hint 2

```csharp
List<Sale> sorted = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).ToList();
```

One read, one sort, one buffer. Everything afterwards indexes or walks the
list: `sorted[0]`, `sorted[^1]`, `sorted.Take(3)`.

Compare with the version that keeps the query lazy:

```csharp
var sorted = sales.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount);   // still a recipe
string top = sorted.First();      // read + sort
string bottom = sorted.Last();    // read + sort AGAIN
```

Naming a deferred query does not cache it. That is the trap this exercise is
really about.

## Hint 3

For `Classify`, `"Distinct"` belongs in `"streaming"` because it yields each new
element as soon as it sees it — it never waits for the end of the input. It does
carry a growing `HashSet` of everything seen, so it is streaming in *latency*
and not in *memory*, which is a distinction worth stating in your comment.

Left to you: whether `"Join"` should appear in your table. It is streaming on
the outer side and buffering on the inner, which is why it is absent — and why
a one-word classification is a simplification.

## Hint 1

Count the work in the original before you touch it. Four sales is nothing; do
it for a million:

- `First()` after a sort: 1,000,000 reads plus a sort.
- `Last()` after a sort: another 1,000,000 plus another sort.
- `Take(3)` after a sort: a third of each.

Three million reads and three sorts for a report that needs one pass and one
sort. Every line looked reasonable in review, which is exactly how this ships.

## Hint 2

There is a subtlety in the rewrite worth catching. `Last()` on a sorted
descending sequence gives the *smallest* — so after materialising, the
equivalent is `sorted[^1]`, not `sorted[0]`. Getting the direction backwards
here produces a plausible-looking string that is wrong, and the gate's data is
chosen so the two differ.

Read the original carefully rather than rewriting from the description.

## Hint 3

Note what you can now skip. Once `sorted` is a `List<Sale>`, `Take(3)` still
allocates an iterator but reads no more than three elements, and `sorted[0]` is
an indexer. If the top three are all you need, `sorted.Take(3)` and a `for`
loop over three indices are equivalent, and one of them reads better.

Left to you: whether to sort at all. For "highest, lowest and top three" a
single pass keeping a small bounded set would do it, and would be considerably
harder to read — a real trade, and at four sales the sort obviously wins.

## Exercise 6 — `GroupBy`, `ToLookup`, `ToDictionary`

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CA05_LinqDeferredCost/Ex6.cs`.

```csharp
public sealed class Item
{
    public Item(string category, string name);
    public string Category { get; set; }   // deliberately mutable
    public string Name { get; }
}

public static class Grouping
{
    public static int GroupByReads(CountingItems items);
    public static int LookupReads(CountingItems items);
    public static string DictionaryOutcome(IEnumerable<Item> items);
    public static string MutatedKeyOutcome();
}
```

Four demonstrations:

- `GroupByReads` builds `items.GroupBy(i => i.Category)` and returns
  `items.Reads` **without enumerating the result** -> `0`, because `GroupBy` is
  deferred
- `LookupReads` calls `items.ToLookup(i => i.Category)` and returns
  `items.Reads` -> the full count, because `ToLookup` is immediate
- `DictionaryOutcome` calls `ToDictionary(i => i.Category)` and returns
  `"ok"` or the exception's type name — with duplicate categories it is
  `"ArgumentException"`
- `MutatedKeyOutcome` builds a lookup, then mutates an item's `Category`, then
  looks it up under the **new** category and returns `"found"` or `"missing"` ->
  `"missing"`

Each of the four is two or three lines. The value is in the comments explaining
what each proves.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3ca05_linq_deferred_cost ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`GroupBy` and `ToLookup` compute the same thing and differ in *when*. `GroupBy`
is deferred and buffers on first use; `ToLookup` runs immediately and hands you
an indexable, reusable `ILookup<TKey, TElement>`.

The rule that follows: if you are going to walk the groups more than once, or
index into them by key, you wanted `ToLookup`.

## Hint 2

`ToDictionary` and duplicate keys:

```csharp
var byCategory = items.ToDictionary(i => i.Category);
// System.ArgumentException: An item with the same key has already been added.
```

That throw is a feature. The alternatives — last wins, first wins — both lose
data silently, and if you genuinely want one of them, `ToLookup` or a
`GroupBy(...).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Last())` says so out loud.

## Hint 3

For the mutated key, the mechanism is lesson 1's hash-container rule: the
lookup placed the item in the bucket for `"tools"`, and changing the property to
`"garden"` does not move it. Asking for `"garden"` searches a different bucket
and finds nothing. Asking for `"tools"` finds it — under a category it no longer
claims to belong to.

Left to you: whether `Item.Category` should be mutable at all. It is mutable
here so the trap can be demonstrated; lesson 1 argued the general case.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach each of the four as an experiment with a hypothesis. Write the
expected number or string in a comment before you run it, then check.

The one people miss is the first: `GroupBy` *feels* eager, because grouping
feels like an operation that has to happen. It is deferred like everything else
— it just happens to read the entire source the instant anyone asks for a
single group.

## Hint 2

The memory difference between `GroupBy` and a streaming operator is worth
stating, since neither the deferral nor the immediacy captures it. A `Lookup`
holds *every source element*, sorted into buckets, for the lifetime of the
result. Grouping a million records and keeping the result keeps a million
records alive.

By contrast `Where` holds one element at a time, and `Distinct` holds one per
distinct key. If a grouping is only used to compute one aggregate per key, a
`Dictionary<TKey, int>` built in a `foreach` holds a thousandth of the memory.

## Hint 3

For `DictionaryOutcome`, catch `ArgumentException` specifically and return
`ex.GetType().Name` rather than hard-coding the string — the same discipline as
lesson 3's array-covariance demonstration. A test that asserts a name you typed
proves nothing about what the runtime did.

Left to you: whether to also demonstrate `ToDictionary`'s overload taking a
value selector. It is the more common form in real code and does not change the
duplicate-key behaviour at all.
